abstract: We describe a neural network, called RufeNet, that learns explicit, sym(cid:173) bolic condition-action rules in a formal string manipulation domain. RuleNet discovers functional categories over elements of the domain, and, at various points during learning, extracts rules that operate on these categories. The rules are then injected back into RuleNet and training continues, in a process called iterative projection. By incorpo(cid:173) rating rules in this way, RuleNet exhibits enhanced learning and gener(cid:173) alization performance over alternative neural net approaches. By integrating symbolic rule learning and subsymbolic category learning, RuleNet has capabilities that go beyond a purely symbolic system. We show how this architecture can be applied to the problem of case-role assignment in natural language processing, yielding a novel rule-based solution.

paragraphs: This paper introduces RuleNet, a neural network that learns explicit condition–action rules in a formal string-manipulation domain. Alongside these symbolic rules, it learns functional categories of domain elements. The categories provide groupings over which rules can operate, connecting learned internal organization to an explicit description of what action should follow a condition.

Learning proceeds through a process called iterative projection. At selected points, the system extracts rules from its developing representations, inserts those rules back into the network, and continues training. Rule extraction therefore changes subsequent learning. The symbolic representation participates in the training process rather than serving only as a final explanation of a trained system.

The authors report improved learning and generalization compared with alternative neural-network approaches. They also argue that learned categories give the architecture capabilities beyond a purely symbolic system. An application to case-role assignment in natural language processing demonstrates a rule-based solution. The contribution is the recurring interaction between category discovery and explicit rules, with each contributing to the system’s continuing development.
summary.tldr: RuleNet improves learning and generalization by repeatedly extracting symbolic rules and feeding them back into neural training.

title: Rule Induction through Integrated Symbolic and Subsymbolic Processing

abstract: In this paper we present NPen ++, a connectionist system for writer independent, large vocabulary on-line cursive handwriting recognition. This system combines a robust input representation, which preserves the dynamic writing information, with a neural network architecture, a so called Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network (MS-TDNN), which integrates rec.ognition and segmen(cid:173) tation in a single framework. Our preprocessing transforms the original coordinate sequence into a (still temporal) sequence offea(cid:173) ture vectors, which combine strictly local features, like curvature or writing direction, with a bitmap-like representation of the co(cid:173) ordinate's proximity. The MS-TDNN architecture is well suited for handling temporal sequences as provided by this input rep(cid:173) resentation. Our system is tested both on writer dependent and writer independent tasks with vocabulary sizes ranging from 400 up to 20,000 words. For example, on a 20,000 word vocabulary we achieve word recognition rates up to 88.9% (writer dependent) and 84.1 % (writer independent) without using any language models.

paragraphs: The paper introduces NPen++, a system for recognizing online cursive handwriting with large vocabularies and across writers. Online input supplies the sequence of pen coordinates, preserving how the writing unfolds. The system builds on that temporal information instead of reducing the input solely to the final written shape.

Preprocessing converts the coordinates into a sequence of feature vectors. These combine local properties, including curvature and writing direction, with a bitmap-like representation of the area near each coordinate. A Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network processes the resulting sequence and integrates recognition with segmentation, so identifying the writing and dividing it into recognizable parts occur within one framework.

Tests cover writer-dependent and writer-independent tasks with vocabularies from 400 to 20,000 words. For the 20,000-word vocabulary, reported word-recognition rates reach 88.9% and 84.1%, respectively, without language models. These results show the usefulness of combining temporal writing information, local spatial context, and joint segmentation and recognition for large-vocabulary handwriting processing.
summary.tldr: NPen++ combines temporal pen features with joint segmentation and recognition, reaching 84.1% writer-independent accuracy on a 20,000-word vocabulary without language models.

title: The Use of Dynamic Writing Information in a Connectionist On-Line Cursive Handwriting Recognition System

paragraphs: The paper studies initialization for speech models fitted with expectation-maximization. Speech is represented as a linear stochastic state-space system whose properties are stationary within successive segments. Poor initialization can produce poor formant trajectories, which track speech resonances important for vowel intelligibility. The authors investigate subspace identification as a better starting procedure.

They compare subspace state-space system identification, called 4SID, with EM. Both estimate a hidden state sequence and then model parameters, but they use different tools: Kalman filtering and least squares for 4SID, versus Kalman smoothing and maximum likelihood for EM. Their structural similarity motivates using 4SID to initialize EM.

4SID requires neither iteration nor initialization, although it is probabilistically suboptimal compared with EM. Experiments on real speech find that the subspace methods compare favorably with conventional initialization techniques, producing smoother formant trajectories, greater frequency resolution, and higher likelihoods. The approach uses a convenient initial estimator to support an iterative probabilistic method, with improvements reported in quantities directly relevant to speech modeling.
summary.tldr: Subspace identification provides effective initialization for EM speech modeling, improving formant trajectories, frequency resolution, and likelihoods in experiments.

title: Speech Modelling Using Subspace and EM Techniques

abstract: The strong correlation between the frequency of words and their naming latency has been well documented. However, as early as 1973, the Age of Acquisition (AoA) of a word was alleged to be the actual variable of interest, but these studies seem to have been ignored in most of the lit(cid:173) erature. Recently, there has been a resurgence of interest in AoA. While some studies have shown that frequency has no effect when AoA is con(cid:173) trolled for, more recent studies have found independent contributions of frequency and AoA. Connectionist models have repeatedly shown strong effects of frequency, but little attention has been paid to whether they can also show AoA effects. Indeed, several researchers have explicitly claimed that they cannot show AoA effects. In this work, we explore these claims using a simple feed forward neural network. We find a sig(cid:173) nificant contribution of AoA to naming latency, as well as conditions under which frequency provides an independent contribution.

paragraphs: Word-naming speed is associated with how frequently a word occurs, but the age at which it was learned may also matter. The paper examines this distinction in connectionist modeling. Earlier models repeatedly showed frequency effects, while some researchers argued that such models could not account for effects of age of acquisition.

The authors investigate that claim with a simple feedforward neural network. Their question is whether the model can exhibit a contribution from when a word is acquired, alongside any contribution from frequency. This separates two influences that can be related in observations but need not have identical effects in the model.

The study finds a significant age-of-acquisition contribution to naming latency and identifies conditions under which frequency contributes independently. The result demonstrates that the tested connectionist setup can express an acquisition-age effect. It also preserves a role for frequency under particular conditions, fitting a picture in which both factors can matter rather than requiring one to account for every observed difference in naming speed.
summary.tldr: A simple feedforward network exhibits age-of-acquisition effects on naming latency, with independent frequency effects under some conditions.

title: The Early Word Catches the Weights

abstract: We investigate Bayesian alternatives to classical Monte Carlo methods for evaluating integrals. Bayesian Monte Carlo (BMC) allows the in- corporation of prior knowledge, such as smoothness of the integrand, into the estimation. In a simple problem we show that this outperforms any classical importance sampling method. We also attempt more chal- lenging multidimensional integrals involved in computing marginal like- lihoods of statistical models (a.k.a. partition functions and model evi- dences). We ﬁnd that Bayesian Monte Carlo outperformed Annealed Importance Sampling, although for very high dimensional problems or problems with massive multimodality BMC may be less adequate. One advantage of the Bayesian approach to Monte Carlo is that samples can be drawn from any distribution. This allows for the possibility of active design of sample points so as to maximise information gain.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a Bayesian approach to estimating integrals from sampled function values. The central idea is to incorporate prior knowledge about the function being integrated, such as its smoothness. That information can influence the estimate, allowing relationships between sampled values to contribute to the calculation.

For one simple problem, the authors show that Bayesian Monte Carlo outperforms any classical importance sampling method. They also investigate harder multidimensional integrals used to compute statistical model evidence, also called marginal likelihoods or partition functions. In those investigations, Bayesian Monte Carlo outperformed Annealed Importance Sampling; these findings concern the problems studied rather than every possible integration task.

The authors identify very high dimensionality and extensive multimodality as settings where the method may be less suitable. They also highlight flexibility in choosing sample distributions. Because samples can come from any distribution, there is a possibility of actively selecting evaluation points to maximize information gain, turning sample placement into part of the estimation strategy.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Monte Carlo uses prior knowledge about integrands to improve integration in studied problems and enables potentially informative sample selection.

title: Bayesian Monte Carlo

abstract: By comparison to some other sensory cortices, the functional proper- ties of cells in the primary auditory cortex are not yet well understood. Recent attempts to obtain a generalized description of auditory cortical responses have often relied upon characterization of the spectrotempo- ral receptive ﬁeld (STRF), which amounts to a model of the stimulus- response function (SRF) that is linear in the spectrogram of the stimulus. How well can such a model account for neural responses at the very ﬁrst stages of auditory cortical processing? To answer this question, we de- velop a novel methodology for evaluating the fraction of stimulus-related response power in a population that can be captured by a given type of SRF model. We use this technique to show that, in the thalamo-recipient layers of primary auditory cortex, STRF models account for no more than 40% of the stimulus-related power in neural responses.

paragraphs: A common way to describe an auditory neuron's response is through its spectrotemporal receptive field, or STRF. This model predicts responses as a linear function of a sound's spectrogram, which represents frequency content over time. The paper asks how much of early auditory cortical activity such a model can explain.

The authors develop a method for measuring the fraction of stimulus-related response power that a chosen type of stimulus-response model captures across a population. Focusing on stimulus-related power makes the question specifically about the response associated with the sound. The method provides a quantitative way to evaluate a model family's explanatory reach.

Applied to the layers of primary auditory cortex that receive thalamic input, the analysis finds that STRF models explain no more than 40% of stimulus-related response power. This places a substantial limit on the linear spectrogram description in the population examined. It shows that even these early cortical processing stages contain sound-related response structure that the tested linear models do not capture.
summary.tldr: Linear spectrogram models explain no more than 40% of stimulus-related response power in the auditory cortical layers examined.

title: How Linear are Auditory Cortical Responses?

abstract: To provide a compact generative representation of the sequential activ- ity of a number of individuals within a group there is a tradeoff between the deﬁnition of individual speciﬁc and global models. This paper pro- poses a linear-time distributed model for ﬁnite state symbolic sequences representing traces of individual user activity by making the assump- tion that heterogeneous user behavior may be ‘explained’ by a relatively small number of common structurally simple behavioral patterns which may interleave randomly in a user-speciﬁc proportion. The results of an empirical study on three different sources of user traces indicates that this modelling approach provides an efﬁcient representation scheme, re- ﬂected by improved prediction performance as well as providing low- complexity and intuitively interpretable representations.

paragraphs: This paper models sequences of user activity while balancing individual differences against patterns shared across a group. A separate model for every person and a single global model represent different ways to organize that information. The authors propose a compact generative representation that combines shared behavioral structure with user-specific proportions.

The key assumption is that heterogeneous behavior can be explained by relatively few common, structurally simple patterns. These patterns may interleave randomly, with each user exhibiting them in different proportions. The resulting distributed model operates in linear time and represents activity as symbolic sequences over a finite set of states.

An empirical study using three sources of user traces indicates improved prediction performance alongside low complexity and intuitively interpretable representations. These findings support the proposed way of sharing patterns across individuals while preserving differences in their behavior. The explanation depends on the stated modeling assumption: variation among users is represented through different mixtures of a small common collection of patterns.
summary.tldr: A linear-time model represents users through interleaved shared behavior patterns, with improved prediction and interpretable representations on three sources of activity traces.

title: Simplicial Mixtures of Markov Chains: Distributed Modelling of Dynamic User Profiles

abstract: We consider the task of tuning hyperparameters in SVM models based on minimizing a smooth performance validation function, e.g., smoothed k-fold crossvalidation error, using non-linear optimization techniques. The key computation in this approach is that of the gradient of the validation function with respect to hyperparameters. We show that for large-scale problems involving a wide choice of kernel-based models and validation functions, this computation can be very efficiently done; often within just a fraction of the training time. Empirical results show that a near-optimal set of hyperparameters can be identified by our approach with very few training rounds and gradient computations. .

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to tune the hyperparameters of support vector machine models using a smooth measure of validation performance. A smoothed version of cross-validation error is one example. The authors treat tuning as a nonlinear optimization problem, so the search can use information about how validation performance changes as the hyperparameters change.

The key computation is the gradient of the validation function with respect to those hyperparameters. That gradient supplies the optimization procedure with directions for adjusting them. The paper shows that, for large problems spanning a broad choice of kernel models and validation functions, this calculation can be efficient, often costing only a fraction of the time needed to train the model.

The empirical results indicate that the method can find a near-optimal hyperparameter setting with very few training rounds and gradient evaluations. The contribution therefore connects an optimization-based tuning strategy with an efficient way to perform its central calculation. The near-optimality and small number of rounds are reported empirical findings, rather than a universal guarantee for every tuning problem.
summary.tldr: Efficient validation gradients let nonlinear optimization tune SVM hyperparameters with few training rounds in the reported experiments.

title: An Efficient Method for Gradient-Based Adaptation of Hyperparameters in SVM Models

abstract: Content-based image suggestion (CBIS) targets the recommendation of products based on user preferences on the visual content of images. In this paper, we mo- tivate both feature selection and model order identiﬁcation as two key issues for a successful CBIS. We propose a generative model in which the visual features and users are clustered into separate classes. We identify the number of both user and image classes with the simultaneous selection of relevant visual features us- ing the message length approach. The goal is to ensure an accurate prediction of ratings for multidimensional non-Gaussian and continuous image descriptors. Experiments on a collected data have demonstrated the merits of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies product recommendation based on users’ preferences for the visual content of images. It identifies two connected modeling choices: which visual features are relevant and how many classes the model should use. Both choices matter when images are represented by many continuous descriptors.

The authors propose a generative model with separate class structure for users and visual features. They use a message-length approach to select relevant features while identifying the numbers of user and image classes. Treating these decisions together lets feature selection and model size be determined within the same modeling procedure.

The target is accurate rating prediction for multidimensional image descriptors whose distributions need not be Gaussian. Experiments on collected data demonstrate merits of the proposed approach. The stated evidence supports the combined modeling strategy in that evaluated setting. Its broader methodological contribution is to make visual relevance and class structure joint parts of recommendation learning, rather than treating the feature set and number of groups as independently fixed inputs.
summary.tldr: A generative recommendation model jointly selects visual features and class counts using message length, with supportive results on collected image-rating data.

title: Unsupervised Feature Selection for Accurate Recommendation of High-Dimensional Image Data

abstract: It has been shown that the problem of $\ell_1$-penalized least-square regression commonly referred to as the Lasso or Basis Pursuit DeNoising leads to solutions that are sparse and therefore achieves model selection. We propose in this paper an algorithm to solve the Lasso with online observations. We introduce an optimization problem that allows us to compute an homotopy from the current solution to the solution after observing a new data point. We compare our method to Lars and present an application to compressed sensing with sequential observations. Our approach can also be easily extended to compute an homotopy from the current solution to the solution after removing a data point, which leads to an efficient algorithm for leave-one-out cross-validation.

We propose in this paper an algorithm to solve the Lasso with online observations. We introduce an optimization problem that allows us to compute an homotopy from the current solution to the solution after observing a new data point. We compare our method to Lars and present an application to compressed sensing with sequential observations. Our approach can also be easily extended to compute an homotopy from the current solution to the solution after removing a data point, which leads to an efficient algorithm for leave-one-out cross-validation.

paragraphs: Lasso fits a regression model using a penalty that encourages some coefficients to become zero. This yields a sparse solution and provides a form of variable selection. The paper considers how to solve this problem when observations arrive sequentially, so the desired fitted model changes whenever a new data point becomes available.

The authors introduce an optimization problem that connects the existing solution to the solution incorporating the new observation. Their algorithm computes a homotopy, meaning a path between these two fitted solutions. The key idea is to make the transition itself the computational object, using the current fit as the starting point for processing an additional observation.

The method is compared with Lars and applied to compressed sensing with sequential measurements. The same approach can also be extended to remove an observation, tracing a path from the current fit to the fit without that point. This removal operation gives an efficient route to leave-one-out cross-validation, where each observation is excluded in turn to assess the fitted model.
summary.tldr: A homotopy algorithm updates Lasso solutions as observations arrive and extends to efficient leave-one-out cross-validation.

title: An Homotopy Algorithm for the Lasso with Online Observations

abstract: We consider bandit problems, motivated by applications in online advertising and news story selection, in which the learner must repeatedly select a slate, that is, a subset of size s from K possible actions, and then receives rewards for just the selected actions. The goal is to minimize the regret with respect to total reward of the best slate computed in hindsight. We consider unordered and ordered versions of the problem, and give efficient algorithms which have regret O(sqrt(T)), where the constant depends on the specific nature of the problem. We also consider versions of the problem where we have access to a number of policies which make recommendations for slates in every round, and give algorithms with O(sqrt(T)) regret for competing with the best such policy as well. We make use of the technique of relative entropy projections combined with the usual multiplicative weight update algorithm to obtain our algorithms.

paragraphs: In a slate bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses a fixed-size subset of available actions and observes rewards only for the selected actions. Online advertising and news selection motivate this setting. The objective is to keep cumulative reward close to that of the best slate that could be chosen after seeing the full sequence.

The paper develops efficient algorithms for both unordered and ordered slates. Their regret grows on the order of the square root of the number of rounds, with constants depending on the particular problem. Because this growth is slower than the number of rounds, the bound implies that regret per round decreases as the interaction continues.

The authors also consider access to policies that recommend slates each round. They obtain square-root regret bounds for competing with the best recommendation policy as well. The algorithms combine multiplicative weight updates with relative entropy projections, extending a common online-learning update technique to the constraints imposed by choosing whole slates.
summary.tldr: Efficient slate-selection algorithms achieve square-root regret against the best fixed slate or recommending policy with feedback only on selected actions.

title: Non-Stochastic Bandit Slate Problems

abstract: A challenging problem in hierarchical classification is to leverage the hierarchical relations among classes for improving classification performance. An even greater challenge is to do so in a manner that is computationally feasible for the large scale problems usually encountered in practice. This paper proposes a set of Bayesian methods to model hierarchical dependencies among class labels using multivari- ate logistic regression. Specifically, the parent-child relationships are modeled by placing a hierarchical prior over the children nodes centered around the parame- ters of their parents; thereby encouraging classes nearby in the hierarchy to share similar model parameters. We present new, efficient variational algorithms for tractable posterior inference in these models, and provide a parallel implementa- tion that can comfortably handle large-scale problems with hundreds of thousands of dimensions and tens of thousands of classes. We run a comparative evaluation on multiple large-scale benchmark datasets that highlights the scalability of our approach, and shows a significant performance advantage over the other state-of- the-art hierarchical methods.

paragraphs: Hierarchical classification places class labels in a structure of parent and child categories. The paper addresses how to use those relationships to improve prediction while keeping computation feasible for large problems. Its Bayesian models incorporate the hierarchy into multivariate logistic regression through relationships among the parameters used for different classes.

Specifically, each child's prior is centered on its parent's parameters. This encourages nearby classes to use similar parameters while still allowing their models to differ. To make inference tractable, the authors develop efficient variational algorithms and a parallel implementation. The implementation can handle problems with hundreds of thousands of dimensions and tens of thousands of classes.

Evaluation on multiple large benchmark datasets highlights scalability and reports a significant performance advantage over the hierarchical methods used for comparison. The findings support the combination of statistical sharing through the class hierarchy and efficient approximate inference. Both elements matter to the stated objective: using relationships among labels in classification problems large enough to make computation a central concern.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Bayesian priors share information across related classes, with variational inference enabling large-scale classification.

title: Bayesian models for Large-scale Hierarchical Classification

abstract: We propose a Deep Boltzmann Machine for learning a generative model of multimodal data. We show how to use the model to extract a meaningful representation of multimodal data. We find that the learned representation is useful for classification and information retreival tasks, and hence conforms to some notion of semantic similarity. The model defines a probability density over the space of multimodal inputs. By sampling from the conditional distributions over each data modality, it possible to create the representation even when some data modalities are missing. Our experimental results on bi-modal data consisting of images and text show that the Multimodal DBM can learn a good generative model of the joint space of image and text inputs that is useful for information retrieval from both unimodal and multimodal queries. We further demonstrate that our model can significantly outperform SVMs and LDA on discriminative tasks. Finally, we compare our model to other deep learning methods, including autoencoders and deep belief networks, and show that it achieves significant gains.

We further demonstrate that our model can significantly outperform SVMs and LDA on discriminative tasks. Finally, we compare our model to other deep learning methods, including autoencoders and deep belief networks, and show that it achieves significant gains.

By modeling their joint probability distribution, the system learns representations that can draw on relationships between visual and textual information.

The model can also form a representation when some modalities are absent by sampling from conditional distributions. This supports retrieval queries containing one modality or multiple modalities. The authors find the learned representations useful for classification and information retrieval, interpreting that usefulness as evidence that they capture some notion of semantic similarity.

These findings support joint generative learning as a way to obtain representations useful across the evaluated prediction and retrieval settings.

title: Multimodal Learning with Deep Boltzmann Machines

abstract: Recent advances in associative memory design through structured pattern sets and graph-based inference algorithms have allowed reliable learning and recall of an exponential number of patterns. Although these designs correct external errors in recall, they assume neurons that compute noiselessly, in contrast to the highly variable neurons in hippocampus and olfactory cortex. Here we consider associative memories with noisy internal computations and analytically characterize performance. As long as the internal noise level is below a specified threshold, the error probability in the recall phase can be made exceedingly small. More surprisingly, we show that internal noise actually improves the performance of the recall phase. Computational experiments lend additional support to our theoretical analysis. This work suggests a functional benefit to noisy neurons in biological neuronal networks.

paragraphs: Associative memories aim to recall stored patterns despite errors in the input. This paper examines what happens when the memory’s own computational units are noisy.

The authors analytically characterize recall performance under internal noise. They show that when the noise level remains below a specified threshold, the probability of recall error can be made extremely small. More surprisingly, their analysis shows that internal noise can improve recall performance. The result therefore concerns a beneficial regime of noise within the studied memory design.

Computational experiments provide additional support for the theoretical analysis. Because biological neurons are highly variable, the authors suggest that their findings point toward a possible functional benefit of neuronal noise. That biological interpretation remains a suggestion: the direct results establish noise tolerance and improved recall in the analyzed associative memories, rather than a general rule that more noise always helps neural computation.
summary.tldr: In the studied associative memories, internal noise below a threshold permits very low recall error and can improve recall performance.

title: Noise-Enhanced Associative Memories

abstract: We develop \textit{parallel predictive entropy search} (PPES), a novel algorithm for Bayesian optimization of expensive black-box objective functions. At each iteration, PPES aims to select a \textit{batch} of points which will maximize the information gain about the global maximizer of the objective. Well known strategies exist for suggesting a single evaluation point based on previous observations, while far fewer are known for selecting batches of points to evaluate in parallel. The few batch selection schemes that have been studied all resort to greedy methods to compute an optimal batch. To the best of our knowledge, PPES is the first non-greedy batch Bayesian optimization strategy. We demonstrate the benefit of this approach in optimization performance on both synthetic and real world applications, including problems in machine learning, rocket science and robotics.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization when evaluating an objective function is expensive and its internal form is unavailable. Bayesian optimization uses previous observations to decide where to evaluate next. Here, the authors focus on choosing several evaluation points at once, so those evaluations can run in parallel.

Their algorithm, parallel predictive entropy search, aims to choose a batch that maximizes information gained about the location of the global maximizer. The selection objective therefore concerns what the entire batch can reveal about the best location. This differs from constructing a batch greedily through successive choices, which the abstract identifies as the approach taken by previously studied batch schemes.

The authors describe PPES as, to their knowledge, the first non-greedy batch strategy for Bayesian optimization. Experiments demonstrate optimization benefits on synthetic and real-world applications, including machine learning, rocket science, and robotics. The contribution links parallel evaluation to joint information gathering: the batch is selected as a collection intended to reduce uncertainty about the optimizer, with the reported experiments supporting the usefulness of that approach.
summary.tldr: PPES jointly selects parallel evaluations to gain information about a global maximizer, with demonstrated benefits across several optimization applications.

title: Parallel Predictive Entropy Search for Batch Global Optimization of Expensive Objective Functions

abstract: Motivated by vision-based reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in particular Atari games from the recent benchmark Aracade Learning Environment (ALE), we consider spatio-temporal prediction problems where future (image-)frames are dependent on control variables or actions as well as previous frames. While not composed of natural scenes, frames in Atari games are high-dimensional in size, can involve tens of objects with one or more objects being controlled by the actions directly and many other objects being influenced indirectly, can involve entry and departure of objects, and can involve deep partial observability. We propose and evaluate two deep neural network architectures that consist of encoding, action-conditional transformation, and decoding layers based on convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. Experimental results show that the proposed architectures are able to generate visually-realistic frames that are also useful for control over approximately 100-step action-conditional futures in some games. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to make and evaluate long-term predictions on high-dimensional video conditioned by control inputs.

paragraphs: Predicting the next image in an interactive environment requires knowing both what has happened and what action will be taken. This paper studies that problem in Atari games, motivated by reinforcement learning from visual inputs. Although these images are not natural scenes, they contain multiple interacting objects, arrivals and departures, and situations where the visible frame does not reveal the full state.

The authors propose two deep network architectures organized around encoding, an action-dependent transformation, and decoding. Convolutional and recurrent neural networks provide the building blocks. This organization connects a representation of previous images to the selected controls, then turns the resulting representation back into predicted images.

The experiments show visually realistic predictions that are also useful for control across futures of approximately 100 steps in some games. That qualification matters: the stated outcome concerns particular games, rather than a universal prediction horizon. The contribution is evidence that high-dimensional visual futures can be modeled over extended periods while explicitly accounting for actions.
summary.tldr: Action-conditioned deep networks generate useful visual predictions roughly 100 steps ahead in some Atari games.

title: Action-Conditional Video Prediction using Deep Networks in Atari Games

abstract: Although the human visual system can recognize many concepts under challengingconditions, it still has some biases. In this paper, we investigate whether wecan extract these biases and transfer them into a machine recognition system.We introduce a novel method that, inspired by well-known tools in humanpsychophysics, estimates the biases that the human visual system might use forrecognition, but in computer vision feature spaces. Our experiments aresurprising, and suggest that classifiers from the human visual system can betransferred into a machine with some success. Since these classifiers seem tocapture favorable biases in the human visual system, we further present an SVMformulation that constrains the orientation of the SVM hyperplane to agree withthe bias from human visual system. Our results suggest that transferring thishuman bias into machines may help object recognition systems generalize acrossdatasets and perform better when very little training data is available.

paragraphs: Human vision recognizes concepts under difficult conditions, but it also brings biases to recognition. This paper investigates whether some of those biases can be estimated and transferred into machine vision. The aim is to capture useful tendencies in human recognition in a form that a computer classifier can incorporate.

The authors introduce a method inspired by tools from human psychophysics that estimates possible human visual biases directly in computer-vision feature spaces. Their experiments suggest that classifiers associated with human vision can be transferred to machines with some success. This provides the basis for incorporating those biases into a learned recognition rule.

They then formulate a support vector machine whose separating hyperplane is constrained to have an orientation consistent with the estimated human bias. This makes the bias an explicit influence on the classifier's decision boundary. The reported results suggest that such transfer may improve generalization across datasets and recognition with very little training data. These are encouraging empirical findings, expressed as possible benefits rather than universal guarantees.
summary.tldr: Estimated human visual biases can guide an SVM's decision boundary and may improve recognition across datasets and with little training data.

title: Learning visual biases from human imagination

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) defines a powerful framework to compare probability distributions in a geometrically faithful way. However, the practical impact of OT is still limited because of its computational burden. We propose a new class of stochastic optimization algorithms to cope with large-scale problems routinely encountered in machine learning applications. These methods are able to manipulate arbitrary distributions (either discrete or continuous) by simply requiring to be able to draw samples from them, which is the typical setup in high-dimensional learning problems. This alleviates the need to discretize these densities, while giving access to provably convergent methods that output the correct distance without discretization error. These algorithms rely on two main ideas: (a) the dual OT problem can be re-cast as the maximization of an expectation; (b) entropic regularization of the primal OT problem results in a smooth dual optimization optimization which can be addressed with algorithms that have a provably faster convergence. We instantiate these ideas in three different computational setups: (i) when comparing a discrete distribution to another, we show that incremental stochastic optimization schemes can beat the current state of the art finite dimensional OT solver (Sinkhorn's algorithm) ; (ii) when comparing a discrete distribution to a continuous density, a re-formulation (semi-discrete) of the dual program is amenable to averaged stochastic gradient descent, leading to better performance than approximately solving the problem by discretization ; (iii) when dealing with two continuous densities, we propose a stochastic gradient descent over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This is currently the only known method to solve this problem, and is more efficient than discretizing beforehand the two densities. We backup these claims on a set of discrete, semi-discrete and continuous benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares probability distributions while accounting for geometry, but its computational cost can limit practical use. This paper develops stochastic optimization methods that work with discrete or continuous distributions through samples. Sampling avoids the need to first replace continuous densities with a discrete approximation and thereby avoids that source of error.

The approach rewrites the dual transport problem as maximizing an expectation. Entropic regularization makes the dual smooth, enabling algorithms with provably faster convergence. The authors instantiate these ideas for three settings: two discrete distributions, a discrete distribution paired with a continuous one, and two continuous densities. The last case uses stochastic gradient descent in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The paper provides convergent methods and benchmark evidence across all three settings. Incremental methods can outperform Sinkhorn's algorithm for discrete problems, while the continuous-data approaches improve on solving discretized approximations in the reported comparisons. The contribution is a sample-based computational framework that accommodates different distribution types without requiring the same preliminary discretization step.
summary.tldr: Sample-based stochastic algorithms scale optimal transport across discrete and continuous settings while avoiding preliminary density discretization.

title: Stochastic Optimization for Large-scale Optimal Transport

abstract: The follow the leader (FTL) algorithm, perhaps the simplest of all online learning algorithms, is known to perform well when the loss functions it is used on are positively curved. In this paper we ask whether there are other "lucky" settings when FTL achieves sublinear, "small" regret. In particular, we study the fundamental problem of linear prediction over a non-empty convex, compact domain. Amongst other results, we prove that the curvature of the boundary of the domain can act as if the losses were curved: In this case, we prove that as long as the mean of the loss vectors have positive lengths bounded away from zero, FTL enjoys a logarithmic growth rate of regret, while, e.g., for polyhedral domains and stochastic data it enjoys finite expected regret. Building on a previously known meta-algorithm, we also get an algorithm that simultaneously enjoys the worst-case guarantees and the bound available for FTL.

In particular, we study the fundamental problem of linear prediction over a non-empty convex, compact domain. paragraphs: Follow the leader chooses a decision based on what has performed best on previous losses. It is a simple online learning method, and curved loss functions are known to support good performance. This paper asks which other favorable conditions can produce small regret, focusing on linear prediction over a nonempty, convex, compact domain.

The authors show that curvature in the boundary of the allowed decision set can play a role similar to curvature in the losses. In this setting, follow the leader has logarithmic regret growth provided the lengths of the mean loss vectors stay bounded away from zero. The geometric property and the condition on the loss vectors both matter to this result.

The paper also gives finite expected regret results for polyhedral domains with stochastic data. Building on an existing meta-algorithm, it obtains a method that combines worst-case guarantees with the available follow-the-leader bound. These findings identify circumstances in which a simple procedure enjoys especially favorable performance while also supporting an algorithm with broader protection.
summary.tldr: Follow the leader can achieve fast regret rates through favorable domain geometry and data conditions, even with linear losses.

title: Following the Leader and Fast Rates in Linear Prediction: Curved Constraint Sets and Other Regularities

abstract: The goal of imitation learning is to mimic expert behavior without access to an explicit reward signal. Expert demonstrations provided by humans, however, often show significant variability due to latent factors that are typically not explicitly modeled. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm that can infer the latent structure of expert demonstrations in an unsupervised way. Our method, built on top of Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning, can not only imitate complex behaviors, but also learn interpretable and meaningful representations of complex behavioral data, including visual demonstrations. In the driving domain, we show that a model learned from human demonstrations is able to both accurately reproduce a variety of behaviors and accurately anticipate human actions using raw visual inputs. Compared with various baselines, our method can better capture the latent structure underlying expert demonstrations, often recovering semantically meaningful factors of variation in the data.

paragraphs: Imitation learning aims to reproduce expert behavior without an explicit reward signal. Human demonstrations often contain substantial variation, however, and some of it reflects hidden factors that are not labeled or directly modeled. InfoGAIL addresses this variation by learning latent structure alongside the behavior being imitated.

The algorithm builds on Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning and infers that structure without supervision. Its aim is to produce both effective imitation and interpretable representations of complex behavioral data, including visual demonstrations. Representing hidden variation gives the model a way to distinguish different patterns within expert behavior instead of treating the demonstrations as one undifferentiated collection.

In driving experiments, a model trained on human demonstrations accurately reproduces a variety of behaviors and anticipates human actions from raw visual inputs. Compared with the evaluated baselines, it better captures the demonstrations' latent structure, often recovering factors with meaningful interpretations. The qualifier matters: the reported results support interpretable variation in these experiments without claiming that every learned latent factor necessarily has a clear semantic meaning.
summary.tldr: InfoGAIL learns hidden variation in expert demonstrations, enabling diverse imitation and often interpretable behavioral representations from visual inputs.

title: InfoGAIL: Interpretable Imitation Learning from Visual Demonstrations

abstract: We propose a framework that learns a representation transferable across different domains and tasks in a data efficient manner. Our approach battles domain shift with a domain adversarial loss, and generalizes the embedding to novel task using a metric learning-based approach. Our model is simultaneously optimized on labeled source data and unlabeled or sparsely labeled data in the target domain. Our method shows compelling results on novel classes within a new domain even when only a few labeled examples per class are available, outperforming the prevalent fine-tuning approach. In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the transfer learning task from image object recognition to video action recognition.

Our model is simultaneously optimized on labeled source data and unlabeled or sparsely labeled data in the target domain. Our method shows compelling results on novel classes within a new domain even when only a few labeled examples per class are available, outperforming the prevalent fine-tuning approach. In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the transfer learning task from image object recognition to video action recognition.

paragraphs: The paper aims to learn representations that remain useful when both the data domain and the task change. Its setting combines labeled source data with target data that are unlabeled or only sparsely labeled. The goal is to make transfer effective when obtaining many labels for the new setting is difficult.

The framework assigns different roles to two learning components. A domain-adversarial loss addresses differences between source and target data, while a metric-learning approach helps the embedding generalize to new tasks. The model is optimized on the source and target data simultaneously, bringing domain adaptation and task transfer into the same training framework.

The authors report strong results on previously unseen classes in a new domain with only a few labeled examples per class, outperforming the prevalent fine-tuning approach. They also demonstrate transfer from recognizing objects in images to recognizing actions in videos. These findings support the framework's usefulness across changes in both data and prediction task, with limited target labels.
summary.tldr: Combining domain-adversarial and metric learning produces transferable representations that perform well with few target labels across domains and tasks.

title: Label Efficient Learning of Transferable Representations acrosss Domains and Tasks

abstract: We suggest a general oracle-based framework that captures parallel stochastic optimization in different parallelization settings described by a dependency graph, and derive generic lower bounds in terms of this graph. We then use the framework and derive lower bounds to study several specific parallel optimization settings, including delayed updates and parallel processing with intermittent communication. We highlight gaps between lower and upper bounds on the oracle complexity, and cases where the ``natural'' algorithms are not known to be optimal.
originalAbstract: We suggest a general oracle-based framework that captures parallel stochastic optimization in different parallelization settings described by a dependency graph, and derive generic lower bounds in terms of this graph. We then use the framework and derive lower bounds to study several specific parallel optimization settings, including delayed updates and parallel processing with intermittent communication. We highlight gaps between lower and upper bounds on the oracle complexity, and cases where the ``natural'' algorithms are not known to be optimal.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic optimization can involve delayed information, multiple workers, and communication that happens only intermittently. These arrangements differ in which computations can depend on which earlier results. The paper introduces an oracle-based framework that represents those dependencies with a graph, giving different parallelization settings a shared mathematical description.

Using this representation, the authors derive generic lower bounds in terms of the dependency graph. Such bounds describe unavoidable demands on oracle access within the modeled setting. They then apply the framework to particular cases, including delayed updates and parallel processing with intermittent communication, to study how those structures constrain optimization.

The analysis also compares lower bounds with available upper bounds on oracle complexity. Gaps between them mark places where current guarantees do not settle the best achievable performance. In some cases, algorithms that appear to be natural choices are not known to be optimal. The paper's value is both a reusable framework for analyzing parallel optimization and a clearer identification of unresolved questions about algorithm quality.
summary.tldr: Dependency graphs provide a common framework for lower bounds in parallel stochastic optimization and expose gaps in known algorithm guarantees.

title: Graph Oracle Models, Lower Bounds, and Gaps for Parallel Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a sample-efficient approach to global optimization that relies on theoretically motivated value heuristics (acquisition functions) to guide its search process. Fully maximizing acquisition functions produces the Bayes' decision rule, but this ideal is difficult to achieve since these functions are frequently non-trivial to optimize. This statement is especially true when evaluating queries in parallel, where acquisition functions are routinely non-convex, high-dimensional, and intractable. We first show that acquisition functions estimated via Monte Carlo integration are consistently amenable to gradient-based optimization. Subsequently, we identify a common family of acquisition functions, including EI and UCB, whose characteristics not only facilitate but justify use of greedy approaches for their maximization.

Fully maximizing acquisition functions produces the Bayes' decision rule, but this ideal is difficult to achieve since these functions are frequently non-trivial to optimize. This statement is especially true when evaluating queries in parallel, where acquisition functions are routinely non-convex, high-dimensional, and intractable. We first show that acquisition functions estimated via Monte Carlo integration are consistently amenable to gradient-based optimization. Subsequently, we identify a common family of acquisition functions, including EI and UCB, whose characteristics not only facilitate but justify use of greedy approaches for their maximization.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function to decide which inputs are worth evaluating next. This makes each search step an optimization problem of its own. Fully maximizing that function gives the Bayesian decision rule, but doing so can be difficult, especially when choosing several evaluations to run in parallel.

The paper addresses this inner optimization problem. Parallel-query acquisition functions can be nonconvex, high-dimensional, and difficult to evaluate directly. The authors show that acquisition functions estimated through Monte Carlo integration are amenable to gradient-based optimization. This provides a principled way to work with sampling-based estimates while searching for useful queries.

They also identify a family of acquisition functions, including expected improvement and upper confidence bound, whose properties justify greedy maximization approaches. The contribution therefore concerns how to implement Bayesian optimization's query-selection step more effectively. It connects the mathematical structure of common acquisition functions with practical optimization strategies, without asserting that every acquisition function can be globally maximized easily.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes support for gradient-based and greedy methods for maximizing important Bayesian optimization acquisition functions.

title: Maximizing acquisition functions for Bayesian optimization

abstract: We prove that ϴ(k d^2 / ε^2) samples are necessary and sufficient for learning a mixture of k Gaussians in R^d, up to error ε in total variation distance. This improves both the known upper bounds and lower bounds for this problem. For mixtures of axis-aligned Gaussians, we show that O(k d / ε^2) samples suffice, matching a known lower bound. The upper bound is based on a novel technique for distribution learning based on a notion of sample compression. Any class of distributions that allows such a sample compression scheme can also be learned with few samples. Moreover, if a class of distributions has such a compression scheme, then so do the classes of products and mixtures of those distributions. The core of our main result is showing that the class of Gaussians in R^d has an efficient sample compression.

Any class of distributions that allows such a sample compression scheme can also be learned with few samples. paragraphs: This paper asks how many observations are needed to learn a mixture of k Gaussian distributions in d dimensions. Accuracy is measured in total variation distance, which compares distributions. The authors establish matching necessary and sufficient sample scaling of Θ(kd²/ε²) for error ε, improving both previously known upper and lower bounds.

For mixtures of axis-aligned Gaussians, they show that O(kd/ε²) samples suffice, matching a known lower bound. The different dependence on dimension distinguishes this more structured family from general Gaussian mixtures. These are sample-complexity results: they quantify the amount of data required to achieve the stated distributional accuracy.

The upper bounds come from a new distribution-learning technique based on sample compression. A distribution class with a suitable compression scheme can be learned from few samples, and the property carries over to products and mixtures. Showing that multivariate Gaussians admit efficient sample compression supplies the key ingredient. This also makes the proof technique useful beyond the single mixture-learning result.
summary.tldr: Sample compression yields nearly tight data requirements for learning Gaussian mixtures and a reusable framework for distribution learning.

title: Nearly tight sample complexity bounds for learning mixtures of Gaussians via sample compression schemes

abstract: To solve complex real-world problems with reinforcement learning, we cannot rely on manually specified reward functions. Instead, we need humans to communicate an objective to the agent directly. In this work, we combine two approaches to this problem: learning from expert demonstrations and learning from trajectory preferences. We use both to train a deep neural network to model the reward function and use its predicted reward to train an DQN-based deep reinforcement learning agent on 9 Atari games. Our approach beats the imitation learning baseline in 7 games and achieves strictly superhuman performance on 2 games. Additionally, we investigate the fit of the reward model, present some reward hacking problems, and study the effects of noise in the human labels.

paragraphs: Communicating an objective to a reinforcement learning agent can be difficult when it requires writing a reward function by hand. This paper combines two forms of human guidance: expert demonstrations and preferences between trajectories. Both are used to learn what behavior should be rewarded, giving the agent an objective derived from human input.

A deep neural network models the reward function from those demonstrations and preferences. Its predicted rewards then train a DQN-based reinforcement learning agent. This separates learning the objective from learning how to act: the reward model interprets the human guidance, and the agent optimizes behavior using that model’s outputs.

Across nine Atari games, the approach beats the imitation-learning baseline in seven and achieves strictly superhuman performance in two. The authors also examine how well the reward model fits, investigate reward hacking, and study noise in human labels. These additional analyses matter because success depends on the learned reward expressing the intended objective. The results demonstrate the potential of combining demonstrations and preferences while also examining failures in that communication process.
summary.tldr: Combining demonstrations and trajectory preferences to learn rewards beats imitation learning in seven of nine Atari games.

title: Reward learning from human preferences and demonstrations in Atari

abstract: Multichannel blind deconvolution is the problem of recovering an unknown signal $f$ and multiple unknown channels $x_i$ from convolutional measurements $y_i=x_i \circledast f$ ($i=1,2,\dots,N$). We consider the case where the $x_i$'s are sparse, and convolution with $f$ is invertible. Our nonconvex optimization formulation solves for a filter $h$ on the unit sphere that produces sparse output $y_i\circledast h$. Under some technical assumptions, we show that all local minima of the objective function correspond to the inverse filter of $f$ up to an inherent sign and shift ambiguity, and all saddle points have strictly negative curvatures. This geometric structure allows successful recovery of $f$ and $x_i$ using a simple manifold gradient descent algorithm with random initialization. Our theoretical findings are complemented by numerical experiments, which demonstrate superior performance of the proposed approach over the previous methods.

paragraphs: Multichannel blind deconvolution tries to recover an unknown shared signal and several unknown channels from their convolutions. The paper considers sparse channels and assumes convolution with the shared signal is invertible. Instead of directly recovering every unknown together, it searches for a filter that makes the filtered observations sparse.

The filter is constrained to the unit sphere, producing a nonconvex optimization problem. Under technical assumptions, the authors prove that every local minimum corresponds to an inverse filter of the shared signal, subject to unavoidable sign and shift ambiguities. They also show that every saddle point has a direction of strictly negative curvature, describing how the objective behaves away from solutions.

This geometry supports recovery using manifold gradient descent from a random initialization. The significance is that the nonconvex formulation has a favorable landscape under the stated assumptions: its local minima represent the desired recovery rather than unrelated alternatives. Numerical experiments complement the analysis and show better performance than previous methods. The recovery claim retains the inherent uncertainty in sign and shift.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, a spherical nonconvex formulation has favorable geometry that enables sparse blind deconvolution from random initialization.

title: Global Geometry of Multichannel Sparse Blind Deconvolution on the Sphere

abstract: Structured prediction provides a general framework to deal with supervised problems where the outputs have semantically rich structure. While classical approaches consider finite, albeit potentially huge, output spaces, in this paper we discuss how structured prediction can be extended to a continuous scenario. Specifically, we study a structured prediction approach to manifold-valued regression. We characterize a class of problems for which the considered approach is statistically consistent and study how geometric optimization can be used to compute the corresponding estimator. Promising experimental results on both simulated and real data complete our study.

While classical approaches consider finite, albeit potentially huge, output spaces, in this paper we discuss how structured prediction can be extended to a continuous scenario. Specifically, we study a structured prediction approach to manifold-valued regression. We characterize a class of problems for which the considered approach is statistically consistent and study how geometric optimization can be used to compute the corresponding estimator. Promising experimental results on both simulated and real data complete our study.

Traditional formulations often use finite output spaces, even when those spaces are enormous. This paper extends the perspective to continuous outputs, concentrating on regression problems whose predictions lie on a manifold, a space with its own geometric structure.

The authors characterize a class of problems for which their structured prediction approach is statistically consistent. This gives a theoretical connection between learning from data and the desired prediction behavior as data increase, within the identified class. They also study geometric optimization as a way to compute the estimator while respecting the structure of its output space.

Experiments on simulated and real data provide promising evidence for the approach. The contribution brings together a continuous structured-output formulation, a consistency analysis, and a computational treatment using geometry. That combination matters because a structured prediction method needs both a statistical justification and a way to obtain predictions. The consistency claim applies to the characterized problems, while the experiments illustrate its practical promise.
summary.tldr: Structured prediction is extended to manifold-valued regression with consistency results for a characterized problem class and geometric optimization methods.

title: Manifold Structured Prediction

abstract: We propose Cormorant, a rotationally covariant neural network architecture for learning the behavior and properties of complex many-body physical systems. We apply these networks to molecular systems with two goals: learning atomic potential energy surfaces for use in Molecular Dynamics simulations, and learning ground state properties of molecules calculated by Density Functional Theory. Some of the key features of our network are that (a) each neuron explicitly corresponds to a subset of atoms; (b) the activation of each neuron is covariant to rotations, ensuring that overall the network is fully rotationally invariant. Furthermore, the non-linearity in our network is based upon tensor products and the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition, allowing the network to operate entirely in Fourier space. Cormorant significantly outperforms competing algorithms in learning molecular Potential Energy Surfaces from conformational geometries in the MD-17 dataset, and is competitive with other methods at learning geometric, energetic, electronic, and thermodynamic properties of molecules on the GDB-9 dataset.

Rotating a molecule changes its coordinates, but should not change a rotation-invariant property predicted from those coordinates. The architecture builds this relationship into its internal representations rather than leaving the network to discover it entirely from examples.

Each neuron corresponds explicitly to a subset of atoms, and its activation changes in a prescribed way when the system rotates. These covariant internal activations support an overall rotationally invariant network. The nonlinear operations use tensor products and Clebsch-Gordan decomposition, allowing the computations to remain entirely in Fourier space.

The authors apply Cormorant to atomic potential energy surfaces for molecular dynamics and to molecular ground-state properties calculated using density functional theory. On MD-17, it significantly outperforms competing algorithms at learning potential energy surfaces from molecular geometries. On GDB-9, it is competitive across geometric, energetic, electronic, and thermodynamic properties. These findings support the usefulness of encoding physical symmetry directly in molecular learning architectures.

title: Cormorant: Covariant Molecular Neural Networks

abstract: Arguably, intelligent agents ought to be able to discover their own questions so that in learning answers for them they learn unanticipated useful knowledge and skills; this departs from the focus in much of machine learning on agents learning answers to externally defined questions. We present a novel method for a reinforcement learning (RL) agent to discover questions formulated as general value functions or GVFs, a fairly rich form of knowledge representation. Specifically, our method uses non-myopic meta-gradients to learn GVF-questions such that learning answers to them, as an auxiliary task, induces useful representations for the main task faced by the RL agent. We demonstrate that auxiliary tasks based on the discovered GVFs are sufficient, on their own, to build representations that support main task learning, and that they do so better than popular hand-designed auxiliary tasks from the literature. Furthermore, we show, in the context of Atari2600 videogames, how such auxiliary tasks, meta-learned alongside the main task, can improve the data efficiency of an actor-critic agent.

paragraphs: An agent can learn more than the answer to its main task: additional prediction problems can help it develop useful internal representations. This paper asks whether the agent can discover those auxiliary questions itself. It expresses questions as general value functions, a flexible form of knowledge representation within reinforcement learning.

The method learns which questions to ask using non-myopic meta-gradients. The guiding criterion is whether learning their answers produces representations that help the main task. This connects the design of an auxiliary task to its downstream learning consequences, rather than selecting it solely because it appears sensible to a human designer.

The authors demonstrate that the discovered auxiliary tasks can, on their own, build representations sufficient for main-task learning. In their evaluations, these representations work better than those produced by popular hand-designed auxiliary tasks. They also show that learning such tasks alongside the main objective can improve an actor-critic agent's data efficiency on Atari2600 games. The findings support discovering useful learning objectives as part of the agent's own training process.
summary.tldr: An agent learns its own auxiliary prediction questions by optimizing how much their answers help it learn the main task.

title: Discovery of Useful Questions as Auxiliary Tasks

abstract: Large-scale industrial recommender systems are usually confronted with computational problems due to the enormous corpus size. To retrieve and recommend the most relevant items to users under response time limits, resorting to an efficient index structure is an effective and practical solution. The previous work Tree-based Deep Model (TDM) \cite{zhu2018learning} greatly improves recommendation accuracy using tree index. By indexing items in a tree hierarchy and training a user-node preference prediction model satisfying a max-heap like property in the tree, TDM provides logarithmic computational complexity w.r.t. the corpus size, enabling the use of arbitrary advanced models in candidate retrieval and recommendation. In tree-based recommendation methods, the quality of both the tree index and the user-node preference prediction model determines the recommendation accuracy for the most part. We argue that the learning of tree index and preference model has interdependence. Our purpose, in this paper, is to develop a method to jointly learn the index structure and user preference prediction model. In our proposed joint optimization framework, the learning of index and user preference prediction model are carried out under a unified performance measure. Besides, we come up with a novel hierarchical user preference representation utilizing the tree index hierarchy. Experimental evaluations with two large-scale real-world datasets show that the proposed method improves recommendation accuracy significantly. Online A/B test results at a display advertising platform also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in production environments.

These findings support treating indexing and preference learning as connected design problems.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a recommendation tree and user-preference model improves accuracy in large-scale evaluations and a production A/B test.

title: Joint Optimization of Tree-based Index and Deep Model for Recommender Systems

abstract: It is becoming increasingly important to understand the vulnerability of machine learning models to adversarial attacks. In this paper we study the feasibility of robust learning from the perspective of computational learning theory, considering both sample and computational complexity. In particular, our definition of robust learnability requires polynomial sample complexity. We start with two negative results. We show that no non-trivial concept class can be robustly learned in the distribution-free setting against an adversary who can perturb just a single input bit. We show moreover that the class of monotone conjunctions cannot be robustly learned under the uniform distribution against an adversary who can perturb $\omega(\log n)$ input bits. However if the adversary is restricted to perturbing $O(\log n)$ bits, then the class of monotone conjunctions can be robustly learned with respect to a general class of distributions (that includes the uniform distribution). Finally, we provide a simple proof of the computational hardness of robust learning on the boolean hypercube. Unlike previous results of this nature, our result does not rely on another computational model (e.g. the statistical query model) nor on any hardness assumption other than the existence of a hard learning problem in the PAC framework.

paragraphs: This paper asks when adversarially robust classification is learnable, considering both the number of examples required and the computation involved. Its definition requires polynomial sample complexity. The setting uses binary inputs, making the adversary's power explicit through the number of input bits it may change.

The authors prove that no nontrivial concept class is robustly learnable in the distribution-free setting even against a one-bit perturbation. For monotone conjunctions under the uniform distribution, robustness is also impossible when the perturbation budget grows faster than log n. However, when the adversary is limited to O(log n) changed bits, these concepts are robustly learnable over a general family of distributions that includes the uniform distribution.

The paper additionally proves computational hardness on the Boolean hypercube, assuming only that a hard learning problem exists in the PAC framework. Together, the results show how distributional assumptions and perturbation budgets change feasibility. The positive result is essential context: the impossibility statements apply to their specified settings, rather than to every form of robust learning.
summary.tldr: Robust learning faces strong sample and computational barriers, with feasibility depending on distributional assumptions and the adversary's perturbation budget.

title: On the Hardness of Robust Classification

abstract: We study two problems in high-dimensional robust statistics: \emph{robust mean estimation} and \emph{outlier detection}. In robust mean estimation the goal is to estimate the mean $\mu$ of a distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ given $n$ independent samples, an $\epsilon$-fraction of which have been corrupted by a malicious adversary. In outlier detection the goal is to assign an \emph{outlier score} to each element of a data set such that elements more likely to be outliers are assigned higher scores. Our algorithms for both problems are based on a new outlier scoring method we call QUE-scoring based on \emph{quantum entropy regularization}. For robust mean estimation, this yields the first algorithm with optimal error rates and nearly-linear running time $\tilde{O}(nd)$ in all parameters, improving on the previous fastest running time $\tilde{O}(\min(nd/\e^6, nd^2))$. For outlier detection, we evaluate the performance of QUE-scoring via extensive experiments on synthetic and real data, and demonstrate that it often performs better than previously proposed algorithms.
