paragraphs: This paper addresses two related problems in high-dimensional statistics. Robust mean estimation seeks the underlying mean even when an adversary has corrupted a fraction of independent samples. Outlier detection instead assigns each observation a score indicating how suspicious it is. The authors develop a shared scoring method, QUE-scoring, based on quantum entropy regularization.

For robust mean estimation, the resulting algorithm combines optimal error rates with running time nearly linear in the number of data entries: approximately n times d, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here n is the sample count and d is the dimension. This improves the previous fastest bound, which carried additional dependence on the corruption fraction or the dimension.

For outlier detection, the evidence is empirical: extensive tests on synthetic and real data show that QUE-scoring often outperforms earlier algorithms. The two contributions have different kinds of support. Mean estimation receives a runtime and accuracy guarantee, while outlier scoring receives broad experimental evaluation demonstrating frequent, rather than universal, improvements.
summary.tldr: Quantum-entropy-based scoring enables optimal-error robust mean estimation in nearly linear time and often improves empirical outlier detection.

title: Quantum Entropy Scoring for Fast Robust Mean Estimation and Improved Outlier Detection

abstract: We theoretically study the landscape of the training error for neural networks in overparameterized cases. We consider three basic methods for embedding a network into a wider one with more hidden units, and discuss whether a minimum point of the narrower network gives a minimum or saddle point of the wider one. Our results show that the networks with smooth and ReLU activation have different partially flat landscapes around the embedded point. We also relate these results to a difference of their generalization abilities in overparameterized realization.
originalAbstract: We theoretically study the landscape of the training error for neural networks in overparameterized cases. We consider three basic methods for embedding a network into a wider one with more hidden units, and discuss whether a minimum point of the narrower network gives a minimum or saddle point of the wider one. Our results show that the networks with smooth and ReLU activation have different partially flat landscapes around the embedded point. We also relate these results to a difference of their generalization abilities in overparameterized realization.

paragraphs: Making a neural network wider introduces additional parameters and changes the space in which training takes place. This paper studies that change theoretically by embedding a narrower network into a wider network with more hidden units. The question is what happens to a parameter setting that was a minimum of the narrower network's training error.

The authors examine three basic embedding methods and analyze whether the embedded point remains a minimum or becomes a saddle point. A saddle point has directions with different local error behavior, while partial flatness means some parameter directions leave the error locally unchanged. The analysis therefore concerns the shape of the training-error landscape around particular embedded solutions.

The results distinguish networks with smooth activations from networks with ReLU activations: their partially flat landscapes differ around the embedded points. The paper also relates these geometric differences to differences in generalization in overparameterized realizations. Its contribution connects a concrete widening operation to local optimization geometry and its relationship with generalization.
summary.tldr: Embedding networks into wider ones reveals activation-dependent differences in partially flat minima and saddle points, with connections to generalization.

title: Semi-flat minima and saddle points by embedding neural networks to overparameterization

abstract: Stack-augmented recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been of interest to the deep learning community for some time. However, the difficulty of training memory models remains a problem obstructing the widespread use of such models. In this paper, we propose the Ordered Memory architecture. Inspired by Ordered Neurons (Shen et al., 2018), we introduce a new attention-based mechanism and use its cumulative probability to control the writing and erasing operation of the memory. We also introduce a new Gated Recursive Cell to compose lower-level representations into higher-level representation. We demonstrate that our model achieves strong performance on the logical inference task (Bowman et al., 2015) and the ListOps (Nangia and Bowman, 2018) task. We can also interpret the model to retrieve the induced tree structure, and find that these induced structures align with the ground truth. Finally, we evaluate our model on the Stanford Sentiment Treebank tasks (Socher et al., 2013), and find that it performs comparatively with the state-of-the-art methods in the literature.

Ordered Memory addresses this problem with an architecture that explicitly controls memory updates and builds higher-level representations from lower-level ones. The design is inspired by the Ordered Neurons approach.

A new attention mechanism governs memory operations through cumulative probabilities. These probabilities control writing and erasing, providing a coordinated mechanism for changing the stored information. A Gated Recursive Cell supplies the complementary composition operation, combining lower-level representations into higher-level representations. Together, the components link memory management with the construction of hierarchical structure.

The authors report strong results on logical inference and ListOps, and performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on Stanford Sentiment Treebank tasks. They also interpret the model to recover its induced tree structures and find alignment with the ground truth. This structural agreement provides evidence that the model’s internal organization captures relevant hierarchy alongside achieving useful task performance.
summary.tldr: Ordered Memory combines attention-controlled memory updates with recursive composition, achieving strong task results and induced trees aligned with ground truth.

title: Ordered Memory

abstract: The exploration bonus is an effective approach to manage the exploration-exploitation trade-off in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). While it has been analyzed in infinite-horizon discounted and finite-horizon problems, we focus on designing and analysing the exploration bonus in the more challenging infinite-horizon undiscounted setting. We first introduce SCAL+, a variant of SCAL (Fruit et al. 2018), that uses a suitable exploration bonus to solve any discrete unknown weakly-communicating MDP for which an upper bound $c$ on the span of the optimal bias function is known. We prove that SCAL+ enjoys the same regret guarantees as SCAL, which relies on the less efficient extended value iteration approach. Furthermore, we leverage the flexibility provided by the exploration bonus scheme to generalize SCAL+ to smooth MDPs with continuous state space and discrete actions. We show that the resulting algorithm (SCCAL+) achieves the same regret bound as UCCRL (Ortner and Ryabko, 2012) while being the first implementable algorithm for this setting.

paragraphs: Exploration bonuses help reinforcement-learning algorithms balance gathering information with using what they already know. This paper studies bonuses in infinite-horizon problems without discounting, where performance concerns long-run average reward. The authors develop and analyze algorithms for this setting, extending the use of bonuses beyond the discounted and finite-horizon cases discussed in the abstract.

Their discrete-state algorithm, SCAL+, applies to unknown weakly communicating MDPs when an upper bound on the span of the optimal bias function is known. They prove that it matches SCAL's regret guarantees. The bonus approach provides an alternative to SCAL's less efficient extended value iteration method while preserving those guarantees.

summary.tldr: Exploration-bonus algorithms match existing regret guarantees for specified discrete and continuous-state average-reward reinforcement-learning problems.

title: Exploration Bonus for Regret Minimization in Discrete and Continuous Average Reward MDPs

abstract: Combinatorial optimization (CO) problems are notoriously challenging for neural networks, especially in the absence of labeled instances. This work proposes an unsupervised learning framework for CO problems on graphs that can provide integral solutions of certified quality. Inspired by Erdos' probabilistic method, we use a neural network to parametrize a probability distribution over sets. Crucially, we show that when the network is optimized w.r.t. a suitably chosen loss, the learned distribution contains, with controlled probability, a low-cost integral solution that obeys the constraints of the combinatorial problem. The probabilistic proof of existence is then derandomized to decode the desired solutions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach to obtain valid solutions to the maximum clique problem and to perform local graph clustering. Our method achieves competitive results on both real datasets and synthetic hard instances.

paragraphs: This paper tackles combinatorial optimization on graphs without labeled solutions. Such problems require discrete choices that satisfy constraints, making it challenging to turn neural predictions into valid answers. The proposed framework uses a neural network to represent a probability distribution over sets, drawing inspiration from the probabilistic method associated with Erdos.

The key is the training objective. The authors show that, with a suitably chosen loss, optimizing the network produces a distribution containing a low-cost, constraint-satisfying integral solution with controlled probability. An integral solution makes the required discrete decisions. The probabilistic existence argument is then derandomized to decode the desired solution.

The framework is demonstrated on maximum clique and local graph clustering, where it produces valid solutions and achieves competitive results on real datasets and difficult synthetic instances. Its significance is the connection between unsupervised neural training and certified solution quality. The guarantee depends on the stated relationship between the loss, the learned distribution, and the decoding procedure.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised neural framework learns distributions over graph solutions and derandomizes an existence guarantee to obtain valid discrete solutions.

title: Erdos Goes Neural: an Unsupervised Learning Framework for Combinatorial Optimization on Graphs

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are a useful probabilistic model for selecting a small diverse subset out of a large collection of items, with applications in summarization, recommendation, stochastic optimization, experimental design and more. Given a kernel function and a subset size k, our goal is to sample k out of n items with probability proportional to the determinant of the kernel matrix induced by the subset (a.k.a. k-DPP). Existing k-DPP sampling algorithms require an expensive preprocessing step which involves multiple passes over all n items, making it infeasible for large datasets. A naïve heuristic addressing this problem is to uniformly subsample a fraction of the data and perform k-DPP sampling only on those items, however this method offers no guarantee that the produced sample will even approximately resemble the target distribution over the original dataset. In this paper, we develop alpha-DPP, an algorithm which adaptively builds a sufficiently large uniform sample of data that is then used to efficiently generate a smaller set of k items, while ensuring that this set is drawn exactly from the target distribution defined on all n items. We show empirically that our algorithm produces a k-DPP sample after observing only a small fraction of all elements, leading to several orders of magnitude faster performance compared to the state-of-the-art. Our implementation of alpha-DPP is provided at https://github.com/guilgautier/DPPy/.
originalAbstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are a useful probabilistic model for selecting a small diverse subset out of a large collection of items, with applications in summarization, recommendation, stochastic optimization, experimental design and more. Given a kernel function and a subset size k, our goal is to sample k out of n items with probability proportional to the determinant of the kernel matrix induced by the subset (a.k.a. k-DPP). Existing k-DPP sampling algorithms require an expensive preprocessing step which involves multiple passes over all n items, making it infeasible for large datasets. A naïve heuristic addressing this problem is to uniformly subsample a fraction of the data and perform k-DPP sampling only on those items, however this method offers no guarantee that the produced sample will even approximately resemble the target distribution over the original dataset. In this paper, we develop alpha-DPP, an algorithm which adaptively builds a sufficiently large uniform sample of data that is then used to efficiently generate a smaller set of k items, while ensuring that this set is drawn exactly from the target distribution defined on all n items. We show empirically that our algorithm produces a k-DPP sample after observing only a small fraction of all elements, leading to several orders of magnitude faster performance compared to the state-of-the-art. Our implementation of alpha-DPP is provided at https://github.com/guilgautier/DPPy/.

paragraphs: A fixed-size determinantal point process, or k-DPP, selects a diverse subset of k items from a larger collection. Each subset's probability is proportional to a determinant computed from its kernel matrix. Existing sampling methods can require expensive preprocessing with repeated passes over the full dataset, making this appealing selection rule difficult to use at large scale.

The paper introduces alpha-DPP, which adaptively constructs a sufficiently large uniform sample and then generates the smaller requested subset from it. Crucially, the final subset follows the exact k-DPP distribution defined over the entire collection. Simple uniform subsampling followed by a k-DPP on the reduced collection does not provide that guarantee.

Empirically, alpha-DPP produces a sample after inspecting only a small fraction of the available items and achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines an exact distributional guarantee with observed computational savings. The small fraction inspected and the magnitude of acceleration are experimental findings rather than universal claims about every dataset.
summary.tldr: Alpha-DPP preserves exact fixed-size determinantal sampling while empirically inspecting only a small fraction of the full collection.

title: Sampling from a k-DPP without looking at all items

abstract: Deep learning methods for graphs achieve remarkable performance on many node-level and graph-level prediction tasks. However, despite the proliferation of the methods and their success, prevailing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) neglect subgraphs, rendering subgraph prediction tasks challenging to tackle in many impactful applications. Further, subgraph prediction tasks present several unique challenges: subgraphs can have non-trivial internal topology, but also carry a notion of position and external connectivity information relative to the underlying graph in which they exist. Here, we introduce SUBGNN, a subgraph neural network to learn disentangled subgraph representations. We propose a novel subgraph routing mechanism that propagates neural messages between the subgraph’s components and randomly sampled anchor patches from the underlying graph, yielding highly accurate subgraph representations. SUBGNN specifies three channels, each designed to capture a distinct aspect of subgraph topology, and we provide empirical evidence that the channels encode their intended properties. We design a series of new synthetic and real-world subgraph datasets. Empirical results for subgraph classification on eight datasets show that SUBGNN achieves considerable performance gains, outperforming strong baseline methods, including node-level and graph-level methods, by 19.8% over the strongest baseline. SUBGNN performs exceptionally well on challenging biomedical datasets where subgraphs have complex topology and even comprise multiple disconnected components.

A subgraph has internal structure, a position within a larger graph, and connections to its surroundings. It may also contain disconnected components. SUBGNN is designed to learn representations that account for these features of subgraphs.

The model routes neural messages between a subgraph's components and randomly sampled anchor patches from the underlying graph. It uses three channels intended to capture distinct aspects of subgraph topology, producing representations that separate those aspects. summary.tldr: SUBGNN learns subgraph representations through topology-specific channels and anchor-patch messaging, improving reported subgraph classification performance.

title: Subgraph Neural Networks

abstract: The search for efficient, sparse deep neural network models is most prominently performed by pruning: training a dense, overparameterized network and removing parameters, usually via following a manually-crafted heuristic. Additionally, the recent Lottery Ticket Hypothesis conjectures that, for a typically-sized neural network, it is possible to find small sub-networks which, when trained from scratch on a comparable budget, match the performance of the original dense counterpart. We revisit fundamental aspects of pruning algorithms, pointing out missing ingredients in previous approaches, and develop a method, Continuous Sparsification, which searches for sparse networks based on a novel approximation of an intractable $\ell_0$ regularization. We compare against dominant heuristic-based methods on pruning as well as ticket search -- finding sparse subnetworks that can be successfully re-trained from an early iterate. Empirical results show that we surpass the state-of-the-art for both objectives, across models and datasets, including VGG trained on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet. In addition to setting a new standard for pruning, Continuous Sparsification also offers fast parallel ticket search, opening doors to new applications of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis.

paragraphs: Neural-network pruning searches for smaller models by removing parameters from a larger network. The related lottery-ticket question asks whether small subnetworks can retain strong performance when trained with a comparable budget. This paper revisits how such subnetworks are found and proposes Continuous Sparsification, a method that makes sparsity part of an optimization objective.

The method uses a new approximation to L0 regularization, which targets the number of nonzero parameters but is otherwise intractable to optimize directly. The authors evaluate it for both pruning and ticket search. In their ticket-search evaluation, the objective is to identify sparse subnetworks that can be successfully retrained from an early training iterate.

Experiments report improvements over leading heuristic methods for both objectives across models and datasets, including VGG on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet. Continuous Sparsification also supports fast parallel ticket search. These findings provide empirical support for the proposed optimization-based sparsity mechanism and its usefulness in discovering retrainable subnetworks; they do not turn the broader Lottery Ticket Hypothesis into a universal theorem.
summary.tldr: Continuous Sparsification approximates L0 regularization to improve neural-network pruning and the search for sparse subnetworks that can be retrained successfully.

title: Winning the Lottery with Continuous Sparsification

abstract: We consider the classical setting of optimizing a nonsmooth Lipschitz continuous convex function over a convex constraint set, when having access to a (stochastic) first-order oracle (FO) for the function and a projection oracle (PO) for the constraint set. It is well known that to achieve $\epsilon$-suboptimality in high-dimensions, $\Theta(\epsilon^{-2})$ FO calls are necessary. This is achieved by the projected subgradient method (PGD). However, PGD also entails $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ PO calls, which may be computationally costlier than FO calls (e.g. nuclear norm constraints). Improving this PO calls complexity of PGD is largely unexplored, despite the fundamental nature of this problem and extensive literature. We present first such improvement. This only requires a mild assumption that the objective function, when extended to a slightly larger neighborhood of the constraint set, still remains Lipschitz and accessible via FO. In particular, we introduce MOPES method, which carefully combines Moreau-Yosida smoothing and accelerated first-order schemes. This is guaranteed to find a feasible $\epsilon$-suboptimal solution using only $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ PO calls and optimal $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ FO calls. Further, instead of a PO if we only have a linear minimization oracle (LMO, a la Frank-Wolfe) to access the constraint set, an extension of our method, MOLES, finds a feasible $\epsilon$-suboptimal solution using $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ LMO calls and FO calls---both match known lower bounds, resolving a question left open since White (1993). Our experiments confirm that these methods achieve significant speedups over the state-of-the-art, for a problem with costly PO and LMO calls.

paragraphs: Optimizing a nonsmooth Lipschitz convex function over a convex set involves learning about the objective and respecting the constraints. Those projections can be much more expensive than evaluating first-order information, making their frequency a separate bottleneck.

The proposed MOPES method combines Moreau-Yosida smoothing with accelerated first-order techniques. It reaches a feasible epsilon-suboptimal solution using O(1/epsilon) projections while retaining the optimal O(1/epsilon²) first-order calls. This requires the objective to remain Lipschitz and accessible through the first-order oracle in a slightly larger neighborhood around the constraint set.

When constraints are accessed through linear minimization instead, the MOLES extension uses O(1/epsilon²) calls to both the linear minimization and first-order oracles, matching known lower bounds. Experiments show significant speedups on a problem with costly constraint-oracle calls. The central benefit is reducing expensive constraint handling without sacrificing the optimal order of objective-information queries.
summary.tldr: MOPES reduces projection calls for nonsmooth convex optimization, while MOLES achieves optimal oracle complexity when using linear minimization.

title: Projection Efficient Subgradient Method and Optimal Nonsmooth Frank-Wolfe Method

abstract: When a toddler is presented a new toy, their instinctual behaviour is to pick it up and inspect it with their hand and eyes in tandem, clearly searching over its surface to properly understand what they are playing with. At any instance here, touch provides high fidelity localized information while vision provides complementary global context. However, in 3D shape reconstruction, the complementary fusion of visual and haptic modalities remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we study this problem and present an effective chart-based approach to multi-modal shape understanding which encourages a similar fusion vision and touch information. To do so, we introduce a dataset of simulated touch and vision signals from the interaction between a robotic hand and a large array of 3D objects. Our results show that (1) leveraging both vision and touch signals consistently improves single- modality baselines; (2) our approach outperforms alternative modality fusion methods and strongly benefits from the proposed chart-based structure; (3) the reconstruction quality increases with the number of grasps provided; and (4) the touch information not only enhances the reconstruction at the touch site but also extrapolates to its local neighborhood.

paragraphs: Vision and touch provide different kinds of evidence about an object's shape. An image supplies broad context, while contact reveals detailed information about a small part of the surface. This paper studies how to combine those signals for three-dimensional reconstruction, using a chart-based representation that organizes surface information into patches.

The researchers introduce a dataset containing simulated visual and touch signals from a robotic hand interacting with many three-dimensional objects. This provides a setting for testing whether the two senses help each other and whether the proposed representation makes their combination more effective. In these experiments, combining vision and touch consistently improves on using either modality alone.

The chart-based method also outperforms alternative ways of combining the modalities, and the results attribute substantial benefit to its surface structure. Reconstruction improves as more grasps become available. Touch also helps reconstruct the neighborhood around a contact point, suggesting that a local measurement can inform a broader surface region rather than correcting only the exact location touched.
summary.tldr: A chart-based reconstruction method combines vision and simulated touch to improve object shapes, including surface regions near contact points.

title: 3D Shape Reconstruction from Vision and Touch

abstract: Reward shaping is an effective technique for incorporating domain knowledge into reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches such as potential-based reward shaping normally make full use of a given shaping reward function. However, since the transformation of human knowledge into numeric reward values is often imperfect due to reasons such as human cognitive bias, completely utilizing the shaping reward function may fail to improve the performance of RL algorithms. In this paper, we consider the problem of adaptively utilizing a given shaping reward function. We formulate the utilization of shaping rewards as a bi-level optimization problem, where the lower level is to optimize policy using the shaping rewards and the upper level is to optimize a parameterized shaping weight function for true reward maximization. We formally derive the gradient of the expected true reward with respect to the shaping weight function parameters and accordingly propose three learning algorithms based on different assumptions. Experiments in sparse-reward cartpole and MuJoCo environments show that our algorithms can fully exploit beneficial shaping rewards, and meanwhile ignore unbeneficial shaping rewards or even transform them into beneficial ones.

paragraphs: Reward shaping adds a learning signal that expresses domain knowledge to a reinforcement learning problem. Human knowledge can be translated imperfectly into numerical rewards, however, so fully following that signal may not improve the actual task. This paper asks how an agent can learn to use a supplied shaping reward selectively.

The approach formulates this choice as a two-level optimization problem. At the lower level, shaping rewards guide policy optimization. At the upper level, a parameterized weighting function is adjusted to maximize the true reward. The authors derive the gradient of expected true reward with respect to the weighting parameters and develop three algorithms under different assumptions.

Experiments use sparse-reward cartpole and MuJoCo environments. The reported results show that the algorithms can exploit helpful shaping rewards while ignoring unhelpful ones or even turning them into useful guidance. This makes the quality of shaping depend on its contribution to the true objective, allowing the learner to adapt how it uses domain knowledge rather than treating every supplied shaping value as equally helpful.
summary.tldr: A two-level optimization learns how to weight shaping rewards according to their effect on true task reward.

title: Learning to Utilize Shaping Rewards: A New Approach of Reward Shaping

abstract: Actor-critic (AC) methods have exhibited great empirical success compared with other reinforcement learning algorithms, where the actor uses the policy gradient to improve the learning policy and the critic uses temporal difference learning to estimate the policy gradient. Under the two time-scale learning rate schedule, the asymptotic convergence of AC has been well studied in the literature. However, the non-asymptotic convergence and finite sample complexity of actor-critic methods are largely open. In this work, we provide a non-asymptotic analysis for two time-scale actor-critic methods under non-i.i.d. setting. We prove that the actor-critic method is guaranteed to find a first-order stationary point (i.e., $\|\nabla J(\bm{\theta})\|_2^2 \le \epsilon$) of the non-concave performance function $J(\bm{\theta})$, with $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-2.5})$ sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work providing finite-time analysis and sample complexity bound for two time-scale actor-critic methods.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning couples two learning processes. The actor improves a policy using policy-gradient information, while the critic uses temporal-difference learning to help estimate that information. With two time scales, their learning rates follow different schedules. Earlier convergence analyses established behavior in the limit, leaving the amount of data needed for a finite accuracy target largely unresolved.

This paper provides a finite-time analysis in a setting where samples are not independent and identically distributed. That distinction matters because the analysis addresses dependent learning data. Its central result bounds the samples needed to reach a first-order stationary point of the policy performance function.

Specifically, the guarantee targets a squared gradient norm at most epsilon, with sample complexity of order epsilon to the power minus 2.5, up to logarithmic factors. Because the performance function is nonconcave, this is a stationarity guarantee rather than a guarantee of a globally best policy. The result gives a quantitative account of how the sample requirement grows as the desired stationarity tolerance becomes stricter.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the samples needed for two-time-scale actor-critic learning to reach approximate stationarity with dependent data.

title: A Finite-Time Analysis of Two Time-Scale Actor-Critic Methods

abstract: We address the problem of learning a decision policy from observational data of past decisions in contexts with features and associated outcomes. The past policy maybe unknown and in safety-critical applications, such as medical decision support, it is of interest to learn robust policies that reduce the risk of outcomes with high costs. In this paper, we develop a method for learning policies that reduce tails of the cost distribution at a specified level and, moreover, provide a statistically valid bound on the cost of each decision. These properties are valid under finite samples -- even in scenarios with uneven or no overlap between features for different decisions in the observed data -- by building on recent results in conformal prediction. The performance and statistical properties of the proposed method are illustrated using both real and synthetic data.

paragraphs: This paper learns decision policies from records of earlier decisions, contextual features, and outcomes. The policy that generated those records may be unknown. The authors focus on reducing the risk of especially costly outcomes, a concern that matters in applications such as medical decision support.

Their method targets the tail of the cost distribution at a specified level and supplies a statistically valid cost bound for each decision. This makes the objective sensitive to high-cost outcomes rather than describing policy quality only through typical costs. The decision-level bounds add a statistical assessment of the costs associated with the choices the policy makes.

The approach builds on conformal prediction, with properties that remain valid for finite samples. The abstract specifically includes cases where feature distributions for different observed decisions overlap unevenly or do not overlap. That is a significant part of the stated result because the available records may represent different decisions in very different contexts. Experiments with real and synthetic data illustrate the method’s performance and statistical properties.
summary.tldr: A conformal-prediction-based method learns policies targeting high-cost outcomes and provides finite-sample statistical bounds for individual decisions.

title: Learning Robust Decision Policies from Observational Data

abstract: In practical instances of nonconvex matrix factorization, the rank of the true solution $r^{\star}$ is often unknown, so the rank $r$of the model can be over-specified as $r>r^{\star}$. This over-parameterized regime of matrix factorization significantly slows down the convergence of local search algorithms, from a linear rate with $r=r^{\star}$ to a sublinear rate when $r>r^{\star}$. We propose an inexpensive preconditioner for the matrix sensing variant of nonconvex matrix factorization that restores the convergence rate of gradient descent back to linear, even in the over-parameterized case, while also making it agnostic to possible ill-conditioning in the ground truth. Classical gradient descent in a neighborhood of the solution slows down due to the need for the model matrix factor to become singular. Our key result is that this singularity can be corrected by $\ell_{2}$ regularization with a specific range of values for the damping parameter. In fact, a good damping parameter can be inexpensively estimated from the current iterate. The resulting algorithm, which we call preconditioned gradient descent or PrecGD, is stable under noise, and converges linearly to an information theoretically optimal error bound. Our numerical experiments find that PrecGD works equally well in restoring the linear convergence of other variants of nonconvex matrix factorization in the over-parameterized regime.

This paper develops an inexpensive preconditioner for matrix sensing that restores linear convergence in the overparameterized setting and avoids sensitivity to possible ill-conditioning of the true matrix.

The abstract distinguishes the matrix-sensing theoretical contribution from that broader experimental evidence, supporting preconditioning as a practical response to the slowdown caused by overspecifying rank.
summary.tldr: PrecGD uses adaptive damping to restore linear convergence in overparameterized matrix sensing while remaining stable under noise.

title: Preconditioned Gradient Descent for Over-Parameterized Nonconvex Matrix Factorization

abstract: Understanding the training dynamics of deep learning models is perhaps a necessary step toward demystifying the effectiveness of these models. In particular, how do training data from different classes gradually become separable in their feature spaces when training neural networks using stochastic gradient descent? In this paper, we model the evolution of features during deep learning training using a set of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that each corresponding to a training sample. As a crucial ingredient in our modeling strategy, each SDE contains a drift term that reflects the impact of backpropagation at an input on the features of all samples. Our main finding uncovers a sharp phase transition phenomenon regarding the intra-class impact: if the SDEs are locally elastic in the sense that the impact is more significant on samples from the same class as the input, the features of training data become linearly separable---meaning vanishing training loss; otherwise, the features are not separable, no matter how long the training time is. In the presence of local elasticity, moreover, an analysis of our SDEs shows the emergence of a simple geometric structure called neural collapse of the features. Taken together, our results shed light on the decisive role of local elasticity underlying the training dynamics of neural networks. We corroborate our theoretical analysis with experiments on a synthesized dataset of geometric shapes as well as on CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: This paper asks how training with stochastic gradient descent gradually makes examples from different classes separable in a neural network’s feature space. The authors model feature evolution using one stochastic differential equation for each training sample. Each equation includes a drift term describing how backpropagation at one input affects the features of other samples.

With local elasticity, features become linearly separable and training loss vanishes; without it, the features remain inseparable regardless of training duration.

The phase-transition statement belongs to the proposed dynamical model, rather than establishing an unrestricted condition for every neural network training procedure.
summary.tldr: A stochastic model of feature learning links stronger within-class update effects to a sharp transition toward linear separability and neural collapse.

title: Imitating Deep Learning Dynamics via Locally Elastic Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: Neural Transducer (e.g., RNN-T) has been widely used in automatic speech recognition (ASR) due to its capabilities of efficiently modeling monotonic alignments between input and output sequences and naturally supporting streaming inputs. Considering that monotonic alignments are also critical to text to speech (TTS) synthesis and streaming TTS is also an important application scenario, in this work, we explore the possibility of applying Transducer to TTS and more. However, it is challenging because it is difficult to trade off the emission (continuous mel-spectrogram prediction) probability and transition (ASR Transducer predicts blank token to indicate transition to next input) probability when calculating the output probability lattice in Transducer, and it is not easy to learn the alignments between text and speech through the output probability lattice. We propose SpeechTransducer (Speech-T for short), a Transformer based Transducer model that 1) uses a new forward algorithm to separate the transition prediction from the continuous mel-spectrogram prediction when calculating the output probability lattice, and uses a diagonal constraint in the probability lattice to help the alignment learning; 2) supports both full-sentence or streaming TTS by adjusting the look-ahead context; and 3) further supports both TTS and ASR together for the first time, which enjoys several advantages including fewer parameters as well as streaming synthesis and recognition in a single model. Experiments on LJSpeech datasets demonstrate that Speech-T 1) is more robust than the attention based autoregressive TTS model due to its inherent monotonic alignments between text and speech; 2) naturally supports streaming TTS with good voice quality; and 3) enjoys the benefit of joint modeling TTS and ASR in a single network.

paragraphs: Transducer models are useful for speech recognition because they align input and output in order and support streaming. Speech-T adapts this idea to speech synthesis, where the output is a continuous mel-spectrogram. A central difficulty is balancing the prediction of acoustic output with the decision to advance to the next text input.

The Transformer-based model uses a new forward algorithm that separates transition prediction from continuous acoustic prediction when computing the probability lattice. A diagonal constraint helps learn the text–speech alignment. Adjusting the available look-ahead context lets the same approach support either full-sentence synthesis or streaming synthesis.

Speech-T also supports synthesis and recognition together in one network, with advantages including fewer parameters and streaming in both directions. Experiments on LJSpeech show greater robustness than an attention-based autoregressive synthesis model, attributed to monotonic alignment, along with good streaming voice quality and benefits from joint modeling. The results connect a structured alignment mechanism to both reliable synthesis and shared speech processing.
summary.tldr: Speech-T adapts transducers to continuous speech output and supports streaming synthesis and recognition in one network.

title: Speech-T: Transducer for Text to Speech and Beyond

abstract: We study the problem of sparse tensor principal component analysis: given a tensor $\pmb Y = \pmb W + \lambda x^{\otimes p}$ with $\pmb W \in \otimes^p \mathbb{R}^n$ having i.i.d. Gaussian entries, the goal is to recover the $k$-sparse unit vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The model captures both sparse PCA (in its Wigner form) and tensor PCA.For the highly sparse regime of $k \leq \sqrt{n}$, we present a family of algorithms that smoothly interpolates between a simple polynomial-time algorithm and the exponential-time exhaustive search algorithm. For any $1 \leq t \leq k$, our algorithms recovers the sparse vector for signal-to-noise ratio $\lambda \geq \tilde{\mathcal{O}} (\sqrt{t} \cdot (k/t)^{p/2})$ in time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{p+t})$, capturing the state-of-the-art guarantees for the matrix settings (in both the polynomial-time and sub-exponential time regimes).Our results naturally extend to the case of $r$ distinct $k$-sparse signals with disjoint supports, with guarantees that are independent of the number of spikes. Even in the restricted case of sparse PCA, known algorithms only recover the sparse vectors for $\lambda \geq \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k \cdot r)$ while our algorithms require $\lambda \geq \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k)$.Finally, by analyzing the low-degree likelihood ratio, we complement these algorithmic results with rigorous evidence illustrating the trade-offs between signal-to-noise ratio and running time. This lower bound captures the known lower bounds for both sparse PCA and tensor PCA. In this general model, we observe a more intricate three-way trade-off between the number of samples $n$, the sparsity $k$, and the tensor power $p$.

paragraphs: Sparse tensor PCA seeks a sparse unit vector hidden in a tensor corrupted by independent Gaussian noise. The model includes both sparse matrix PCA and tensor PCA, allowing the paper to examine how sparsity and tensor order jointly affect recovery. Its central question is how much computation is needed at different signal strengths.

For sparsity at most the square root of the ambient dimension, the authors give a family of algorithms ranging from polynomial-time methods toward exhaustive search. A tuning parameter trades longer runtime for recovery at weaker signal-to-noise ratios. The guarantees recover leading matrix-case results and extend to multiple sparse signals when their supports are disjoint, without dependence on the number of signals in the recovery threshold.

The paper complements these algorithms with low-degree likelihood-ratio analysis, providing rigorous evidence for signal-strength versus runtime tradeoffs. This is evidence through a particular analytical framework, rather than an unrestricted computational impossibility claim. Together, the results connect known sparse PCA and tensor PCA behavior and reveal a more intricate interaction among dimension, sparsity, and tensor order.
summary.tldr: A family of sparse tensor PCA algorithms trades computation for weaker signal requirements, supported by low-degree evidence about computational limits.

title: The Complexity of Sparse Tensor PCA

abstract: For certain infinitely-wide neural networks, the neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory fully characterizes generalization, but for the networks used in practice, the empirical NTK only provides a rough first-order approximation. Still, a growing body of work keeps leveraging this approximation to successfully analyze important deep learning phenomena and design algorithms for new applications. In our work, we provide strong empirical evidence to determine the practical validity of such approximation by conducting a systematic comparison of the behavior of different neural networks and their linear approximations on different tasks. We show that the linear approximations can indeed rank the learning complexity of certain tasks for neural networks, even when they achieve very different performances. However, in contrast to what was previously reported, we discover that neural networks do not always perform better than their kernel approximations, and reveal that the performance gap heavily depends on architecture, dataset size and training task. We discover that networks overfit to these tasks mostly due to the evolution of their kernel during training, thus, revealing a new type of implicit bias.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernel theory fully describes generalization for certain infinitely wide networks, but its empirical counterpart is only a first-order approximation for practical networks. This paper tests how informative that approximation remains by systematically comparing neural networks with their linearized versions across tasks. It distinguishes usefulness as an analytical guide from agreement in predictive performance.

The authors find that linear approximations can rank the learning difficulty of some tasks even when their actual performance differs substantially from the networks'. They also find that neural networks do not consistently outperform their kernel approximations. The size and direction of the gap depend strongly on architecture, dataset size, and the training task.

In the studied tasks, the authors attribute most network overfitting to changes in the kernel during training, identifying a form of implicit bias. The results support a qualified use of linearized models: they can reveal relative task difficulty while missing consequential training behavior. Their practical relevance therefore depends on which aspect of learning is being explained.
summary.tldr: Linearized networks can rank some tasks' difficulty, but performance gaps depend strongly on architecture, data size, and training task.

title: What can linearized neural networks actually say about generalization?

abstract: Several queries and scores have recently been proposed to explain individual predictions over ML models. Examples include queries based on “anchors”, which are parts of an instance that are sufficient to justify its classification, and “feature-perturbation” scores such as SHAP. Given the need for flexible, reliable, and easy-to-apply interpretability methods for ML models, we foresee the need for developing declarative languages to naturally specify different explainability queries. We do this in a principled way by rooting such a language in a logic called FOIL, which allows for expressing many simple but important explainability queries, and might serve as a core for more expressive interpretability languages. We study the computational complexity of FOIL queries over two classes of ML models often deemed to be easily interpretable: decision trees and more general decision diagrams. Since the number of possible inputs for an ML model is exponential in its dimension, tractability of the FOIL evaluation problem is delicate but can be achieved by either restricting the structure of the models, or the fragment of FOIL being evaluated. We also present a prototype implementation of FOIL wrapped in a high-level declarative language and perform experiments showing that such a language can be used in practice.

paragraphs: Questions about a model's predictions take many forms, including which parts of an input suffice to justify a classification. This paper develops a logical foundation for expressing such explanation requests through a declarative language. The aim is to let users specify the explanation they want in a systematic way.

The proposed logic, FOIL, can express many simple but useful interpretability queries and could underpin richer languages. The authors analyze the computational cost of evaluating these queries on decision trees and more general decision diagrams. These models may seem easy to interpret, but the number of possible inputs grows exponentially with input dimension, making some explanation questions computationally delicate.

The analysis identifies ways to obtain tractable evaluation by restricting either model structure or the portion of the language being used. A prototype wraps FOIL in a higher-level declarative interface, and experiments demonstrate practical use. The contribution links expressiveness to computational feasibility: a common language can organize explanation requests, while its supported queries and target models determine how efficiently those requests can be answered.
summary.tldr: FOIL provides a logical language for model explanations and identifies restrictions that make explanation queries computationally tractable.

title: Foundations of Symbolic Languages for Model Interpretability

abstract: The CSGM framework (Bora-Jalal-Price-Dimakis'17) has shown that deepgenerative priors can be powerful tools for solving inverse problems.However, to date this framework has been empirically successful only oncertain datasets (for example, human faces and MNIST digits), and itis known to perform poorly on out-of-distribution samples. In thispaper, we present the first successful application of the CSGMframework on clinical MRI data. We train a generative prior on brainscans from the fastMRI dataset, and show that posterior sampling viaLangevin dynamics achieves high quality reconstructions. Furthermore,our experiments and theory show that posterior sampling is robust tochanges in the ground-truth distribution and measurement process.Our code and models are available at: \url{https://github.com/utcsilab/csgm-mri-langevin}.

paragraphs: This paper applies deep generative priors to reconstructing clinical MRI images within the CSGM framework. Such priors had shown promise for inverse problems, but their empirical successes had been concentrated on particular datasets, and poor performance on out-of-distribution samples was a known concern. The authors present what they describe as the framework's first successful clinical MRI application.

They train a generative prior on brain scans from fastMRI and reconstruct images using posterior sampling through Langevin dynamics. The prior supplies learned image information, while the posterior sampling procedure incorporates the reconstruction problem's measurements. The authors report that this combination produces high-quality reconstructions, extending the framework to the clinical imaging data studied.

The paper also examines robustness when either the ground-truth distribution or the measurement process changes. Both experiments and theory support robustness of posterior sampling to these changes. This makes the contribution broader than applying a learned prior to another dataset: it addresses the distribution and measurement sensitivity that motivated concern about the earlier framework.
summary.tldr: A learned brain-scan prior combined with Langevin posterior sampling yields high-quality MRI reconstructions and supported robustness to distribution and measurement changes.

title: Robust Compressed Sensing MRI with Deep Generative Priors

abstract: Hyperbolic space is particularly useful for embedding data with hierarchical structure; however, representing hyperbolic space with ordinary floating-point numbers greatly affects the performance due to its \emph{ineluctable} numerical errors. Simply increasing the precision of floats fails to solve the problem and incurs a high computation cost for simulating greater-than-double-precision floats on hardware such as GPUs, which does not support them. In this paper, we propose a simple, feasible-on-GPUs, and easy-to-understand solution for numerically accurate learning on hyperbolic space. We do this with a new approach to represent hyperbolic space using multi-component floating-point (MCF) in the Poincar{\'e} upper-half space model. Theoretically and experimentally we show our model has small numerical error, and on embedding tasks across various datasets, models represented by multi-component floating-points gain more capacity and run significantly faster on GPUs than prior work.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic space is useful for embedding hierarchical data, but its numerical representation can undermine learning. Ordinary floating-point arithmetic introduces errors that affect performance. The paper argues that simply increasing precision does not resolve the problem and can be expensive on GPUs that lack native support for precision beyond double.

The proposed solution represents hyperbolic space using multi-component floating-point values in the Poincaré upper-half-space model. This changes how the geometry is represented numerically while remaining feasible on GPUs. The authors present it as a simple approach to accurate learning in hyperbolic space, addressing the numerical representation directly.

Theoretical analysis and experiments show small numerical error for the proposed model. On embedding tasks across multiple datasets, representations using multi-component floats gain capacity and run significantly faster on GPUs than prior work. The findings connect numerical accuracy to practical modeling ability: a useful geometry must also be represented in a way that computation can handle reliably and efficiently.
summary.tldr: Multi-component floats enable accurate hyperbolic representations that improve embedding capacity and GPU speed in the evaluated tasks.

title: Representing Hyperbolic Space Accurately using Multi-Component Floats

abstract: Existing approaches for training neural networks with user-level differential privacy (e.g., DP Federated Averaging) in federated learning (FL) settings involve bounding the contribution of each user's model update by {\em clipping} it to some constant value. However there is no good {\em a priori} setting of the clipping norm across tasks and learning settings: the update norm distribution depends on the model architecture and loss, the amount of data on each device, the client learning rate, and possibly various other parameters. We propose a method wherein instead of a fixed clipping norm, one clips to a value at a specified quantile of the update norm distribution, where the value at the quantile is itself estimated online, with differential privacy. The method tracks the quantile closely, uses a negligible amount of privacy budget, is compatible with other federated learning technologies such as compression and secure aggregation, and has a straightforward joint DP analysis with DP-FedAvg. Experiments demonstrate that adaptive clipping to the median update norm works well across a range of federated learning tasks, eliminating the need to tune any clipping hyperparameter.

paragraphs: Federated learning with user-level differential privacy limits how much each user's model update can contribute. A common mechanism clips updates to a fixed maximum norm. Choosing that threshold beforehand is difficult because update sizes depend on the model, loss, data available on devices, learning rate, and other training choices.

This paper replaces the fixed threshold with an adaptive value drawn from a chosen quantile of the update-norm distribution. The quantile is estimated during training using differential privacy, so adaptation itself is included in the privacy accounting. The authors report that the estimate tracks the desired quantile closely while consuming a negligible amount of the privacy budget.

The method is compatible with compression and secure aggregation, and its privacy analysis can be combined directly with DP Federated Averaging. Experiments find that clipping at the median update norm works well across a range of federated tasks. In those evaluations, this removes the need to tune a clipping hyperparameter, simplifying an otherwise task-dependent part of private training.
summary.tldr: Privately tracking a quantile of user-update sizes provides an adaptive clipping threshold that works well across tested federated learning tasks.

title: Differentially Private Learning with Adaptive Clipping

abstract: Pre-training (PT) followed by fine-tuning (FT) is an effective method for training neural networks, and has led to significant performance improvements in many domains. PT can incorporate various design choices such as task and data reweighting strategies, augmentation policies, and noise models, all of which can significantly impact the quality of representations learned. The hyperparameters introduced by these strategies therefore must be tuned appropriately. However, setting the values of these hyperparameters is challenging. Most existing methods either struggle to scale to high dimensions, are too slow and memory-intensive, or cannot be directly applied to the two-stage PT and FT learning process. In this work, we propose an efficient, gradient-based algorithm to meta-learn PT hyperparameters. We formalize the PT hyperparameter optimization problem and propose a novel method to obtain PT hyperparameter gradients by combining implicit differentiation and backpropagation through unrolled optimization. We demonstrate that our method improves predictive performance on two real-world domains. First, we optimize high-dimensional task weighting hyperparameters for multitask pre-training on protein-protein interaction graphs and improve AUROC by up to 3.9%. Second, we optimize a data augmentation neural network for self-supervised PT with SimCLR on electrocardiography data and improve AUROC by up to 1.9%.

paragraphs: Pretraining depends on choices such as task weights, data weights, augmentation policies, and noise models. Those choices affect the representations a network later uses during fine-tuning. This paper asks how to learn their hyperparameters efficiently within the complete pretraining-then-fine-tuning process, including cases with many adjustable values.

The authors formulate the optimization problem and introduce a gradient-based meta-learning algorithm. It obtains pretraining hyperparameter gradients by combining implicit differentiation with backpropagation through unrolled optimization. The approach addresses a setting where existing techniques can struggle with dimensionality, computational cost, memory use, or the separation between the two training stages.

The method improves predictive performance in two applications. Learning high-dimensional task weights for multitask pretraining on protein-protein interaction graphs improves AUROC by up to 3.9%. Learning an augmentation network for SimCLR pretraining on electrocardiography data improves AUROC by up to 1.9%. These results support treating pretraining design choices as learnable components whose values can be optimized for the subsequent learning process.
summary.tldr: A gradient-based meta-learning method tunes pretraining hyperparameters and improves performance in graph and electrocardiography applications.

title: Meta-learning to Improve Pre-training

abstract: Reweighting adversarial data during training has been recently shown to improve adversarial robustness, where data closer to the current decision boundaries are regarded as more critical and given larger weights. However, existing methods measuring the closeness are not very reliable: they are discrete and can take only a few values, and they are path-dependent, i.e., they may change given the same start and end points with different attack paths. In this paper, we propose three types of probabilistic margin (PM), which are continuous and path-independent, for measuring the aforementioned closeness and reweighing adversarial data. Specifically, a PM is defined as the difference between two estimated class-posterior probabilities, e.g., such a probability of the true label minus the probability of the most confusing label given some natural data. Though different PMs capture different geometric properties, all three PMs share a negative correlation with the vulnerability of data: data with larger/smaller PMs are safer/riskier and should have smaller/larger weights. Experiments demonstrated that PMs are reliable and PM-based reweighting methods outperformed state-of-the-art counterparts.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can place greater weight on examples near a classifier's decision boundary, where predictions are more vulnerable. The challenge is measuring that closeness reliably. This paper identifies weaknesses in existing measures: they take only a few discrete values and can change with the attack path even when its endpoints stay the same.

The authors propose three probabilistic margins that are continuous and independent of the attack path. Each uses a difference between estimated class probabilities. One example subtracts the probability of the most confusing class from that of the true class. Although the three margins capture different geometric properties, all are negatively correlated with vulnerability.

This relationship supplies a weighting rule: smaller margins indicate riskier examples that should receive greater training weight, while larger margins indicate safer examples that should receive less. Experiments find the margins reliable and report that the resulting reweighting methods outperform state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution is a smoother, path-independent basis for directing adversarial training toward more vulnerable data.
summary.tldr: Continuous, path-independent probability margins improve how adversarial training identifies and emphasizes vulnerable examples.

title: Probabilistic Margins for Instance Reweighting in Adversarial Training

abstract: To promote better performance-bandwidth trade-off for multi-agent perception, we propose a novel distilled collaboration graph (DiscoGraph) to model trainable, pose-aware, and adaptive collaboration among agents. Our key novelties lie in two aspects. First, we propose a teacher-student framework to train DiscoGraph via knowledge distillation. The teacher model employs an early collaboration with holistic-view inputs; the student model is based on intermediate collaboration with single-view inputs. Our framework trains DiscoGraph by constraining post-collaboration feature maps in the student model to match the correspondences in the teacher model. Second, we propose a matrix-valued edge weight in DiscoGraph. In such a matrix, each element reflects the inter-agent attention at a specific spatial region, allowing an agent to adaptively highlight the informative regions. During inference, we only need to use the student model named as the distilled collaboration network (DiscoNet). Attributed to the teacher-student framework, multiple agents with the shared DiscoNet could collaboratively approach the performance of a hypothetical teacher model with a holistic view. Our approach is validated on V2X-Sim 1.0, a large-scale multi-agent perception dataset that we synthesized using CARLA and SUMO co-simulation. Our quantitative and qualitative experiments in multi-agent 3D object detection show that DiscoNet could not only achieve a better performance-bandwidth trade-off than the state-of-the-art collaborative perception methods, but also bring more straightforward design rationale. Our code is available on https://github.com/ai4ce/DiscoNet.

paragraphs: When multiple agents perceive a scene together, exchanging information can improve detection but consumes communication bandwidth. This paper learns a collaboration graph that adapts information sharing to agents' poses and the spatial regions that matter. Its aim is a better balance between perception performance and the amount of information agents must communicate.

Training uses a teacher with holistic-view inputs and early collaboration to guide a student that collaborates through intermediate features from single-view inputs. The student's features after collaboration are encouraged to match the teacher's corresponding features. Graph edges have matrix-valued weights, allowing attention between agents to vary across spatial regions instead of assigning one uniform importance to an entire connection.

At inference, only the student network, DiscoNet, is needed. The authors evaluate multi-agent 3D object detection on V2X-Sim 1.0, a dataset synthesized through CARLA and SUMO co-simulation. They report a better performance-bandwidth trade-off than state-of-the-art collaborative methods. The findings suggest that agents sharing the student model can approach a holistic-view teacher's performance through selective, learned collaboration.
summary.tldr: DiscoNet learns spatially selective collaboration from a holistic-view teacher to improve multi-agent perception's performance-bandwidth trade-off.

title: Learning Distilled Collaboration Graph for Multi-Agent Perception

abstract: Large-scale pre-trained language models have achieved tremendous success across a wide range of natural language understanding (NLU) tasks, even surpassing human performance. However, recent studies reveal that the robustness of these models can be challenged by carefully crafted textual adversarial examples. While several individual datasets have been proposed to evaluate model robustness, a principled and comprehensive benchmark is still missing. In this paper, we present Adversarial GLUE (AdvGLUE), a new multi-task benchmark to quantitatively and thoroughly explore and evaluate the vulnerabilities of modern large-scale language models under various types of adversarial attacks. In particular, we systematically apply 14 textual adversarial attack methods to GLUE tasks to construct AdvGLUE, which is further validated by humans for reliable annotations. Our ﬁndings are summarized as follows. (i) Most existing adversarial attack algorithms are prone to generating invalid or ambiguous adversarial examples, with around 90% of them either changing the original semantic meanings or misleading human annotators as well. Therefore, we perform a careful ﬁltering process to curate a high-quality benchmark. (ii) All the language models and robust training methods we tested perform poorly on AdvGLUE, with scores lagging far behind the benign accuracy. We hope our work will motivate the development of new adversarial attacks that are more stealthy and semantic-preserving, as well as new robust language models against sophisticated adversarial attacks. AdvGLUE is available at https://adversarialglue.github.io.

AdvGLUE addresses this issue with a benchmark spanning multiple GLUE tasks and different adversarial attacks. The authors apply 14 attack methods and use human validation to check the resulting examples and annotations.

That validation exposes a problem with the attacks themselves. Around 90% of generated examples either alter the original meaning or also mislead human annotators. Such examples complicate interpretation because an apparent model failure may involve an invalid or ambiguous test item. The authors therefore carefully filter the generated material to construct the benchmark.

All language models and robust training methods tested perform poorly on the curated AdvGLUE examples relative to their accuracy on ordinary inputs. This finding establishes a vulnerability among the evaluated systems while also showing why attack quality matters for measuring robustness. The benchmark supports research on both meaning-preserving attacks and models that remain reliable under those attacks.
summary.tldr: AdvGLUE uses human-filtered adversarial examples to reveal robustness weaknesses across tested language models and training methods.

title: Adversarial GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark for Robustness Evaluation of Language Models

abstract: In this paper, we address the "dual problem" of multi-view scene reconstruction in which we utilize single-view images captured under different point lights to learn a neural scene representation. Different from existing single-view methods which can only recover a 2.5D scene representation (i.e., a normal / depth map for the visible surface), our method learns a neural reflectance field to represent the 3D geometry and BRDFs of a scene. Instead of relying on multi-view photo-consistency, our method exploits two information-rich monocular cues, namely shading and shadow, to infer scene geometry. Experiments on multiple challenging datasets show that our method is capable of recovering 3D geometry, including both visible and invisible parts, of a scene from single-view images. Thanks to the neural reflectance field representation, our method is robust to depth discontinuities. It supports applications like novel-view synthesis and relighting. Our code and model can be found at https://ywq.github.io/s3nerf.

paragraphs: Recovering a three-dimensional scene usually benefits from viewing it from different positions. S³-NeRF instead uses multiple images taken from one viewpoint under different point lights. The changing illumination supplies evidence through shading and shadows, even though the camera position stays fixed.

The method learns a neural reflectance field representing both scene geometry and how surfaces reflect light. This goes beyond a depth or normal map describing only the visible surface. Its reconstruction process uses the two lighting cues to infer geometry, replacing the reliance on agreement between images captured from multiple viewpoints.

Experiments on challenging datasets show recovery of both visible and invisible portions of scene geometry. The representation is also reported to handle depth discontinuities robustly and support rendering from new viewpoints and under new lighting. These findings demonstrate the information available in changing illumination under the tested conditions. The input remains a set of differently lit images, so the single-view claim refers to a fixed viewpoint rather than a single photograph.
summary.tldr: S³-NeRF reconstructs geometry and reflectance from a fixed viewpoint under changing point lights by using shading and shadow cues.

title: S$^3$-NeRF: Neural Reflectance Field from Shading and Shadow under a Single Viewpoint

abstract: Latency is of utmost importance in safety-critical systems. In neural networks, lowest theoretical latency is dependent on the depth of the network. This begs the question -- is it possible to build high-performing ``non-deep" neural networks? We show that it is. To do so, we use parallel subnetworks instead of stacking one layer after another. This helps effectively reduce depth while maintaining high performance. By utilizing parallel substructures, we show, for the first time, that a network with a depth of just 12 can achieve top-1 accuracy over 80% on ImageNet, 96% on CIFAR10, and 81% on CIFAR100. We also show that a network with a low-depth (12) backbone can achieve an AP of 48% on MS-COCO. We analyze the scaling rules for our design and show how to increase performance without changing the network's depth. Finally, we provide a proof of concept for how non-deep networks could be used to build low-latency recognition systems. Code is available at https://github.com/imankgoyal/NonDeepNetworks.

paragraphs: Network depth places a constraint on the lowest theoretical latency because successive layers create a chain of dependent computations. This paper asks whether strong recognition performance can be achieved with relatively few such stages. Its proposed networks use parallel subnetworks to reduce depth while retaining high predictive performance.

The central architectural choice is to expand through parallel substructures rather than repeatedly adding successive layers. The authors also analyze scaling rules for this design, showing how performance can increase while depth remains fixed. This makes the arrangement of computation an explicit part of the tradeoff between recognition quality and potential latency.

A depth-12 network achieves top-1 accuracy above 80% on ImageNet, 96% on CIFAR10, and 81% on CIFAR100. A depth-12 backbone also achieves 48% average precision on MS-COCO. The paper provides a proof of concept for low-latency recognition systems using these networks. Together, these results demonstrate that the tested recognition tasks can support high performance with shallow sequential depth and substantial parallel structure.
summary.tldr: Parallel subnetworks enable strong image recognition with only 12 layers of depth and offer a route toward low-latency systems.

title: Non-deep Networks

abstract: We introduce HandMeThat, a benchmark for a holistic evaluation of instruction understanding and following in physical and social environments. While previous datasets primarily focused on language grounding and planning, HandMeThat considers the resolution of human instructions with ambiguities based on the physical (object states and relations) and social (human actions and goals) information. HandMeThat contains 10,000 episodes of human-robot interactions. In each episode, the robot first observes a trajectory of human actions towards her internal goal. Next, the robot receives a human instruction and should take actions to accomplish the subgoal set through the instruction. In this paper, we present a textual interface for our benchmark, where the robot interacts with a virtual environment through textual commands. We evaluate several baseline models on HandMeThat, and show that both offline and online reinforcement learning algorithms perform poorly on HandMeThat, suggesting significant room for future work on physical and social human-robot communications and interactions.

paragraphs: A robot may need more than the words of an instruction to understand what a person wants. HandMeThat evaluates instruction following when meaning depends on physical context, such as object states and relationships, and social context, such as the person's previous actions and goals. Resolving ambiguity is therefore part of the task itself.

The benchmark contains 10,000 episodes of human-robot interaction. In each episode, the robot observes a sequence of human actions directed toward an internal goal. The person then gives an instruction, and the robot must act to accomplish the requested subgoal. The paper presents a textual interface, through which the robot issues commands to a virtual environment.

This setup connects interpreting language with understanding an ongoing activity and planning appropriate actions. The evaluated baseline models include offline and online reinforcement learning algorithms, both of which perform poorly on the benchmark. Those results indicate substantial room for improvement on these tasks and motivate studying physical and social context together when evaluating human-robot communication.
summary.tldr: HandMeThat benchmarks whether robots can resolve ambiguous instructions using object information and the context of a person's actions and goals.

title: HandMeThat: Human-Robot Communication in Physical and Social Environments

abstract: We develop an algorithm which can learn from partially labeled and unsegmented sequential data. Most sequential loss functions, such as Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC), break down when many labels are missing. We address this problem with Star Temporal Classification (STC) which uses a special star token to allow alignments which include all possible tokens whenever a token could be missing. We express STC as the composition of weighted finite-state transducers (WFSTs) and use GTN (a framework for automatic differentiation with WFSTs) to compute gradients. We perform extensive experiments on automatic speech recognition. These experiments show that STC can close the performance gap with supervised baseline to about 1% WER when up to 70% of the labels are missing. We also perform experiments in handwriting recognition to show that our method easily applies to other temporal classification tasks.

paragraphs: Sequential training data can be incomplete in two ways: labels may lack timing information, and some labels may be missing altogether. Standard sequence losses such as Connectionist Temporal Classification struggle when many labels are absent. Star Temporal Classification, or STC, is designed to learn under both conditions.

STC introduces a special star token into the possible alignments between inputs and labels. Where a token may be missing, the star permits alternatives covering all possible tokens. The loss therefore accommodates unknown portions of the sequence. The authors express the computation using weighted finite-state transducers and use GTN to differentiate through those structures.

In speech-recognition experiments, STC narrows the gap to a supervised baseline to about 1% word error rate with up to 70% of labels missing. This describes a gap to the baseline, not an absolute error rate of 1%. Handwriting-recognition experiments also demonstrate applicability beyond speech. The results support incorporating missing-label possibilities directly into sequence alignment as a useful way to train from incomplete supervision.
summary.tldr: STC uses a wildcard-like star token to train sequence models when labels are missing and unaligned.

title: Star Temporal Classification: Sequence Modeling with Partially Labeled Data

abstract: Dealing with non-stationarity in environments (e.g., in the transition dynamics) and objectives (e.g., in the reward functions) is a challenging problem that is crucial in real-world applications of reinforcement learning (RL). While most current approaches model the changes as a single shared embedding vector, we leverage insights from the recent causality literature to model non-stationarity in terms of individual latent change factors, and causal graphs across different environments. In particular, we propose Factored Adaptation for Non-Stationary RL (FANS-RL), a factored adaption approach that learns jointly both the causal structure in terms of a factored MDP, and a factored representation of the individual time-varying change factors. We prove that under standard assumptions, we can completely recover the causal graph representing the factored transition and reward function, as well as a partial structure between the individual change factors and the state components. Through our general framework, we can consider general non-stationary scenarios with different function types and changing frequency, including changes across episodes and within episodes. Experimental results demonstrate that FANS-RL outperforms existing approaches in terms of return, compactness of the latent state representation, and robustness to varying degrees of non-stationarity.
