paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may encounter changes in how its environment behaves or in what it is rewarded for doing. Representing all such changes with one shared vector can obscure their separate influences. FANS-RL instead models non-stationarity through individual hidden change factors and causal relationships across environments.

The method jointly learns a factored representation of the decision process and representations of the time-varying factors. Under the paper's stated standard assumptions, the authors prove complete recovery of the causal graph describing factored transitions and rewards. They also establish recovery of a partial structure linking individual change factors to state components; that second recovery claim is explicitly more limited.

The framework accommodates different kinds and frequencies of change, including changes between episodes and during an episode. Experiments report better returns, more compact latent state representations, and greater robustness to differing degrees of non-stationarity than existing approaches. Together, the theory and experiments support separating sources of change as a useful way to adapt, while the structural recovery guarantee remains conditional on its assumptions.
summary.tldr: FANS-RL learns separate hidden change factors and causal structure to improve adaptation when reinforcement learning environments or rewards change.

title: Factored Adaptation for Non-Stationary Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Safe exploration is a challenging and important problem in model-free reinforcement learning (RL). Often the safety cost is sparse and unknown, which unavoidably leads to constraint violations - a phenomenon ideally to be avoided in safety-critical applications. We tackle this problem by augmenting the state-space with a safety state, which is nonnegative if and only if the constraint is satisfied. The value of this state also serves as a distance toward constraint violation, while its initial value indicates the available safety budget. This idea allows us to derive policies for scheduling the safety budget during training. We call our approach Simmer (Safe policy IMproveMEnt for RL) to reflect the careful nature of these schedules. We apply this idea to two safe RL problems: RL with constraints imposed on an average cost, and RL with constraints imposed on a cost with probability one. Our experiments suggest that "simmering" a safe algorithm can improve safety during training for both settings. We further show that Simmer can stabilize training and improve the performance of safe RL with average constraints.

paragraphs: Safe exploration is difficult when a reinforcement-learning agent encounters safety costs only occasionally and does not know them beforehand. The agent must learn while trying to respect constraints. This paper introduces an additional safety state that makes the available safety budget part of the information used during learning.

The safety state is nonnegative exactly when the constraint is satisfied. Its value also indicates distance toward a violation, and its starting value specifies the available budget. This representation lets the authors derive policies for scheduling that budget during training. Their approach, Simmer, therefore treats the management of safety allowance as an explicit part of the learning process.

The paper considers both constraints on average cost and constraints that must hold with probability one. Experiments suggest that adding Simmer to a safe-learning algorithm can improve training-time safety in both settings. For average-cost constraints, the authors also report more stable training and better performance. These findings support budget scheduling as a useful mechanism for safer learning, without establishing that exploratory violations disappear.
summary.tldr: Simmer adds a safety-budget state and schedules that budget to improve safety during reinforcement-learning training.

title: Enhancing Safe Exploration Using Safety State Augmentation

abstract: Periodic graphs are graphs consisting of repetitive local structures, such as crystal nets and polygon mesh. Their generative modeling has great potential in real-world applications such as material design and graphics synthesis. Classical models either rely on domain-specific predefined generation principles (e.g., in crystal net design), or follow geometry-based prescribed rules. Recently, deep generative models have shown great promise in automatically generating general graphs. However, their advancement into periodic graphs has not been well explored due to several key challenges in 1) maintaining graph periodicity; 2) disentangling local and global patterns; and 3) efficiency in learning repetitive patterns. To address them, this paper proposes Periodical-Graph Disentangled Variational Auto-encoder (PGD-VAE), a new deep generative model for periodic graphs that can automatically learn, disentangle, and generate local and global graph patterns. Specifically, we develop a new periodic graph encoder consisting of global-pattern encoder and local-pattern encoder that ensures to disentangle the representation into global and local semantics. We then propose a new periodic graph decoder consisting of local structure decoder, neighborhood decoder, and global structure decoder, as well as the assembler of their outputs that guarantees periodicity. Moreover, we design a new model learning objective that helps ensure the invariance of local-semantic representations for the graphs with the same local structure. Comprehensive experimental evaluations have been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Periodic graphs contain local structures that repeat, as in crystal networks and polygon meshes. Generating them requires more than producing plausible connections: the output must preserve repetition while representing both local structure and global organization. The paper addresses these requirements with a generative model intended to learn such patterns automatically.

PGD-VAE separates its encoder into components for local and global patterns. Its decoder likewise divides the work among local structure, neighborhood, and global structure components. An assembler combines their outputs in a way that guarantees periodicity. This architecture gives the repeated building blocks and their larger arrangement distinct roles in the generation process.

The training objective additionally encourages graphs with the same local structure to receive invariant local representations. That supports the intended separation between what repeats locally and how the overall graph is organized. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is an architecture that incorporates periodic structure into both representation learning and output construction, addressing obstacles that general graph generation alone does not resolve.
summary.tldr: PGD-VAE separately learns local and global graph patterns and assembles generated structures with guaranteed periodicity.

title: Deep Generative Model for Periodic Graphs

abstract: Understanding convergence of SGD-based optimization algorithms can help deal with enormous machine learning problems. To ensure last-iterate convergence of SGD and momentum-based SGD (mSGD), the existing studies usually constrain the step size $\epsilon_{n}$ to decay as $\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty}\epsilon_{n}^{2}<+\infty$, which however is rather conservative and may lead to slow convergence in the early stage of the iteration. In this paper, we relax this requirement by studying an alternate step size for the mSGD. First, we relax the requirement of the decay on step size to $\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty}\epsilon_{n}^{2+\eta_{0}}<+\infty\ (0\le\eta_{0}<1/2)$. This implies that a larger step size, such as $\epsilon_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ can be utilized for accelerating the mSGD in the early stage. Under this new step size and some common conditions, we prove that the gradient norm of mSGD for non-convex loss functions asymptotically decays to zero. In addition, we show that this step size can indeed help make the convergence into a neighborhood of the stationary points quicker in the early stage. In addition, we establish the convergence of mSGD under a constant step size $\epsilon_n\equiv\epsilon>0$ by removing the common requirement in the literature on the strong convexity of the loss function. Some experiments are given to illustrate the developed results.

paragraphs: Convergence analyses for stochastic gradient descent with momentum often require learning rates whose squared values have a finite sum. This forces the step size to shrink sufficiently quickly, potentially slowing early progress. This paper relaxes that requirement while studying convergence of the last iterate.

The new condition requires summability of step sizes raised to a power of two plus a parameter between zero and one-half, excluding one-half. With a suitable positive parameter, this permits a schedule proportional to one divided by the square root of the iteration count. Under this condition and additional common assumptions, the authors prove that gradient norms approach zero for nonconvex losses. They also show faster early arrival near stationary points.

A separate result studies constant step sizes and establishes convergence without the strong convexity requirement commonly imposed in prior work. Experiments illustrate the theoretical findings. The contribution broadens the step-size choices supported by analysis; the vanishing-gradient result for decaying steps should be distinguished from the separate constant-step convergence claim.
summary.tldr: The paper relaxes step-size decay requirements for momentum SGD while proving conditional convergence results and faster early progress.

title: Revisit last-iterate convergence of mSGD under milder requirement on step size

abstract: Many real-world domains require safe decision making in uncertain environments. In this work, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework for approaching this important problem. We consider a distribution over transition models, and apply a risk-averse perspective towards model uncertainty through the use of coherent distortion risk measures. We provide robustness guarantees for this framework by showing it is equivalent to a specific class of distributionally robust safe reinforcement learning problems. Unlike existing approaches to robustness in deep reinforcement learning, however, our formulation does not involve minimax optimization. This leads to an efficient, model-free implementation of our approach that only requires standard data collection from a single training environment. In experiments on continuous control tasks with safety constraints, we demonstrate that our framework produces robust performance and safety at deployment time across a range of perturbed test environments.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when decisions must satisfy safety constraints despite uncertainty about environmental dynamics. It represents that uncertainty with a distribution over transition models. A risk-averse perspective then accounts for unfavorable possibilities within this uncertainty, using coherent distortion risk measures.

The authors prove that their framework is equivalent to a specific class of distributionally robust safe reinforcement learning problems. This equivalence provides robustness guarantees for the formulation. At the same time, it avoids minimax optimization, enabling an efficient model-free implementation that uses standard data collection from a single training environment.

Experiments examine continuous-control tasks with safety constraints and test the learned behavior in perturbed environments. The reported results show robust performance and safety across a range of those deployment conditions. The significance is the combination of a theoretical robustness interpretation with a comparatively accessible training procedure. The guarantees concern the identified problem class, while the deployment findings provide empirical evidence across the tested perturbations.
summary.tldr: A risk-averse treatment of uncertain dynamics yields a safe reinforcement learning framework with distributional robustness guarantees and no minimax optimization.

title: Risk-Averse Model Uncertainty for Distributionally Robust Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Solar power harbors immense potential in mitigating climate change by substantially reducing CO$_{2}$ emissions. Nonetheless, the inherent variability of solar irradiance poses a significant challenge for seamlessly integrating solar power into the electrical grid. While the majority of prior research has centered on employing purely time series-based methodologies for solar forecasting, only a limited number of studies have taken into account factors such as cloud cover or the surrounding physical context.In this paper, we put forth a deep learning architecture designed to harness spatio-temporal context using satellite data, to attain highly accurate day-ahead time-series forecasting for any given station, with a particular emphasis on forecasting Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI). We also suggest a methodology to extract a distribution for each time step prediction, which can serve as a very valuable measure of uncertainty attached to the forecast. When evaluating models, we propose a testing scheme in which we separate particularly difficult examples from easy ones, in order to capture the model performances in crucial situations, which in the case of this study are the days suffering from varying cloudy conditions. Furthermore, we present a new multi-modal dataset gathering satellite imagery over a large zone and time series for solar irradiance and other related physical variables from multiple geographically diverse solar stations. Our approach exhibits robust performance in solar irradiance forecasting, including zero-shot generalization tests at unobserved solar stations, and holds great promise in promoting the effective integration of solar power into the grid.

paragraphs: Solar irradiance varies in ways that complicate the integration of solar power into electricity grids. A forecast based only on a station's time series may miss useful information about clouds and surrounding conditions. This paper develops a deep learning architecture that incorporates spatial and temporal context from satellite data for day-ahead forecasting, emphasizing Global Horizontal Irradiance.

The approach also extracts a predictive distribution for each forecast time step, providing uncertainty information alongside the forecast. Its evaluation separates difficult examples from easier ones, with changing cloud conditions defining particularly important challenging days. This makes performance in demanding conditions visible instead of folding it entirely into an overall result.

abstract: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) are a popular approach for safe control of nonlinear systems. In CBF-based control, the desired safety properties of the system are mapped to nonnegativity of a CBF, and the control input is chosen to ensure that the CBF remains nonnegative for all time. Recently, machine learning methods that represent CBFs as neural networks (neural control barrier functions, or NCBFs) have shown great promise due to the universal representability of neural networks. However, verifying that a learned CBF guarantees safety remains a challenging research problem. This paper presents novel exact conditions and algorithms for verifying safety of feedforward NCBFs with ReLU activation functions. The key challenge in doing so is that, due to the piecewise linearity of the ReLU function, the NCBF will be nondifferentiable at certain points, thus invalidating traditional safety verification methods that assume a smooth barrier function. We resolve this issue by leveraging a generalization of Nagumo's theorem for proving invariance of sets with nonsmooth boundaries to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for safety. Based on this condition, we propose an algorithm for safety verification of NCBFs that first decomposes the NCBF into piecewise linear segments and then solves a nonlinear program to verify safety of each segment as well as the intersections of the linear segments. We mitigate the complexity by only considering the boundary of the safe region and by pruning the segments with Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) and linear relaxation. We evaluate our approach through numerical studies with comparison to state-of-the-art SMT-based methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongchaoZhang-HZ/exactverif-reluncbf-nips23.

paragraphs: Control barrier functions describe safety through a nonnegative value that a controller must maintain over time. Neural networks can represent these functions flexibly, but learning a candidate does not itself verify safety. With ReLU networks, a specific obstacle is that the barrier has corners where derivatives are undefined, so verification methods requiring smoothness do not apply.

The paper derives necessary and sufficient safety conditions using a version of Nagumo's theorem that handles sets with nonsmooth boundaries. Its verification algorithm decomposes the neural barrier into linear pieces and solves nonlinear programs to check the pieces and their intersections. Checking intersections is central because they include the places where smooth reasoning breaks down.

To reduce computation, the algorithm concentrates on the safe region's boundary and prunes pieces using interval bound propagation and linear relaxation. Numerical studies compare it with state-of-the-art SMT-based approaches. The main contribution is an exact verification framework tailored to feedforward ReLU barriers, including their nondifferentiable structure.
summary.tldr: The paper derives exact safety conditions and verification algorithms that account for the corners in ReLU neural control barrier functions.

title: Exact Verification of ReLU Neural Control Barrier Functions

abstract: We consider the problem of Learning from Label Proportions (LLP), a weakly supervised classification setup where instances are grouped into i.i.d. “bags”, and only the frequency of class labels at each bag is available. Albeit, the objective of the learner is to achieve low task loss at an individual instance level. Here we propose EASYLLP, a flexible and simple-to-implement debiasing approach based on aggregate labels, which operates on arbitrary loss functions. Our technique allows us to accurately estimate the expected loss of an arbitrary model at an individual level. We elucidate the differences between our method and standard methods based on label proportion matching, in terms of applicability and optimality conditions. We showcase the flexibility of our approach compared to alternatives by applying our method to popular learning frameworks, like Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with provable guarantees on instance level performance. Finally, we validate our theoretical results on multiple datasets, empirically illustrating the conditions under which our algorithm is expected to perform better or worse than previous LLP approaches

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions provides group-level supervision: examples arrive in independently and identically distributed bags, and only each bag’s class frequencies are known. The learner nevertheless needs to classify individual examples well. This creates a mismatch between the information available during training and the individual-level loss that the learner ultimately wants to minimize.

EASYLLP addresses that mismatch through a debiasing method based on aggregate labels. It can operate with arbitrary loss functions and accurately estimate a model’s expected individual-level loss. The paper contrasts this approach with methods that train by matching bag proportions, examining differences in where the methods apply and the conditions under which they are optimal.

The authors integrate their method into empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent, with provable guarantees for performance on individual instances. Experiments across multiple datasets support the theory and illustrate circumstances where EASYLLP should do better or worse than earlier approaches. The contribution is thus a flexible way to train against the desired individual objective, with explicitly conditional comparative benefits.
summary.tldr: EASYLLP uses aggregate class proportions to debias individual-level loss estimates and support standard learning methods with performance guarantees.

title: Easy Learning from Label Proportions

abstract: Attractor networks require neuronal connections to be highly structured in order to maintain attractor states that represent information, while excitation and inhibition balanced networks (E-INNs) require neuronal connections to be random and sparse to generate irregular neuronal firings. Despite being regarded as canonical models of neural circuits, both types of networks are usually studied in isolation, and it remains unclear how they coexist in the brain, given their very different structural demands. In this study, we investigate the compatibility of continuous attractor neural networks (CANNs) and E-INNs. In line with recent experimental data, we find that a neural circuit can exhibit both the traits of CANNs and E-INNs if the neuronal synapses consist of two sets: one set is strong and fast for irregular firing, and the other set is weak and slow for attractor dynamics. Our results from simulations and theoretical analysis reveal that the network also exhibits enhanced performance compared to the case of using only one set of synapses, with accelerated convergence of attractor states and retained E-I balanced condition for localized input. We also apply the network model to solve a real-world tracking problem and demonstrate that it can track fast-moving objects well. We hope that this study provides insight into how structured neural computations are realized by irregular firings of neurons.

paragraphs: Attractor networks represent information through persistent activity states supported by structured connections. Excitation–inhibition balanced networks instead use sparse, random connections to generate irregular firing. This paper asks how those two familiar descriptions of neural circuits can coexist despite their different structural demands.

The proposed circuit uses two sets of synapses with different strengths and timescales. Strong, fast connections support irregular firing, while weak, slow connections support continuous attractor dynamics. Simulations and theoretical analysis show that this arrangement can exhibit both kinds of behavior within the same network, consistent with the experimental picture described by the authors.

Compared with using only one set of synapses, the combined network reaches attractor states faster and preserves excitation–inhibition balance under localized input. The authors also apply it to a real-world tracking problem and demonstrate successful tracking of fast-moving objects. These findings offer a mechanism by which structured computation and irregular neural activity can work together, with their coexistence improving the studied network’s computational behavior.
summary.tldr: Separate fast, strong and slow, weak synapses allow a neural circuit to combine irregular balanced firing with useful attractor computation.

title: Slow and Weak Attractor Computation Embedded in Fast and Strong E-I Balanced Neural Dynamics

abstract: We present D$^2$CSG, a neural model composed of two dual and complementary network branches, with dropouts, for unsupervised learning of compact constructive solid geometry (CSG) representations of 3D CAD shapes. Our network is trained to reconstruct a 3D shape by a fixed-order assembly of quadric primitives, with both branches producing a union of primitive intersections or inverses. A key difference between D$^2$CSG and all prior neural CSG models is its dedicated residual branch to assemble the potentially complex shape complement, which is subtracted from an overall shape modeled by the cover branch. With the shape complements, our network is provably general, while the weight dropout further improves compactness of the CSG tree by removing redundant primitives. We demonstrate both quantitatively and qualitatively that D$^2$CSG produces compact CSG reconstructions with superior quality and more natural primitives than all existing alternatives, especially over complex and high-genus CAD shapes.

paragraphs: Constructive solid geometry represents a shape through combinations of simpler geometric pieces. D²CSG learns compact representations of 3D CAD shapes without supervision, training a neural network to reconstruct shapes through a fixed sequence of operations on quadric primitives. The aim is to recover both the shape and a concise construction describing it.

The network has two complementary branches. A cover branch builds an overall shape, while a residual branch constructs a potentially complicated complement that is subtracted from that cover. Each branch assembles unions of primitive intersections or inverses. The authors prove generality of the representation using these complements, making subtraction a central source of expressive power.

Weight dropout helps remove redundant primitives, improving the compactness of the resulting construction tree. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show better reconstruction quality, more natural primitives, and compact representations compared with the existing alternatives considered. The reported strengths are especially apparent for complex CAD shapes and shapes with many holes. The method combines an expressive representation with a mechanism for reducing unnecessary geometric components.
summary.tldr: D²CSG reconstructs CAD shapes using complementary geometric branches and dropout to produce expressive, compact construction trees.

title: D$^2$CSG: Unsupervised Learning of Compact CSG Trees with Dual Complements and Dropouts

abstract: We present a new combinatorial bandit model, the \textit{cascading contextual assortment bandit}. This model serves as a generalization of both existing cascading bandits and assortment bandits, broadening their applicability in practice. For this model, we propose our first UCB bandit algorithm, UCB-CCA. We prove that this algorithm achieves a $T$-step regret upper-bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{1}{\kappa}d\sqrt{T})$, sharper than existing bounds for cascading contextual bandits by eliminating dependence on cascade length $K$. To improve the dependence on problem-dependent constant $\kappa$, we introduce our second algorithm, UCB-CCA+, which leverages a new Bernstein-type concentration result. This algorithm achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ without dependence on $\kappa$ in the leading term. We substantiate our theoretical claims with numerical experiments, demonstrating the practical efficacy of our proposed methods.

We prove that this algorithm achieves a $T$-step regret upper-bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{1}{\kappa}d\sqrt{T})$, sharper than existing bounds for cascading contextual bandits by eliminating dependence on cascade length $K$. paragraphs: This paper introduces a bandit model that brings together cascading bandits and assortment bandits. The combined model, called cascading contextual assortment bandits, broadens the decision settings these existing formulations can represent. The authors develop two algorithms and analyze regret, which measures the accumulated cost of learning rather than making the best decisions throughout.

The first algorithm, UCB-CCA, has a regret upper bound scaling as d times the square root of T, divided by a problem-dependent constant kappa, up to logarithmic factors. Its improvement over existing cascading contextual bandit bounds is the removal of dependence on cascade length K. Thus, cascade length no longer appears as a factor in this guarantee.

The second algorithm, UCB-CCA+, uses a new Bernstein-type concentration result to sharpen the treatment of uncertainty. Its leading regret term scales as d times the square root of T without dependence on kappa, again up to logarithmic factors. This is specifically a leading-term improvement. Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms for a unified cascading assortment bandit model improve regret bounds by removing cascade-length and leading-term kappa dependence.

title: Cascading Contextual Assortment Bandits

abstract: Recent advances in egocentric video understanding models are promising, but their heavy computational expense is a barrier for many real-world applications. To address this challenge, we propose EgoDistill, a distillation-based approach that learns to reconstruct heavy ego-centric video clip features by combining the semantics from a sparse set of video frames with head motion from lightweight IMU readings. We further devise a novel IMU-based self-supervised pretraining strategy. Our method leads to significant improvements in efficiency, requiring 200× fewer GFLOPs than equivalent video models. We demonstrate its effectiveness on the Ego4D and EPIC- Kitchens datasets, where our method outperforms state-of-the-art efficient video understanding methods.

paragraphs: Understanding video captured from a person's viewpoint can require computationally expensive models. EgoDistill addresses this cost by combining information from a sparse set of video frames with head-motion measurements from an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. The aim is to preserve useful information from a heavy video model while requiring substantially less computation.

The approach uses distillation: it learns to reconstruct the video-clip features produced by the heavier model. Sparse frames supply semantic information about the scene, while lightweight IMU readings supply head-motion information. Their combination provides the inputs for reconstructing those features. The authors also introduce an IMU-based self-supervised pretraining strategy as another component of the method.

Evaluations on Ego4D and EPIC-KITCHENS show that EgoDistill outperforms the compared state-of-the-art efficient video-understanding methods. The paper reports requiring 200 times fewer GFLOPs than equivalent video models. This is a reduction in computational operations, and the stated findings support the value of combining visual semantics with motion measurements for efficient egocentric understanding. The result specifically concerns an approach that has access to both frames and IMU readings.
summary.tldr: EgoDistill combines sparse video frames with IMU head-motion readings to reconstruct heavy video features using 200 times fewer GFLOPs.

title: EgoDistill: Egocentric Head Motion Distillation for Efficient Video Understanding

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has great potential for molecular representation learning given the complexity of molecular graphs, the large amounts of unlabelled data available, the considerable cost of obtaining labels experimentally, and the hence often only small training datasets. The importance of the topic is reflected in the variety of paradigms and architectures that have been investigated recently, most focus on designing views for contrastive learning.In this paper, we study SSL based on persistent homology (PH), a mathematical tool for modeling topological features of data that persist across multiple scales. It has several unique features which particularly suit SSL, naturally offering: different views of the data, stability in terms of distance preservation, and the opportunity to flexibly incorporate domain knowledge.We (1) investigate an autoencoder, which shows the general representational power of PH, and (2) propose a contrastive loss that complements existing approaches. We rigorously evaluate our approach for molecular property prediction and demonstrate its particular features in improving the embedding space:after SSL, the representations are better and offer considerably more predictive power than the baselines over different probing tasks; our loss increases baseline performance, sometimes largely; and we often obtain substantial improvements over very small datasets, a common scenario in practice.

paragraphs: Molecular learning often has plentiful unlabeled data but few experimentally obtained labels. Self-supervised learning can help, although choosing useful views of a molecule is a central design problem. This paper studies persistent homology, a mathematical tool that describes topological features surviving across multiple scales, as a foundation for learning molecular representations.

Persistent homology offers multiple views of data, stability in preserving distances, and flexibility for incorporating domain knowledge. The authors investigate an autoencoder to assess its representational power and propose a contrastive loss that complements existing methods. These two components examine both what the topological representation can capture and how it can improve other self-supervised approaches.

Evaluations on molecular property prediction find more predictive representations across different probing tasks after self-supervised learning. Adding the proposed loss improves baseline performance, sometimes substantially, and the method often produces substantial gains on very small datasets. These qualified findings are especially relevant to molecular applications where obtaining labels is costly and the available supervised training set is limited.
summary.tldr: Persistent homology supplies multiscale molecular representations and a complementary contrastive loss that improve property prediction, often on very small datasets.

title: Improving Self-supervised Molecular Representation Learning using Persistent Homology

abstract: In-context learning is a surprising and important phenomenon that emerged when modern language models were scaled to billions of learned parameters. Without modifying a large language model's weights, it can be tuned to perform various downstream natural language tasks simply by including concatenated training examples of these tasks in its input. Though disruptive for many practical applications of large language models, this emergent learning paradigm is not well understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we propose a first-of-its-kind PAC based framework for in-context learnability, and use it to provide the first finite sample complexity results for the in-context learning setup. Our framework includes an initial pretraining phase, which fits a function to the pretraining distribution, and then a second in-context learning phase, which keeps this function constant and concatenates training examples of the downstream task in its input. We use our framework in order to prove that, under mild assumptions, when the pretraining distribution is a mixture of latent tasks (a model often considered for natural language pretraining), these tasks can be efficiently learned via in-context learning, even though the model's weights are unchanged and the input significantly diverges from the pretraining distribution. Our theoretical analysis reveals that in this setting, in-context learning is more about identifying the task than about learning it, a result which is in line with a series of recent empirical findings. We hope that the in-context learnability framework presented in this paper will facilitate future progress towards a deeper understanding of this important new learning paradigm.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model respond to task examples placed in its input without changing its weights. This paper gives the phenomenon a theoretical framework based on probably approximately correct learning. The framework supports finite-sample complexity results, addressing how much example data is needed for the analyzed learning setup.

The model has two stages: pretraining fits a function to a distribution, and the in-context stage holds that function fixed while adding downstream examples to its input. Under mild assumptions, the authors prove efficient in-context learnability when pretraining data come from a mixture of latent tasks. This holds even though the resulting input differs substantially from the pretraining distribution.

The analysis indicates that, in this setting, the examples primarily help identify which task is being requested. This explains how useful adaptation can occur with unchanged weights: pretraining has already established the relevant task structure. The conclusion is specific to the analyzed latent-task setting and agrees with empirical findings cited by the authors, providing a theoretical basis for understanding this form of adaptation.
summary.tldr: A PAC framework proves efficient in-context learning under latent-task assumptions and explains it primarily as identifying the task.

title: The Learnability of In-Context Learning

abstract: We reconsider the challenge of non-convex optimization under differential privacy constraint. Building upon the previous variance-reduced algorithm SpiderBoost, we propose a novel framework that employs two types of gradient oracles: one that estimates the gradient at a single point and a more cost-effective option that calculates the gradient difference between two points. Our framework can ensure continuous accuracy of gradient estimations and subsequently enhances the rates of identifying second-order stationary points.Additionally, we consider a more challenging task by attempting to locate the global minima of a non-convex objective via the exponential mechanism without almost any assumptions. Our preliminary results suggest that the regularized exponential mechanism can effectively emulate previous empirical and population risk bounds, negating the need for smoothness assumptions for algorithms with polynomial running time. Furthermore, with running time factors excluded, the exponential mechanism demonstrates promising population risk bound performance, and we provide a nearly matching lower bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies non-convex optimization under differential privacy, where learning must satisfy a privacy constraint while navigating an objective that can have multiple local structures. One focus is finding second-order stationary points. Building on SpiderBoost, the authors seek to improve the accuracy of gradient information used throughout optimization.

Their framework combines two gradient oracles: one estimates the gradient at a single point, while a cheaper oracle estimates the gradient difference between two points. Maintaining accurate gradient estimates through this combination improves the rates for identifying second-order stationary points. The contribution concerns how optimization obtains and reuses gradient information under privacy requirements.

The paper separately investigates global minimization using the exponential mechanism under very few assumptions. Preliminary results suggest that a regularized version can match previous empirical and population risk bounds without smoothness assumptions for polynomial-time algorithms. When running-time factors are set aside, the authors also obtain promising population risk bounds and a nearly matching lower bound. These conclusions distinguish computationally constrained results from statistical performance considered without those time factors.
summary.tldr: A two-oracle framework improves private non-convex optimization rates, while exponential-mechanism results explore global risk guarantees under weak assumptions.

title: Private (Stochastic) Non-Convex Optimization Revisited: Second-Order Stationary Points and Excess Risks

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a powerful tool for generating high-quality images from textual descriptions. Despite their successes, these models often exhibit limited diversity in the sampled images, particularly when sampling with a high classifier-free guidance weight. To address this issue, we present Kaleido, a novel approach that enhances the diversity of samples by incorporating autoregressive latent priors. Kaleido integrates an autoregressive language model that encodes the original caption and generates latent variables, serving as abstract and intermediary representations for guiding and facilitating the image generation process.In this paper, we explore a variety of discrete latent representations, including textual descriptions, detection bounding boxes, object blobs, and visual tokens. These representations diversify and enrich the input conditions to the diffusion models, enabling more diverse outputs.Our experimental results demonstrate that Kaleido effectively broadens the diversity of the generated image samples from a given textual description while maintaining high image quality. Furthermore, we show that Kaleido adheres closely to the guidance provided by the generated latent variables, demonstrating its capability to effectively control and direct the image generation process.

These representations diversify and enrich the input conditions to the diffusion models, enabling more diverse outputs.Our experimental results demonstrate that Kaleido effectively broadens the diversity of the generated image samples from a given textual description while maintaining high image quality. Furthermore, we show that Kaleido adheres closely to the guidance provided by the generated latent variables, demonstrating its capability to effectively control and direct the image generation process.

paragraphs: Text-conditioned diffusion models can produce high-quality images while showing limited variety across samples from the same description. The paper highlights this issue particularly when classifier-free guidance is strong. Kaleido addresses it by introducing generated intermediate representations between the original caption and the image-generation process.

An autoregressive language model encodes the caption and generates latent variables that provide additional guidance to the diffusion model. The authors investigate several discrete forms for these variables: textual descriptions, detection bounding boxes, object blobs, and visual tokens. These intermediates enrich and diversify the conditions supplied to the image generator, allowing one caption to lead to different guided outputs.

Experiments show greater diversity among images generated from a given description while maintaining high image quality. The generated images also closely follow the latent guidance. That finding matters because the intermediate representations serve two related purposes: they introduce variation and provide a way to direct the result. Kaleido therefore connects diversity improvements with controllability through the same generated conditioning stage.
summary.tldr: Kaleido generates intermediate latent guidance from captions to increase diffusion-image diversity while maintaining quality and control.

title: Kaleido Diffusion: Improving Conditional Diffusion Models with Autoregressive Latent Modeling

abstract: Capitalizing on the complementary advantages of generative and discriminative models has always been a compelling vision in machine learning, backed by a growing body of research. This work discloses the hidden semantic structure within score-based generative models, unveiling their potential as effective discriminative priors. Inspired by our theoretical findings, we propose DUSA to exploit the structured semantic priors underlying diffusion score to facilitate the test-time adaptation of image classifiers or dense predictors. Notably, DUSA extracts knowledge from a single timestep of denoising diffusion, lifting the curse of Monte Carlo-based likelihood estimation over timesteps. We demonstrate the efficacy of our DUSA in adapting a wide variety of competitive pre-trained discriminative models on diverse test-time scenarios. Additionally, a thorough ablation study is conducted to dissect the pivotal elements in DUSA. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/BIT-DA/DUSA.

This paper investigates that connection through the score used in score-based generative models. Its theoretical findings reveal semantic structure within the score, suggesting that generative knowledge can serve as a useful prior for discriminative prediction.

The proposed method, DUSA, uses these structured semantic priors to adapt pretrained classifiers and dense predictors at test time. A central design feature is that it extracts knowledge from a single denoising timestep. This avoids relying on Monte Carlo likelihood estimation across diffusion timesteps, making that single-step source of semantic information central to the approach.

The authors demonstrate adaptation across a variety of competitive pretrained discriminative models and diverse test-time scenarios. They also conduct ablations to examine which components matter to DUSA. The reported findings support the usefulness of diffusion-score structure beyond generation: information within a generative model can guide adaptation of existing predictors when they encounter test-time data.
summary.tldr: DUSA uses semantic structure in a diffusion model's score to adapt pretrained visual predictors using knowledge from one denoising timestep.

title: Exploring Structured Semantic Priors Underlying Diffusion Score for Test-time Adaptation

abstract: Articulated object manipulation in real images is a fundamental step in computer and robotic vision tasks. Recently, several image editing methods based on diffusion models have been proposed to manipulate articulated objects according to text prompts. However, these methods often generate weird artifacts or even fail in real images. To this end, we introduce the Part-Aware Diffusion Model to approach the manipulation of articulated objects in real images. First, we develop Abstract 3D Models to represent and manipulate articulated objects efficiently. Then we propose dynamic feature maps to transfer the appearance of objects from input images to edited ones, meanwhile generating the novel-appearing parts reasonably. Extensive experiments are provided to illustrate the advanced manipulation capabilities of our method concerning state-of-the-art editing works. Additionally, we verify our method on 3D articulated object understanding forembodied robot scenarios and the promising results prove that our method supports this task strongly. The project page is https://mvig-rhos.com/pa_diffusion.

paragraphs: Editing the pose of an articulated object requires coordinating its movable parts while preserving a convincing image. The paper observes that text-driven diffusion editors can produce artifacts or fail when attempting such changes in real images. It introduces a Part-Aware Diffusion Model that explicitly represents the object's articulated structure during manipulation.

The approach uses Abstract 3D Models to represent and manipulate articulated objects efficiently. It then uses dynamic feature maps to transfer the object's appearance from the original image to the edited result. These maps also help generate parts that become newly visible after manipulation. This addresses both the structural change and the need to make newly appearing content fit the object.

The authors report extensive experiments demonstrating advanced manipulation capabilities relative to state-of-the-art image-editing work. They also evaluate the method for understanding 3D articulated objects in embodied robot scenarios, obtaining promising results. Together, these findings support the value of combining a manipulable 3D abstraction with appearance transfer for image editing and the tested object-understanding task.
summary.tldr: Part-aware diffusion combines abstract 3D structure and appearance transfer to edit articulated objects in real images.

title: General Articulated Objects Manipulation in Real Images via Part-Aware Diffusion Process

abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has become the standard for customising Foundation Models (FMs) to user-specific downstream tasks. However, typical PEFT methods require storing multiple task-specific adapters, creating scalability issues as these adapters must be housed and run at the FM server. Traditional prompt tuning offers a potential solution by customising them through task-specific input prefixes, but it under-performs compared to other PEFT methods like LoRA. To address this gap, we propose Low-Rank Prompt Adaptation (LoPA), a prompt-tuning-based approach that performs on par with state-of-the-art PEFT methods and full fine-tuning while being more parameter-efficient and not requiring a server-based adapter. LoPA generates soft prompts by balancing between sharing task-specific information across instances and customization for each instance. It uses a low-rank decomposition of the soft-prompt component encoded for each instance to achieve parameter efficiency. We provide a comprehensive evaluation on multiple natural language understanding and code generation and understanding tasks across a wide range of foundation models with varying sizes.

paragraphs: Customizing foundation models with small task-specific adapters reduces training costs, but those adapters still need to be stored and run at the model server. Prompt tuning offers another route by placing task-specific information in input prefixes. Its drawback is that traditional approaches perform worse than alternatives such as LoRA.

Low-Rank Prompt Adaptation, or LoPA, aims to close that performance gap while retaining prompt-based customization. It generates soft prompts that combine information shared across a task with information tailored to each individual instance. A low-rank decomposition of the instance-specific prompt component keeps the number of parameters small.

The authors evaluate LoPA across natural-language understanding and code generation and understanding tasks, using foundation models of different sizes. They report performance comparable to leading parameter-efficient methods and full fine-tuning, with greater parameter efficiency and no need for a server-based adapter. The approach matters because it connects effective customization to the input interface while explicitly balancing reusable task knowledge with adaptation to the current example.
summary.tldr: LoPA uses low-rank, instance-adapted soft prompts to achieve competitive model customization without server-based adapters.

title: Prompt Tuning Strikes Back: Customizing Foundation Models with Low-Rank Prompt Adaptation

abstract: Neural functional networks (NFNs) have recently gained significant attention due to their diverse applications, ranging from predicting network generalization and network editing to classifying implicit neural representation. Previous NFN designs often depend on permutation symmetries in neural networks' weights, which traditionally arise from the unordered arrangement of neurons in hidden layers. However, these designs do not take into account the weight scaling symmetries of $\operatorname{ReLU}$ networks, and the weight sign flipping symmetries of $\operatorname{sin}$ or $\operatorname{Tanh}$ networks. In this paper, we extend the study of the group action on the network weights from the group of permutation matrices to the group of monomial matrices by incorporating scaling/sign-flipping symmetries. Particularly, we encode these scaling/sign-flipping symmetries by designing our corresponding equivariant and invariant layers. We name our new family of NFNs the Monomial Matrix Group Equivariant Neural Functional Networks (Monomial-NFN). Because of the expansion of the symmetries, Monomial-NFN has much fewer independent trainable parameters compared to the baseline NFNs in the literature, thus enhancing the model's efficiency. Moreover, for fully connected and convolutional neural networks, we theoretically prove that all groups that leave these networks invariant while acting on their weight spaces are some subgroups of the monomial matrix group. We provide empirical evidences to demonstrate the advantages of our model over existing baselines, achieving competitive performance and efficiency. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MathematicalAI-NUS/Monomial-NFN.

Their design often accounts for the fact that reordering hidden neurons can preserve a network's function. This paper expands that treatment to additional weight symmetries associated with different activation functions.

Monomial-NFN incorporates scaling symmetries of ReLU networks and sign-flipping symmetries of sine or Tanh networks. It does so through equivariant and invariant layers built around monomial matrix groups, which extend permutation groups. Encoding these additional relationships reduces the number of independent trainable parameters relative to the baseline neural functional networks considered.

Experiments show competitive performance and efficiency against existing baselines. The broader design lesson is that recognizing more ways to represent the same underlying network function can impose useful structure on a model that operates on network weights.
summary.tldr: Monomial-NFN incorporates permutation, scaling, and sign-flipping symmetries to process neural-network weights with fewer independent parameters.

title: Monomial Matrix Group Equivariant Neural Functional Networks

abstract: A natural strategy for continual learning is to weigh a Bayesian ensemble of fixed functions. This suggests that if a (single) neural network could be interpreted as an ensemble, one could design effective algorithms that learn without forgetting. To realize this possibility, we observe that a neural network classifier with N parameters can be interpreted as a weighted ensemble of N classifiers, and that in the lazy regime limit these classifiers are fixed throughout learning. We call these classifiers the *neural tangent experts* and show they output valid probability distributions over the labels. We then derive the likelihood and posterior probability of each expert given past data. Surprisingly, the posterior updates for these experts are equivalent to a scaled and projected form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) over the network weights. Away from the lazy regime, networks can be seen as ensembles of adaptive experts which improve over time. These results offer a new interpretation of neural networks as Bayesian ensembles of experts, providing a principled framework for understanding and mitigating catastrophic forgetting in continual learning settings.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires incorporating new observations while retaining useful information from earlier ones. This paper approaches that problem by interpreting a single neural-network classifier as a Bayesian ensemble. The motivating idea is that updating weights over fixed predictors offers a principled way to accumulate evidence from successive data without changing the predictors themselves.

The authors show that a network with N parameters can be represented as a weighted collection of N neural tangent experts. Each expert produces a valid probability distribution over labels. In the lazy-regime limit, these experts remain fixed during learning. The paper derives their likelihoods and posterior probabilities given previously observed data.

The resulting Bayesian posterior updates correspond to a scaled and projected version of stochastic gradient descent on the network weights. Outside the lazy regime, the interpretation changes to an ensemble of adaptive experts that improve over time. This connection provides a framework for understanding and mitigating forgetting, while making clear that the fixed-expert interpretation depends on the lazy-regime limit.
summary.tldr: A neural network can be interpreted as a Bayesian ensemble whose expert updates connect to modified stochastic gradient descent.

title: Continual learning with the neural tangent ensemble

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a cornerstone of large language model (LLM) functionality, yet its theoretical foundations remain elusive due to the complexity of transformer architectures. In particular, most existing work only theoretically explains how the attention mechanism facilitates ICL under certain data models. It remains unclear how the other building blocks of the transformer contribute to ICL. To address this question, we study how a two-attention-layer transformer is trained to perform ICL on $n$-gram Markov chain data, where each token in the Markov chain statistically depends on the previous n tokens. We analyze a sophisticated transformer model featuring relative positional embedding, multi-head softmax attention, and a feed-forward layer with normalization. We prove that the gradient flow with respect to a cross-entropy ICL loss converges to a limiting model that performs a generalized version of the "induction head" mechanism with a learned feature, resulting from the congruous contribution of all the building blocks. Specifically, the first attention layer acts as a copier, copying past tokens within a given window to each position, and the feed-forward network with normalization acts as a selector that generates a feature vector by only looking at informationally relevant parents from the window. Finally, the second attention layer is a classifier thatcompares these features with the feature at the output position, and uses the resulting similarity scores to generate the desired output. Our theory is further validated by simulation experiments.

summary.tldr: For a two-attention-layer transformer on Markov-chain data, the authors prove that training yields coordinated copying, feature selection, and induction-style prediction.

title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers

abstract: Embedders play a central role in machine learning, projecting any object into numerical representations that can, in turn, be leveraged to perform various downstream tasks. The evaluation of embedding models typically depends on domain-specific empirical approaches utilizing downstream tasks, primarily because of the lack of a standardized framework for comparison. However, acquiring adequately large and representative datasets for conducting these assessments is not always viable and can prove to be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. In this paper, we present a unified approach to evaluate embedders. First, we establish theoretical foundations for comparing embedding models, drawing upon the concepts of sufficiency and informativeness. We then leverage these concepts to devise a tractable comparison criterion (information sufficiency), leading to a task-agnostic and self-supervised ranking procedure. We demonstrate experimentally that our approach aligns closely with the capability of embedding models to facilitate various downstream tasks in both natural language processing and molecular biology. This effectively offers practitioners a valuable tool for prioritizing model trials.

paragraphs: Embedding models convert objects into numerical representations that can support many downstream tasks. Comparing them usually requires task-specific experiments and sufficiently representative datasets. Those evaluations can be expensive or difficult to organize. This paper develops a common comparison framework intended to help identify promising embedding models before investing in extensive downstream testing.

The theoretical foundation uses sufficiency and informativeness to reason about the information represented by different embedders. From these concepts, the authors derive a tractable criterion called information sufficiency. This criterion supports a self-supervised ranking procedure that is independent of a particular downstream task, offering a shared basis for comparison across candidate models.

Experiments in natural language processing and molecular biology show that the resulting rankings align closely with embedding models' ability to support downstream tasks. This empirical alignment makes the method useful for prioritizing model trials. The stated result is a practical screening tool supported across these domains; it does not establish that the ranking must identify the best model for every possible task.
summary.tldr: An information-sufficiency criterion ranks embedding models without a specific downstream task and empirically helps identify promising models to test.

title: When is an Embedding Model More Promising than Another?

abstract: The distribution of pedestrian trajectories is highly complex and influenced by the scene, nearby pedestrians, and subjective intentions. This complexity presents challenges for modeling and generalizing trajectory prediction. Previous methods modeled the feature space of future trajectories based on the high-dimensional feature space of historical trajectories, but this approach is suboptimal because it overlooks the similarity between historical and future trajectories. Our proposed method, TrajCLIP, utilizes contrastive learning and idempotent generative networks to address this issue. By pairing historical and future trajectories and applying contrastive learning on the encoded feature space, we enforce same-space consistency constraints. To manage complex distributions, we use idempotent loss and tightness loss to control over-expansion in the latent space. Additionally, we have developed a trajectory interpolation algorithm and synthetic trajectory data to enhance model capacity and improve generalization. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate that TrajCLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance and excels in scene-to-scene transfer, few-shot transfer, and online learning tasks.

paragraphs: TrajCLIP predicts pedestrian trajectories in settings where movement depends on the scene, nearby people, and individual intentions. The authors argue that earlier approaches underuse similarities between past and future trajectories when modeling their feature spaces. Their method makes that relationship an explicit part of representation learning.

Historical and future trajectories are paired, encoded, and trained with a contrastive objective that enforces consistency within a shared feature space. The model also uses idempotent generative networks, with idempotent and tightness losses designed to control excessive expansion of the latent space. These components address both the relationship between observed and future motion and the complexity of the distribution being modeled.

The findings support combining shared trajectory representations, latent-space constraints, and added trajectory data to improve prediction across these evaluated learning settings.
summary.tldr: TrajCLIP combines contrastive past–future alignment, constrained latent modeling, and synthetic trajectories to improve pedestrian prediction and transfer.

title: TrajCLIP: Pedestrian trajectory prediction method using contrastive learning and idempotent networks

abstract: The online reconstruction of dynamic scenes from multi-view streaming videos faces significant challenges in training, rendering and storage efficiency. Harnessing superior learning speed and real-time rendering capabilities, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently demonstrated considerable potential in this field. However, 3DGS can be inefficient in terms of storage and prone to overfitting by excessively growing Gaussians, particularly with limited views. This paper proposes an efficient framework, dubbed HiCoM, with three key components. First, we construct a compact and robust initial 3DGS representation using a perturbation smoothing strategy. Next, we introduce a Hierarchical Coherent Motion mechanism that leverages the inherent non-uniform distribution and local consistency of 3D Gaussians to swiftly and accurately learn motions across frames. Finally, we continually refine the 3DGS with additional Gaussians, which are later merged into the initial 3DGS to maintain consistency with the evolving scene. To preserve a compact representation, an equivalent number of low-opacity Gaussians that minimally impact the representation are removed before processing subsequent frames. Extensive experiments conducted on two widely used datasets show that our framework improves learning efficiency of the state-of-the-art methods by about 20% and reduces the data storage by 85%, achieving competitive free-viewpoint video synthesis quality but with higher robustness and stability. Moreover, by parallel learning multiple frames simultaneously, our HiCoM decreases the average training wall time to <2 seconds per frame with negligible performance degradation, substantially boosting real-world applicability and responsiveness.

abstract: In machine learning research, it is common to evaluate algorithms via their performance on standard benchmark datasets. While a growing body of work establishes guidelines for---and levies criticisms at---data and benchmarking practices in machine learning, comparatively less attention has been paid to the data repositories where these datasets are stored, documented, and shared. In this paper, we analyze the landscape of these _benchmark data repositories_ and the role they can play in improving benchmarking. This role includes addressing issues with both datasets themselves (e.g., representational harms, construct validity) and the manner in which evaluation is carried out using such datasets (e.g., overemphasis on a few datasets and metrics, lack of reproducibility). To this end, we identify and discuss a set of considerations surrounding the design and use of benchmark data repositories, with a focus on improving benchmarking practices in machine learning.

paragraphs: Machine learning benchmarks depend on more than the datasets researchers choose. They also depend on the repositories that store, document, and distribute those datasets. This paper examines that infrastructure, arguing that repository design and use deserve more attention in discussions about how to make algorithm evaluation more meaningful.

The analysis connects repositories to two kinds of problems. Some concern the datasets themselves, including representational harms and construct validity: whether a dataset actually captures what an evaluation is intended to measure. Others concern research practices, such as repeatedly emphasizing a small collection of datasets and metrics or making results difficult to reproduce.

The authors survey the repository landscape and identify considerations for designing and using repositories to improve benchmarking. The contribution is an analysis of how shared data infrastructure can help address these issues. It broadens the focus of benchmarking reform from individual datasets and evaluations to the systems through which researchers discover, understand, and reuse data.
summary.tldr: The paper examines how dataset repositories can improve the quality, reproducibility, and breadth of machine learning benchmarking.

title: Benchmark Data Repositories for Better Benchmarking

abstract: Existing approaches to differentiable structure learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) rely on strong identifiability assumptions in order to guarantee that global minimizers of the acyclicity-constrained optimization problem identifies the true DAG. Moreover, it has been observed empirically that the optimizer may exploit undesirable artifacts in the loss function. We explain and remedy these issues by studying the behavior of differentiable acyclicity-constrained programs under general likelihoods with multiple global minimizers. By carefully regularizing the likelihood, it is possible to identify the sparsest model in the Markov equivalence class, even in the absence of an identifiable parametrization. We first study the Gaussian case in detail, showing how proper regularization of the likelihood defines a score that identifies the sparsest model. Assuming faithfulness, it also recovers the Markov equivalence class. These results are then generalized to general models and likelihoods, where the same claims hold. These theoretical results are validated empirically, showing how this can be done using standard gradient-based optimizers (without resorting to approximations such as Gumbel-Softmax), thus paving the way for differentiable structure learning under general models and losses. Open-source code is available at \url{https://github.com/duntrain/dagrad}.

This paper examines the broader situation of likelihoods with multiple global minimizers and addresses undesirable loss-function artifacts that optimizers can exploit.

title: Markov Equivalence and Consistency in Differentiable Structure Learning

abstract: Continuous action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL) are commonly defined as multidimensional intervals. While intervals usually reflect the action boundaries for tasks well, they can be challenging for learning because the typically large global action space leads to frequent exploration of irrelevant actions. Yet, little task knowledge can be sufficient to identify significantly smaller state-specific sets of relevant actions. Focusing learning on these relevant actions can significantly improve training efficiency and effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to focus learning on the set of relevant actions and introduce three continuous action masking methods for exactly mapping the action space to the state-dependent set of relevant actions. Thus, our methods ensure that only relevant actions are executed, enhancing the predictability of the RL agent and enabling its use in safety-critical applications. We further derive the implications of the proposed methods on the policy gradient. Using proximal policy optimization ( PPO), we evaluate our methods on four control tasks, where the relevant action set is computed based on the system dynamics and a relevant state set. Our experiments show that the three action masking methods achieve higher final rewards and converge faster than the baseline without action masking.

This paper asks how task knowledge can narrow the choices available at each state so that learning spends less effort exploring actions that do not help.

The authors introduce three continuous action-masking methods that map the action space exactly onto a state-dependent set of relevant actions. This ensures that executed actions belong to that specified set. They also derive how the mappings affect the policy gradient, connecting the restriction on available actions to the learning updates used to improve the policy.

The methods are evaluated with proximal policy optimization on four control tasks. Relevant action sets are computed from system dynamics and a relevant state set. All three methods converge faster and achieve higher final rewards than the unmasked baseline in these experiments. The action restriction also supports more predictable behavior, with safety-related usefulness depending on the relevant sets supplied to the method.
summary.tldr: Three continuous action-masking methods restrict agents to state-relevant actions and improve convergence and final rewards in four control tasks.

title: Excluding the Irrelevant: Focusing Reinforcement Learning through Continuous Action Masking

abstract: The pre-trained point cloud model based on Masked Point Modeling (MPM) has exhibited substantial improvements across various tasks. However, these models heavily rely on the Transformer, leading to quadratic complexity and limited decoder, hindering their practice application. To address this limitation, we first conduct a comprehensive analysis of existing Transformer-based MPM, emphasizing the idea that redundancy reduction is crucial for point cloud analysis. To this end, we propose a Locally constrained Compact point cloud Model (LCM) consisting of a locally constrained compact encoder and a locally constrained Mamba-based decoder. Our encoder replaces self-attention with our local aggregation layers to achieve an elegant balance between performance and efficiency. Considering the varying information density between masked and unmasked patches in the decoder inputs of MPM, we introduce a locally constrained Mamba-based decoder. This decoder ensures linear complexity while maximizing the perception of point cloud geometry information from unmasked patches with higher information density. Extensive experimental results show that our compact model significantly surpasses existing Transformer-based models in both performance and efficiency, especially our LCM-based Point-MAE model, compared to the Transformer-based model, achieved an improvement of 1.84%, 0.67%, and 0.60% in performance on the three variants of ScanObjectNN while reducing parameters by 88% and computation by 73%. The code is available at https://github.com/zyh16143998882/LCM.

This paper analyzes those models and argues that reducing redundancy is important for efficient point-cloud processing.

The proposed LCM has a compact encoder and a locally constrained Mamba-based decoder. The encoder replaces self-attention with local aggregation layers to balance predictive performance and efficiency. These results suggest that a more compact architecture can use point-cloud geometry effectively without retaining the computational burden of the original Transformer design.
summary.tldr: LCM replaces Transformer components with local aggregation and a Mamba-based decoder to improve point-cloud performance while cutting model size and computation.

title: LCM: Locally Constrained Compact Point Cloud Model for Masked Point Modeling

abstract: In image classification, it is common to utilize a pretrained model to extract meaningful features of the input images, and then to train a classifier on top of it to make predictions for any downstream task. Trained on enormous amounts of data, these models have been shown to contain harmful biases which can hurt their performance when adapted for a downstream classification task. Further, very often they may be blackbox, either due to scale, or because of unavailability of model weights or architecture. Thus, during a downstream task, we cannot debias such models by updating the weights of the feature encoder, as only the classifier can be finetuned. In this regard, we investigate the suitability of some existing debiasing techniques and thereby motivate the need for more focused research towards this problem setting. Furthermore, we propose a simple method consisting of a clustering-based adaptive margin loss with a blackbox feature encoder, with no knowledge of the bias attribute. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: A common image-classification workflow uses a pretrained model to extract features and trains a separate classifier on those features. Biases inherited from the pretrained model can hurt downstream performance. Addressing them becomes more difficult when the feature extractor is a black box whose weights or architecture are unavailable, or whose scale prevents updating it.

This paper studies debiasing under that restriction: the classifier can be fine-tuned, but the feature encoder cannot. The authors examine how suitable existing debiasing methods are for this setting and propose a clustering-based adaptive margin loss. Their method works with the black-box encoder and does not require knowing which attribute is responsible for the bias.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness. The contribution focuses attention on a practical distinction between changing a representation and improving a classifier that must use a fixed representation. By operating within the latter constraint and without bias-attribute knowledge, the approach addresses a setting where direct modification of the pretrained model is unavailable.
summary.tldr: A clustering-based adaptive margin loss helps debias downstream image classifiers when the feature extractor is fixed and the bias attribute is unknown.

title: Mitigating Biases in Blackbox Feature Extractors for Image Classification Tasks

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an actively growing field that is seeing increased usage in real-world, safety-critical applications -- making it paramount to ensure the robustness of RL algorithms against adversarial attacks. In this work we explore a particularly stealthy form of training-time attacks against RL -- backdoor poisoning. Here the adversary intercepts the training of an RL agent with the goal of reliably inducing a particular action when the agent observes a pre-determined trigger at inference time. We uncover theoretical limitations of prior work by proving their inability to generalize across domains and MDPs. Motivated by this, we formulate a novel poisoning attack framework which interlinks the adversary's objectives with those of finding an optimal policy -- guaranteeing attack success in the limit. Using insights from our theoretical analysis we develop "SleeperNets" as a universal backdoor attack which exploits a newly proposed threat model and leverages dynamic reward poisoning techniques. We evaluate our attack in 6 environments spanning multiple domains and demonstrate significant improvements in attack success over existing methods, while preserving benign episodic return.
