paragraphs: A backdoor attack on reinforcement learning aims to make an agent behave normally until it encounters a predetermined trigger, then take an attacker-chosen action. The attack is introduced during training but activated during inference. This paper studies the theoretical reach of such attacks and develops SleeperNets within a newly proposed threat model.

The authors prove limitations in earlier approaches that prevent them from generalizing across domains and Markov decision processes. Their framework links the attacker's objective to the search for an optimal policy, producing an attack-success guarantee in the limit. SleeperNets draws on this analysis and uses dynamic reward poisoning as its attack mechanism.

Experiments span six environments across multiple domains. The attack achieves substantially higher success than existing methods while preserving benign episodic return, meaning normal task performance remains intact in the reported evaluations. The theoretical guarantee is asymptotic, while the experiments provide separate evidence of practical effectiveness. Together, these results show how ordinary performance can coexist with a learned trigger-dependent vulnerability.
summary.tldr: SleeperNets strengthens trigger-based attacks on reinforcement learning, with an asymptotic success guarantee and improved empirical success while preserving normal returns.

title: SleeperNets: Universal Backdoor Poisoning Attacks Against Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: Large vision language models, such as CLIP, demonstrate impressive robustness to spurious features than single-modal models trained on ImageNet. However, existing test datasets are typically curated based on ImageNet-trained models, which aim to capture the spurious features inherited in ImageNet. Benchmarking CLIP models based on the ImageNet-oriented spurious features may not be sufficient to reflect the extent to which CLIP models are robust to spurious correlations within CLIP training data, e.g., LAION. To this end, we craft a new challenging dataset named CounterAnimal designed to reveal the reliance of CLIP models on realistic spurious features. Specifically, we split animal photos into groups according to the backgrounds, and then identify a pair of groups for each class where a CLIP model shows high-performance drops across the two groups. Our evaluations show that the spurious features captured by CounterAnimal are generically learned by CLIP models with different backbones and pre-train data, yet have limited influence for ImageNet models. We provide theoretical insights that the CLIP objective cannot offer additional robustness. Furthermore, we also re-evaluate strategies such as scaling up parameters and high-quality pre-trained data. We find that they still help mitigate the spurious features, providing a promising path for future developments.

paragraphs: A model can recognize an animal partly by its background rather than by the animal itself. Tests of such misleading associations often target shortcuts found in ImageNet-trained models. The paper asks whether CLIP's strong performance on those tests adequately reveals shortcuts associated with its own training data.

The authors construct CounterAnimal by grouping animal photographs according to their backgrounds. For each animal class, they identify two groups between which a CLIP model's performance drops substantially. This makes the benchmark sensitive to realistic background associations that conventional tests may miss. Evaluations show that these associations affect CLIP models with different architectures and pretraining data, while having limited influence on ImageNet models.

The paper also provides theoretical insights indicating that CLIP's training objective cannot itself supply additional robustness. Its experiments nevertheless find that larger models and higher-quality pretraining data help reduce the problem. The findings make robustness evaluation more specific: success against one model family's shortcuts does not establish resistance to the shortcuts learned by another.
summary.tldr: CounterAnimal reveals background shortcuts shared across CLIP models, showing why ImageNet-oriented tests can give an incomplete picture of their robustness.

title: A Sober Look at the Robustness of CLIPs to Spurious Features

abstract: Approximate Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) methods are an important family of optimisers for deep learning models, which use approximate Fisher information matrices to pre-condition gradients during training. The empirical Fisher (EF) method approximates the Fisher information matrix empirically by reusing the per-sample gradients collected during back-propagation. Despite its ease of implementation, the EF approximation has its theoretical and practical limitations. This paper investigates the *inversely-scaled projection* issue of EF, which is shown to be a major cause of its poor empirical approximation quality. An improved empirical Fisher (iEF) method is proposed to address this issue, which is motivated as a generalised NGD method from a loss reduction perspective, meanwhile retaining the practical convenience of EF. The exact iEF and EF methods are experimentally evaluated using practical deep learning setups, including widely-used setups for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained models (T5-base with LoRA and Prompt-Tuning on GLUE tasks, and ViT with LoRA for CIFAR100). Optimisation experiments show that applying exact iEF directly as an optimiser provides strong convergence and generalisation. It achieves the best test performance and the lowest training loss for the majority of the tasks, even when compared to well-tuned AdamW/Adafactor baselines. Additionally, under a novel empirical evaluation framework, the proposed iEF method shows consistently better approximation quality to exact Natural Gradient updates than both the EF and the more expensive sampled Fisher methods, meanwhile demonstrating the superior property of being robust to the choice of damping across tasks and training stages. Improving existing approximate NGD optimisers with iEF is expected to lead to better convergence and robustness. Furthermore, the iEF method also serves as a better approximation method to the Fisher information matrix itself, which enables the improvement of a variety of Fisher-based methods, not limited to the scope of optimisation.

Benefits from incorporating iEF into other approximate optimizers remain an expectation; the reported experiments directly establish results for the evaluated implementations.
summary.tldr: Improved empirical Fisher corrects a problematic scaling effect and yields stronger natural-gradient approximations and optimization results.

title: An Improved Empirical Fisher Approximation for Natural Gradient Descent

abstract: We study stochastic approximation algorithms with Markovian noise and constant step-size $\alpha$. We develop a method based on infinitesimal generator comparisons to study the bias of the algorithm, which is the expected difference between $\theta_n$ ---the value at iteration $n$--- and $\theta^*$ ---the unique equilibrium of the corresponding ODE. We show that, under some smoothness conditions, this bias is of order $O(\alpha)$. Furthermore, we show that the time-averaged bias is equal to $\alpha V + O(\alpha^2)$, where $V$ is a constant characterized by a Lyapunov equation, showing that $E[\bar{\theta}_n] \approx \theta^*+V\alpha + O(\alpha^2)$, where $\bar{\theta}_n$ is the Polyak-Ruppert average. We also show that $\bar{\theta}_n$ converges with high probability around $\theta^*+\alpha V$. We illustrate how to combine this with Richardson-Romberg extrapolation to derive an iterative scheme with a bias of order $O(\alpha^2)$.

paragraphs: This paper studies iterative estimation algorithms that keep a constant update size while their noise follows a Markov process. Its central question is how far the algorithm’s expected value lies from the unique equilibrium of the corresponding ordinary differential equation. That expected displacement is the bias the authors seek to characterize.

Using comparisons of infinitesimal generators, the researchers show that the bias is of order O(α) under smoothness conditions, where α is the step size. They give a more precise description for the time-averaged iterates: the leading bias is αV, with a remainder of order O(α²). The coefficient V is characterized through a Lyapunov equation.

The average also concentrates with high probability around the shifted value θ* + αV. Thus, averaging can leave a systematic displacement from the target equilibrium. By combining their characterization with Richardson–Romberg extrapolation, the authors illustrate an iterative scheme that cancels the leading bias term and achieves bias of order O(α²).
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes constant-step estimation bias under Markovian noise and shows how extrapolation can reduce its leading order.

title: Computing the Bias of Constant-step Stochastic Approximation with Markovian Noise

abstract: Modern video generation frameworks based on Latent Diffusion Models suffer from inefficiencies in tokenization due to the Frame-Proportional Information Assumption. Existing tokenizers provide fixed temporal compression rates, causing the computational cost of the diffusion model to scale linearly with the frame rate. The paper proposes the Duration-Proportional Information Assumption: the upper bound on the information capacity of a video is proportional to the duration rather than the number of frames. Based on this insight, the paper introduces VFRTok, a Transformer-based video tokenizer, that enables variable frame rate encoding and decoding through asymmetric frame rate training between the encoder and decoder. Furthermore, the paper proposes Partial Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to decouple position and content modeling, which groups correlated patches into unified tokens. The Partial RoPE effectively improves content-awareness, enhancing the video generation capability. Benefiting from the compact and continuous spatio-temporal representation, VFRTok achieves competitive reconstruction quality and state-of-the-art generation fidelity while using only $1/8$ tokens compared to existing tokenizers.

paragraphs: Video diffusion models operate on compact tokens, but fixed temporal compression makes their computational cost grow with frame rate. VFRTok starts from a different proposed assumption: the upper bound on a video’s information capacity scales with its duration rather than its number of frames. This motivates representing videos without automatically adding proportional token capacity for every additional frame.

The transformer-based tokenizer supports variable frame rates by training its encoder and decoder with asymmetric frame rates. It also introduces Partial Rotary Position Embeddings to separate position modeling from content modeling. This helps group correlated patches into shared tokens and improves content awareness, producing a compact representation across space and time.

The authors report competitive reconstruction quality and state-of-the-art generation fidelity while using one-eighth as many tokens as existing tokenizers. These findings support the proposed representation’s efficiency in the evaluated settings. The duration-based information claim is the assumption guiding the design; the reported empirical result is that much smaller token representations can still support strong reconstruction and generation.
summary.tldr: VFRTok supports variable video frame rates and reports strong generation quality using one-eighth as many tokens as existing tokenizers.

title: VFRTok: Variable Frame Rates Video Tokenizer with Duration-Proportional Information Assumption

abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video (T2V) generation, exemplified by models such as Sora and Kling, have demonstrated strong potential for constructing world simulators. However, existing T2V models still struggle to understand abstract physical principles and to generate videos that faithfully obey physical laws. This limitation stems primarily from the lack of explicit physical guidance, caused by a significant gap between high-level physical concepts and the generative capabilities of current models. To address this challenge, we propose the **W**orld **S**imulator **A**ssistant (**WISA**), a novel framework designed to systematically decompose and integrate physical principles into T2V models. Specifically, WISA decomposes physical knowledge into three hierarchical levels: textual physical descriptions, qualitative physical categories, and quantitative physical properties. It then incorporates several carefully designed modules—such as Mixture-of-Physical-Experts Attention (MoPA) and a Physical Classifier—to effectively encode these attributes and enhance the model’s adherence to physical laws during generation. In addition, most existing video datasets feature only weak or implicit representations of physical phenomena, limiting their utility for learning explicit physical principles. To bridge this gap, we present **WISA-80K**, a new dataset comprising 80,000 human-curated videos that depict 17 fundamental physical laws across three core domains of physics: dynamics, thermodynamics, and optics. Experimental results show that WISA substantially improves the alignment of T2V models (such as CogVideoX and Wan2.1) with real-world physical laws, achieving notable gains on the VideoPhy benchmark. Our data, code, and models are available in the [Project Page](https://wisav1.github.io/WISA/).

To bridge this gap, we present **WISA-80K**, a new dataset comprising 80,000 human-curated videos that depict 17 fundamental physical laws across three core domains of physics: dynamics, thermodynamics, and optics. Experimental results show that WISA substantially improves the alignment of T2V models (such as CogVideoX and Wan2.1) with real-world physical laws, achieving notable gains on the VideoPhy benchmark. Our data, code, and models are available in the [Project Page](https://wisav1.github.io/WISA/).

The paper attributes this partly to a gap between abstract physical concepts and the guidance available to generative models. It introduces both a framework for representing physical knowledge and a dataset with explicit physical content.

The framework organizes physical knowledge into textual descriptions, qualitative categories, and quantitative properties. Modules including Mixture-of-Physical-Experts Attention and a Physical Classifier encode these attributes to guide generation. This decomposition gives the model several forms of physical information, connecting verbal descriptions with categorical and numerical representations of the same underlying principles.

WISA-80K contains 80,000 human-curated videos depicting 17 fundamental laws across dynamics, thermodynamics, and optics. It addresses the weak or implicit representation of physics in many existing video datasets. Experiments with models including CogVideoX and Wan2.1 report substantially improved physical alignment and notable gains on VideoPhy. These findings demonstrate better adherence in the evaluated setting, rather than a guarantee that generated videos always satisfy physical laws.
summary.tldr: WISA combines structured physical guidance with a curated physics-video dataset to improve physical consistency in text-to-video generation.

title: WISA: World simulator assistant for physics-aware text-to-video generation

abstract: We introduce ITTO, a challenging new benchmark suite for evaluating and diagnosing the capabilities and limitations of point tracking methods. Our videos are sourced from existing datasets and egocentric real-world recordings, with high-quality human annotations collected through a multi-stage pipeline. ITTO captures the motion complexity, occlusion patterns, and object diversity characteristic of real-world scenes -- factors that are largely absent in current benchmarks. We conduct a rigorous analysis of state-of-the-art tracking methods on ITTO, breaking down performance along key axes of motion complexity. Our findings reveal that existing trackers struggle with these challenges, particularly in re-identifying points after occlusion, highlighting critical failure modes. These results point to the need for new modeling approaches tailored to real-world dynamics. We envision ITTO as a foundation testbed for advancing point tracking and guiding the development of more robust tracking algorithms.

paragraphs: Point tracking follows particular locations through a video as objects and cameras move. ITTO is a benchmark suite designed to test this capability under complex real-world dynamics. Its videos combine material from existing datasets with egocentric recordings, and its human annotations are collected through multiple stages to support high-quality evaluation.

The benchmark emphasizes complicated motion, varied objects, and patterns of occlusion, where a tracked point temporarily disappears from view. The authors argue that these factors are largely absent from current benchmarks. They analyze state-of-the-art trackers along specific dimensions of motion complexity, making the evaluation useful for diagnosing where a method struggles.

The results reveal substantial difficulties, especially when trackers must identify the same point again after an occlusion. This finding separates maintaining a visible track from recovering its identity after a gap. ITTO therefore contributes both an evaluation resource and evidence of concrete failure modes, intended to guide modeling approaches that better handle the dynamics present in real-world videos.
summary.tldr: ITTO tests point tracking under complex real-world motion and exposes particular weaknesses in recovering points after occlusion.

title: Is This Tracker On? A Benchmark Protocol for Dynamic Tracking

abstract: Many decision-making processes involve evaluating and selecting items, including scientific peer review, job hiring, school admissions, and investment decisions. These domains feature error-prone evaluations and uncertainty about outcomes, which undermine deterministic selection rules. Consequently, randomized selection mechanisms are gaining traction. However, current randomized approaches are ad hoc and, as we prove, inappropriate for their purported objectives. We propose a principled framework for randomized decision-making based on interval estimates of item quality. We introduce MERIT (Maximin Efficient Randomized Interval Top-$k$), which maximizes the worst-case expected number of top candidates selected under uncertainty represented by overlapping intervals. MERIT provides optimal resource allocation under an interpretable robustness notion. We develop a polynomial-time, practically efficient algorithm and prove our approach satisfies desirable axiomatic properties not guaranteed by existing methods. Experiments on synthetic peer review data from grant funding and conferences demonstrate that MERIT matches existing algorithms' expected utility under fully probabilistic models while outperforming them under our worst-case formulation.

paragraphs: Selecting papers or grant proposals requires judging quality from imperfect evidence. A fixed ranking can conceal this uncertainty, while introducing randomness does not automatically produce a selection rule suited to its intended goal. This paper develops a framework in which each candidate’s quality is described by an interval, allowing uncertainty and overlapping assessments to enter the decision directly.

The proposed method, MERIT, chooses a randomized selection that maximizes the worst-case expected number of top candidates selected. Its robustness criterion asks how well the selection performs under the least favorable quality assignments consistent with the intervals. The authors provide a polynomial-time algorithm and prove desirable axiomatic properties that existing methods do not guarantee.

Experiments use synthetic peer-review data representing conference and grant-funding settings. MERIT matches existing algorithms’ expected utility under fully probabilistic models and performs better under the paper’s worst-case objective. These findings support a specific benefit: randomness can be designed around an explicit, interpretable protection against uncertainty instead of being introduced through an ad hoc lottery.
summary.tldr: MERIT randomizes selection using quality intervals to maximize the worst-case expected number of top candidates chosen.

title: A Principled Approach to Randomized Selection under Uncertainty: Applications to Peer Review and Grant Funding

abstract: Recent advances in multimodal training have significantly improved the integration of image understanding and generation within a unified model. This study investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) handle image-understanding tasks, focusing on how visual information is processed and transferred to the textual domain. We compare *native multimodal VLMs*, models trained from scratch on multimodal data to generate both text and images, and *non-native multimodal VLMs*, models adapted from pre-trained large language models or capable of generating only text, highlighting key differences in information flow. We find that in native multimodal VLMs, image and text embeddings are more separated within the residual stream. Moreover, VLMs differ in how visual information reaches text: non-native multimodal VLMs exhibit a distributed communication pattern, where information is exchanged through multiple image tokens, whereas models trained natively for joint image and text generation tend to rely on a single post-image token that acts as a *narrow gate* for visual information. We show that ablating this single token significantly deteriorates image-understanding performance, whereas targeted, token-level interventions reliably steer image semantics and downstream text with fine-grained control.

The authors find greater separation between image and text embeddings in the residual stream of native models. They also identify different communication patterns. These findings connect an internal information-flow pattern with both a vulnerability to ablation and an opportunity to influence the model’s interpretation.
summary.tldr: Native image-and-text generators tend to channel visual information through one post-image token whose removal or modification strongly affects understanding.

title: The Narrow Gate: Localized Image-Text Communication in Native Multimodal Models

abstract: Compositional training has been the de-facto paradigm in existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), where pre-trained vision encoders are connected with pre-trained LLMs through continuous multimodal pre-training. However, the multimodal scaling property of this paradigm remains difficult to explore due to the separated training. In this paper, we focus on the native training of MLLMs in an end-to-end manner and systematically study its design space and scaling property under a practical setting, i.e., data constraint. Through careful study of various choices in MLLM, we obtain the optimal meta-architecture that best balances performance and training cost. After that, we further explore the scaling properties of the native MLLM and indicate the positively correlated scaling relationship between visual encoders and LLMs. Based on these findings, we propose a native MLLM called NaViL, combined with a simple and cost-effective recipe. Experimental results on 14 multimodal benchmarks confirm the competitive performance of NaViL against existing MLLMs. Besides that, our findings and results provide in-depth insights for the future study of native MLLMs.

paragraphs: Many multimodal language models connect a separately pretrained vision encoder to a separately pretrained language model. Because these components have different training histories, studying how the combined system scales is difficult. This paper examines native, end-to-end multimodal training under a practical constraint: the amount of available data is limited.

The authors systematically study architectural choices and identify the meta-architecture that best balances performance and training cost in their investigation. They then examine how the visual encoder and language model scale together, finding a positively correlated scaling relationship. The result treats the sizes of the two components as connected design choices within the jointly trained system.

These findings lead to NaViL, a native multimodal model paired with a simple, cost-effective training recipe. Evaluation on 14 multimodal benchmarks shows competitive performance against existing models. The paper contributes both a working model and empirical guidance about allocating model capacity under data constraints. Its architectural conclusions come from the studied design space and setting, while the benchmark results establish competitiveness rather than uniform superiority.
summary.tldr: NaViL studies joint vision–language scaling under limited data and turns its findings into a competitively performing native multimodal model.

title: NaViL: Rethinking Scaling Properties of Native Multimodal Large Language Models under Data Constraints

abstract: Foundation models (FMs) trained with different objectives and data learn diverse representations, making some more effective than others for specific downstream tasks. Existing adaptation strategies, such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning, focus on individual models and do not exploit the complementary strengths across models. Probing methods offer a promising alternative by extracting information from frozen models, but current techniques do not scale well with large feature sets and often rely on dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning. We propose Combined backBones (ComBo), a simple and scalable probing-based adapter that effectively integrates features from multiple models and layers. ComBo compresses activations from layers of one or more FMs into compact token-wise representations and processes them with a lightweight transformer for task-specific prediction. Crucially, ComBo does not require dataset-specific tuning or backpropagation through the backbone models. However, not all models are equally relevant for all tasks. To address this, we introduce a mechanism that leverages ComBo’s joint multi-backbone probing to efficiently evaluate each backbone’s task-relevance, enabling both practical model comparison and improved performance through selective adaptation. On the 19 tasks of the VTAB-1k benchmark, ComBo outperforms previous probing methods, matches or surpasses more expensive alternatives, such as distillation-based model merging, and enables efficient probing of tuned models. Our results demonstrate that ComBo offers a practical and general-purpose framework for combining diverse representations from multiple FMs.

paragraphs: Foundation models learn different representations because their training data and objectives differ. A downstream task may therefore benefit from information distributed across several models or layers. ComBo addresses the challenge of combining that information efficiently, using frozen backbone models rather than requiring training updates to pass through each large model.

The adapter compresses layer activations into compact representations for individual tokens, then uses a lightweight transformer to make task-specific predictions. It requires neither dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning nor backpropagation through the backbones. A related mechanism evaluates each backbone’s relevance through joint probing, allowing selective adaptation when some models contribute more useful information than others.

Across the 19 VTAB-1k tasks, ComBo outperforms previous probing methods and matches or exceeds more expensive alternatives, including distillation-based model merging. It also supports efficient probing of tuned models. These results indicate that combining representations can be practical without updating every source model, and that selecting relevant backbones can improve the value of the combination.
summary.tldr: ComBo efficiently combines frozen features from multiple models and layers, achieving strong results across 19 VTAB-1k tasks.

title: Fantastic Features and Where to Find Them: A Probing Method to combine Features from Multiple Foundation Models

abstract: Overparameterized neural networks can interpolate a given dataset in many different ways, prompting the fundamental question: which among these solutions should we prefer, and what explicit regularization strategies will provably yield these solutions? This paper addresses the challenge of finding the sparsest interpolating ReLU network—i.e., the network with the fewest nonzero parameters or neurons—a goal with wide-ranging implications for efficiency, generalization, interpretability, theory, and model compression. Unlike post hoc pruning approaches, we propose a continuous, almost-everywhere differentiable training objective whose global minima are guaranteed to correspond to the sparsest single-hidden-layer ReLU networks that fit the data. This result marks a conceptual advance: it recasts the combinatorial problem of sparse interpolation as a smooth optimization task, potentially enabling the use of gradient-based training methods. Our objective is based on minimizing $\ell^p$ quasinorms of the weights for $0 < p < 1$, a classical sparsity-promoting strategy in finite-dimensional settings. However, applying these ideas to neural networks presents new challenges: the function class is infinite-dimensional, and the weights are learned using a highly nonconvex objective. We prove that, under our formulation, global minimizers correspond exactly to sparsest solutions. Our work lays a foundation for understanding when and how continuous sparsity-inducing objectives can be leveraged to recover sparse networks through training.

paragraphs: Many different overparameterized networks can fit the same training data exactly. This paper asks how to select the sparsest such network, measured through nonzero parameters or neurons. Instead of first fitting a large network and pruning it afterward, the authors study a training objective designed to make sparsity part of the optimization problem itself.

Their formulation uses weight penalties based on ℓᵖ quasinorms with p strictly between zero and one. These penalties promote sparsity, but transferring that idea to neural networks requires handling an infinite-dimensional function class and a highly nonconvex objective. The authors prove that, under their formulation, global minimizers correspond exactly to the sparsest interpolating single-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

The result connects a discrete selection problem with a continuous objective that is differentiable almost everywhere. This potentially opens the problem to gradient-based training methods. Crucially, the guarantee concerns global minima; it does not state that ordinary training will necessarily find them. The contribution is a theoretical characterization of which solutions the objective selects when globally minimized.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that global minima of its ℓᵖ-based objective recover the sparsest interpolating single-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

title: Global Minimizers of $\ell^p$-Regularized Objectives Yield the Sparsest ReLU Neural Networks

abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is marked by cognitive decline along with the widespread of tau aggregates across the brain cortex. Due to the challenges of imaging pathology spreading flows *in vivo*, however, quantitative analysis on the cortical pathways of tau propagation and its interaction with the cascade of amyloid-beta (A$\beta$) plaques lags behind the experimental insights of underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. To address this challenge, we present a physics-informed neural network, empowered by mean-field theory, to uncover the biologically meaningful spreading pathways of tau aggregates between two longitudinal snapshots. Following the notion of `prion-like' mechanism in AD, we first formulate the dynamics of tau propagation as a mean-field game (MFG), where the spread of tau aggregate at each location (aka. agent) depends on the collective behavior of the surrounding agents as well as the potential field formed by amyloid burden. Given the governing equation of propagation dynamics, MFG reaches an equilibrium that allows us to model the evolution of tau aggregates as an optimal transport with the lowest cost in *Wasserstein* space. By leveraging the variational primal-dual structure in MFG, we propose a *Wasserstein*-1 Lagrangian generative adversarial network (GAN), in which a Lipschitz critic seeks the appropriate transport cost at the population level and a generator parameterizes the flow fields of optimal transport across individuals. Additionally, we incorporate a symbolic regression module to derive an explicit formulation capturing the A$\beta$-tau crosstalk. Experimental results on public neuroimaging datasets demonstrate that our explainable deep model not only yields precise and reliable predictions of future tau progression for unseen new subjects but also provides a new window to uncover new understanding of pathology propagation in AD through learning-based approaches.

summary.tldr: A mean-field-game model learns tau propagation pathways and an explicit amyloid–tau relationship from longitudinal brain imaging.

title: Uncover Governing Law of Pathology Propagation Mechanism Through A Mean-Field Game

abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery in reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn diverse behaviors without relying on external rewards. However, current methods often overlook the periodic nature of learned skills, focusing instead on increasing the mutual dependency between states and skills or maximizing the distance traveled in latent space. Considering that many robotic tasks—particularly those involving locomotion—require periodic behaviors across varying timescales, the ability to discover diverse periodic skills is essential. Motivated by this, we propose Periodic Skill Discovery (PSD), a framework that discovers periodic behaviors in an unsupervised manner. The key idea of PSD is to train an encoder that maps states to a circular latent space, thereby naturally encoding periodicity in the latent representation. By capturing temporal distance, PSD can effectively learn skills with diverse periods in complex robotic tasks, even with pixel-based observations. We further show that these learned skills achieve high performance on downstream tasks such as hurdling. Moreover, integrating PSD with an existing skill discovery method offers more diverse behaviors, thus broadening the agent’s repertoire. Our code and demos are available at https://jonghaepark.github.io/psd

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery aims to teach reinforcement learning agents varied behaviors without externally supplied rewards. Periodic Skill Discovery focuses on a particular kind of variety: repeated behaviors with different cycle lengths. This matters for robotic tasks such as locomotion, where useful behavior often involves recurring movement rather than simply reaching distinct states.

The framework trains an encoder to map states into a circular latent space. A circular representation naturally accommodates repetition, while information about temporal distance helps the method distinguish and learn skills with different periods. The authors show that this approach can discover periodic skills in complex robotic tasks, including settings where observations are images.

The learned skills achieve high performance on downstream tasks such as hurdling. Combining PSD with an existing skill-discovery method also produces more diverse behaviors. Together, these findings support explicitly representing periodicity as a useful complement to other discovery objectives. The contribution expands the kinds of behavior an agent can acquire, particularly when repeated motion at different timescales is important.
summary.tldr: Periodic Skill Discovery uses a circular latent representation to learn repeated robotic behaviors with diverse cycle lengths without external rewards.

title: Periodic Skill Discovery

abstract: Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) have markedly advanced the quality of image inpainting and local editing. However, the inherent latent compression often introduces pixel-level inconsistencies, such as chromatic shifts, texture mismatches, and visible seams along editing boundaries. Existing remedies, including background-conditioned latent decoding and pixel-space harmonization, usually fail to fully eliminate these artifacts in practice and do not generalize well across different latent representations or tasks. We introduce PixPerfect, a pixel‐level refinement framework that delivers seamless, high-fidelity local edits across diverse LDM architectures and tasks. PixPerfect leverages (i) a differentiable discriminative pixel space that amplifies and suppresses subtle color and texture discrepancies, (ii) a comprehensive artifact simulation pipeline that exposes the refiner to realistic local editing artifacts during training, and (iii) a direct pixel-space refinement scheme that ensures broad applicability across diverse latent representations and tasks. Extensive experiments on inpainting, object removal, and insertion benchmarks demonstrate that PixPerfect substantially enhances perceptual fidelity and downstream editing performance, establishing a new standard for robust and high-fidelity localized image editing.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion models can produce convincing local edits while leaving small inconsistencies where edited and original content meet. Compression into a latent representation can introduce color shifts, mismatched textures, and visible seams. PixPerfect addresses these pixel-level problems with a refinement framework intended to work across different latent diffusion architectures and editing tasks.

The framework uses a differentiable discriminative pixel space to make subtle color and texture discrepancies more apparent and support their suppression. A training pipeline simulates realistic editing artifacts so the refiner encounters the problems it will need to repair. Refinement then operates directly in pixel space, supporting applicability across different latent representations.

Experiments cover inpainting, object removal, and object insertion. The authors report substantial improvements in perceptual fidelity and downstream editing performance across these benchmarks. The approach matters because successful local editing requires both a plausible changed region and visual consistency with its surroundings. PixPerfect makes that consistency a direct training and refinement target, with reported benefits across several forms of localized image manipulation.
summary.tldr: PixPerfect refines edited images in pixel space to reduce seams, color shifts, and texture mismatches across latent diffusion editing tasks.

title: PixPerfect: Seamless Latent Diffusion Local Editing with Discriminative Pixel-Space Refinement

abstract: Pretraining a policy on offline data followed by fine-tuning through online interactions, known as Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning (O2O RL), has emerged as a promising paradigm for real-world RL deployment. However, both offline datasets and online interactions in practical environments are often noisy or even maliciously corrupted, severely degrading the performance of O2O RL. Existing works primarily focus on mitigating the conservatism of offline policies via online exploration, while the robustness of O2O RL under data corruption, including states, actions, rewards, and dynamics, is still unexplored. In this work, we observe that data corruption induces heavy-tailed behavior in the policy, thereby substantially degrading the efficiency of online exploration. To address this issue, we incorporate Inverse Probability Weighted (IPW) into the online exploration policy to alleviate heavy-tailedness, and propose a novel, simple yet effective method termed $\textbf{RPEX}$: $\textbf{R}$obust $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{EX}$pansion. Extensive experimental results on D4RL datasets demonstrate that RPEX achieves SOTA O2O performance across a wide range of data corruption scenarios.
originalAbstract: Pretraining a policy on offline data followed by fine-tuning through online interactions, known as Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning (O2O RL), has emerged as a promising paradigm for real-world RL deployment. However, both offline datasets and online interactions in practical environments are often noisy or even maliciously corrupted, severely degrading the performance of O2O RL. Existing works primarily focus on mitigating the conservatism of offline policies via online exploration, while the robustness of O2O RL under data corruption, including states, actions, rewards, and dynamics, is still unexplored. In this work, we observe that data corruption induces heavy-tailed behavior in the policy, thereby substantially degrading the efficiency of online exploration. To address this issue, we incorporate Inverse Probability Weighted (IPW) into the online exploration policy to alleviate heavy-tailedness, and propose a novel, simple yet effective method termed $\textbf{RPEX}$: $\textbf{R}$obust $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{EX}$pansion. Extensive experimental results on D4RL datasets demonstrate that RPEX achieves SOTA O2O performance across a wide range of data corruption scenarios.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts with a policy trained on stored data and then improves it through interactions with an environment. Both stages can encounter noisy or maliciously corrupted information. This paper studies corruption involving states, actions, rewards, and dynamics, extending attention beyond the usual challenge of overcoming an offline policy's conservatism during online exploration.

The authors observe that corruption induces heavy-tailed behavior in the policy and substantially reduces exploration efficiency. Their proposed method, Robust Policy Expansion, or RPEX, incorporates inverse probability weighting into the online exploration policy to alleviate that behavior. The intervention therefore targets how the agent explores after pretraining, where corrupted learning can impede further improvement.

Extensive experiments on D4RL datasets report state-of-the-art offline-to-online performance across a wide range of corruption scenarios. These findings support inverse probability weighting as a simple, effective component for robust policy expansion in the tested settings. The paper's central connection is between corruption-induced policy behavior and inefficient exploration, providing a specific mechanism to address when adapting offline policies online.
summary.tldr: RPEX uses inverse probability weighting to reduce corruption-induced heavy-tailed policy behavior and improve offline-to-online reinforcement learning.

title: Robust Policy Expansion for Offline-to-Online RL under Diverse Data Corruption

abstract: Latent stochastic differential equation (SDE) models are important tools for the unsupervised discovery of dynamical systems from data, with applications ranging from engineering to neuroscience. In these complex domains, exact posterior inference of the latent state path is typically intractable, motivating the use of approximate methods such as variational inference (VI). However, existing VI methods for inference in latent SDEs often suffer from slow convergence and numerical instability. Here, we propose SDE Inference via Natural Gradients (SING), a method that leverages natural gradient VI to efficiently exploit the underlying geometry of the model and variational posterior. SING enables fast and reliable inference in latent SDE models by approximating intractable integrals and parallelizing computations in time. We provide theoretical guarantees that SING will approximately optimize the intractable, continuous-time objective of interest. Moreover, we demonstrate that better state inference enables more accurate estimation of nonlinear drift functions using, for example, Gaussian process SDE models. SING outperforms prior methods in state inference and drift estimation on a variety of datasets, including a challenging application to modeling neural dynamics in freely behaving animals. Altogether, our results illustrate the potential of SING as a tool for accurate inference in complex dynamical systems, especially those characterized by limited prior knowledge and non-conjugate structure.

paragraphs: Latent stochastic differential equations describe evolving systems whose internal states are only indirectly observed. Recovering a distribution over their hidden state trajectories is typically intractable, so researchers use approximations. SING addresses slow convergence and numerical instability in variational inference methods used for this task.

The method uses natural gradients to account for the geometry of the model and its approximate posterior distribution. It also approximates otherwise intractable integrals and parallelizes calculations across time. The paper provides theoretical guarantees of approximate optimization of the continuous-time objective, connecting the computational procedure to the inference problem it is intended to solve.

SING outperforms prior methods on state inference and drift estimation across multiple datasets, including neural dynamics in freely behaving animals. The findings support its potential for learning complex dynamics, particularly with limited prior knowledge and structures that resist convenient inference formulas.
summary.tldr: SING uses natural-gradient variational inference to improve hidden-state recovery and dynamics estimation in stochastic differential equation models.

title: SING: SDE Inference via Natural Gradients

abstract: Spatio-temporal trajectory representation learning plays a crucial role in various urban applications such as transportation systems, urban planning, and environmental monitoring. Existing methods can be divided into single-view and multi-view approaches, with the latter offering richer representations by integrating multiple sources of spatio-temporal data. However, these methods often struggle to generalize across diverse urban scenes due to multi-city structural heterogeneity, which arises from the disparities in road networks, grid layouts, and traffic regulations across cities, and the amplified seesaw phenomenon, where optimizing for one city, view, or task can degrade performance in others. These challenges hinder the deployment of trajectory learning models across multiple cities, limiting their real-world applicability. In this work, we propose SMARTraj$^2$, a novel stable multi-city adaptive method for multi-view spatio-temporal trajectory representation learning. Specifically, we introduce a feature disentanglement module to separate domain-invariant and domain-specific features, and a personalized gating mechanism to dynamically stabilize the contributions of different views and tasks. Our approach achieves superior generalization across heterogeneous urban scenes while maintaining robust performance across multiple downstream tasks. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SMARTraj$^2$ in enhancing cross-city generalization and outperforming state-of-the-art methods. See our project website at \url{https://github.com/GestaltCogTeam/SMARTraj}.

Combining multiple views of trajectory data can enrich a representation, but it introduces competing demands. Improving performance for one city, view, or task may worsen it for another, creating the paper's seesaw problem.

SMARTraj² addresses these issues through feature disentanglement and personalized gating. The disentanglement module separates features shared across environments from features specific to an environment. The findings support treating transfer and training balance as connected problems: a representation needs to capture common patterns while controlling how competing sources of information contribute. This is relevant to deploying trajectory models across heterogeneous cities for transportation, planning, and environmental applications.
summary.tldr: SMARTraj² separates shared and city-specific features while balancing data views and tasks to improve cross-city trajectory learning.

title: SMARTraj$^2$: A Stable Multi-City Adaptive Method for Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Trajectory Representation Learning

abstract: Feature encoding with an overcomplete dictionary has demonstrated good performance in many applications, especially computer vision. In this paper we analyze the classification accuracy with respect to dictionary size by linking the encoding stage to kernel methods and \nystrom sampling, and obtain useful bounds on accuracy as a function of size. The \nystrom method also inspires us to revisit dictionary learning from local patches, and we propose to learn the dictionary in an end-to-end fashion taking into account pooling, a common computational layer in vision. We validate our contribution by showing how the derived bounds are able to explain the observed behavior of multiple datasets, and show that the pooling aware method efficiently reduces the dictionary size by a factor of two for a given accuracy.

paragraphs: Feature encoding with a large, overcomplete dictionary can work well in computer vision, but dictionary size raises a practical question: how much representation is needed for a particular classification accuracy? This paper analyzes that relationship by connecting feature encoding to kernel methods and Nyström sampling, producing bounds that relate accuracy to dictionary size.

The same connection motivates a change in dictionary learning. Dictionaries are often learned from local image patches, but their encoded outputs later pass through a pooling stage. The authors propose learning the dictionary in an end-to-end fashion that takes pooling into account, so the dictionary reflects how its features will ultimately be combined.

Experiments show that the derived bounds can explain observed behavior across multiple datasets. The pooling-aware method also reduces dictionary size by a factor of two for a given accuracy in the reported evaluation. The paper thus links an explanation of the size–accuracy relationship with a concrete way to obtain more compact pooled representations.
summary.tldr: Kernel-based analysis explains dictionary size effects, while pooling-aware dictionary learning halves dictionary size at a given accuracy in the reported evaluation.

title: On Compact Codes for Spatially Pooled Features

abstract: In this work, we focus on Online Sparse Kernel Learning that aims to online learn a kernel classifier with a bounded number of support vectors. Although many online learning algorithms have been proposed to learn a sparse kernel classifier, most of them fail to bound the number of support vectors used by the final solution which is the average of the intermediate kernel classifiers generated by online algorithms. The key idea of the proposed algorithm is to measure the difficulty in correctly classifying a training example by the derivative of a smooth loss function, and give a more chance to a difficult example to be a support vector than an easy one via a sampling scheme. Our analysis shows that when the loss function is smooth, the proposed algorithm yields similar performance guarantee as the standard online learning algorithm but with a near optimal number of support vectors (up to a poly(lnT) factor). Our empirical study shows promising performance of the proposed algorithm compared to the state-of-the-art algorithms for online sparse kernel learning.

paragraphs: Online kernel learning updates a classifier as examples arrive, while sparse versions try to limit the number of retained support vectors. The paper highlights a difficulty with existing approaches: controlling intermediate classifiers does not necessarily bound the support vectors in the final classifier, which is formed by averaging those intermediate solutions.

The proposed algorithm uses the derivative of a smooth loss function to assess how difficult an example is to classify correctly. A sampling scheme then gives difficult examples a greater chance of becoming support vectors than easy examples. This makes the selection of stored examples responsive to the classifier's learning difficulty.

For smooth loss functions, the analysis gives a performance guarantee similar to standard online learning while using a near-optimal number of support vectors, up to a polynomial factor in the logarithm of the number of steps. Experiments show promising performance against existing sparse online kernel methods. The contribution specifically addresses sparsity of the final averaged solution alongside learning performance.
summary.tldr: Difficulty-based sampling gives online kernel learning a near-optimal support-vector bound under a smooth-loss assumption.

title: Online Kernel Learning with a Near Optimal Sparsity Bound

abstract: We study the problem of ordinal embedding: given a set of ordinal constraints of the form distance(i,j) < distance(k,l) for some_quadruples (i,j,k,l) of indices, the goal is to construct a point configuration \hat\bmx_1, ..., \hat\bmx_n in \R^p that preserves these constraints as well as possible. Our first contribution is to suggest a simple new algorithm for this problem, Soft Ordinal Embedding. The key feature of the algorithm is that it recovers not only the ordinal constraints, but even the density structure of the underlying data set. As our second contribution we prove that in the large sample limit it is enough to know “local ordinal information” in order to perfectly reconstruct a given point configuration. This leads to our Local Ordinal Embedding algorithm, which can also be used for graph drawing.

The key feature of the algorithm is that it recovers not only the ordinal constraints, but even the density structure of the underlying data set. paragraphs: Ordinal embedding constructs point locations from comparisons between distances rather than from the distances themselves. For example, the input may say that one pair is closer together than another pair. The task is to find a configuration in a chosen-dimensional space that preserves these comparisons as well as possible.

The paper first introduces Soft Ordinal Embedding. Its highlighted feature is recovering the density structure of the underlying data as well as the supplied ordering constraints. This means the representation retains information about how points are concentrated, adding geometric content beyond whether individual distance comparisons are satisfied.

The second contribution is a theoretical result about local information. In the large-sample limit, local ordinal comparisons are sufficient to reconstruct a given point configuration perfectly. This is an asymptotic sufficiency statement, rather than a guarantee of perfect reconstruction from any finite collection of comparisons. The result leads to Local Ordinal Embedding, an algorithm that also has an application to graph drawing.
summary.tldr: New ordinal embedding algorithms recover geometric structure from distance comparisons, with a theorem showing local comparisons suffice in the large-sample limit.

title: Local Ordinal Embedding

abstract: Nuclear norm regularization has been shown very promising for pursing a low rank matrix solution in various machine learning problems. Many efforts have been devoted to develop efficient algorithms for solving the optimization problem in nuclear norm regularization. Solving it for large-scale matrix variables, however, is still a challenging task since the complexity grows fast with the size of matrix variable. In this work, we propose a novel method called safe subspace screening (SSS), to improve the efficiency of the solver for nuclear norm regularized least squares problems. Motivated by the fact that the low rank solution can be represented by a few subspaces, the proposed method accurately discards a predominant percentage of inactive subspaces prior to solving the problem to reduce problem size. Consequently, a much smaller problem is required to solve, making it more efficient than optimizing the original problem. The proposed SSS is safe, in that its solution is identical to the solution from the solver. In addition, the proposed SSS can be used together with any existing nuclear norm solver since it is independent of the solver. Extensive results on several synthetic and real data sets show that the proposed SSS is very effective in inactive subspace screening.

paragraphs: Nuclear norm regularization encourages low-rank matrix solutions, but optimization can still become expensive when the matrix variables are large. This paper introduces safe subspace screening for nuclear-norm-regularized least squares. Its purpose is to shrink the optimization problem before an existing solver begins its main work.

The approach uses the fact that a low-rank solution can be represented through relatively few subspaces. It identifies and discards a large proportion of inactive subspaces, leaving a smaller problem to solve. The screening is safe in the stated sense that the resulting solution is identical to the solution obtained by the solver on the original problem.

Because screening is independent of the solver, the authors state that it can be combined with any existing nuclear norm solver. Experiments on several synthetic and real datasets demonstrate effective removal of inactive subspaces. The contribution is a way to reduce computational burden while preserving the solution, making the preprocessing step useful alongside existing optimization methods.
summary.tldr: Safe subspace screening reduces nuclear-norm least-squares problems before optimization while preserving the solver's solution.

title: Safe Subspace Screening for Nuclear Norm Regularized Least Squares Problems

abstract: Approximate Message Passing (AMP) has been shown to be a superior method for inference problems, such as the recovery of signals from sets of noisy, lower-dimensionality measurements, both in terms of reconstruction accuracy and in computational efficiency. However, AMP suffers from serious convergence issues in contexts that do not exactly match its assumptions. We propose a new approach to stabilizing AMP in these contexts by applying AMP updates to individual coefficients rather than in parallel. Our results show that this change to the AMP iteration can provide theoretically expected, but hitherto unobtainable, performance for problems on which the standard AMP iteration diverges. Additionally, we find that the computational costs of this swept coefficient update scheme is not unduly burdensome, allowing it to be applied efficiently to signals of large dimensionality.

paragraphs: Approximate Message Passing can recover signals from noisy measurements that contain fewer dimensions than the original signal. It offers strong reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency, but its iterations can fail to converge when a problem does not closely match its assumptions. This paper targets that instability without abandoning the AMP approach.

The proposed change concerns the update schedule. Standard AMP updates coefficients in parallel, whereas the swept version applies updates to individual coefficients. The authors show that this modification can stabilize problems on which the standard iteration diverges. In those cases, it makes theoretically expected reconstruction performance attainable when the original iteration could not deliver it.

The paper also examines whether the altered schedule imposes an excessive computational cost. Its results indicate that the added burden is manageable, allowing efficient application to high-dimensional signals. The contribution is therefore a practical change to the iteration that can recover AMP's expected benefits in difficult settings while retaining useful computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: Updating AMP coefficients individually can stabilize otherwise divergent problems while keeping high-dimensional signal recovery computationally practical.

title: Swept Approximate Message Passing for Sparse Estimation

abstract: The Cross Domain Collaborative Filtering (CDCF) exploits the rating matrices from multiple domains to make better recommendations. Existing CDCF methods adopt the sub-structure sharing technique that can only transfer linearly correlated knowledge between domains. In this paper, we propose the notion of Hyper-Structure Transfer (HST) that requires the rating matrices to be explained by the projections of some more complex structure, called the hyper-structure, shared by all domains, and thus allows the non-linearly correlated knowledge between domains to be identified and transferred. Extensive experiments are conducted and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our HST models empirically.

paragraphs: Cross-domain collaborative filtering uses rating information from several domains to improve recommendations. Its usefulness depends on what relationships a model can transfer between those domains. This paper argues that existing approaches based on sharing substructures are limited to transferring knowledge with linear correlations, leaving nonlinear relationships outside their representational scope.

The proposed Hyper-Structure Transfer approach introduces a more complex structure shared across all domains. Each domain's rating matrix must be explainable as a projection of that common structure. Sharing happens through this underlying object, allowing the model to identify and transfer relationships that are nonlinearly correlated across the observed rating matrices.

This changes the form of the connection imposed between domains: the common explanation can be richer than a directly shared substructure. The authors conduct extensive experiments and report empirical evidence that their HST models are effective. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling proposal for nonlinear knowledge transfer and an experimental demonstration of its usefulness for cross-domain recommendation.
summary.tldr: Hyper-Structure Transfer connects rating matrices through a shared complex structure to transfer nonlinear relationships across recommendation domains.

title: Non-Linear Cross-Domain Collaborative Filtering via Hyper-Structure Transfer

abstract: Ordinary least squares (OLS) is the default method for fitting linear models, but is not applicable for problems with dimensionality larger than the sample size. For these problems, we advocate the use of a generalized version of OLS motivated by ridge regression, and propose two novel three-step algorithms involving least squares fitting and hard thresholding. The algorithms are methodologically simple to understand intuitively, computationally easy to implement efficiently, and theoretically appealing for choosing models consistently. Numerical exercises comparing our methods with penalization-based approaches in simulations and data analyses illustrate the great potential of the proposed algorithms.

The algorithms are methodologically simple to understand intuitively, computationally easy to implement efficiently, and theoretically appealing for choosing models consistently. Numerical exercises comparing our methods with penalization-based approaches in simulations and data analyses illustrate the great potential of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper considers linear regression when the number of potential predictors exceeds the number of observations. Ordinary least squares is not directly applicable in the usual way in this regime. The authors advocate a generalized version inspired by ridge regression, aiming to retain the intuitive and computational appeal of least-squares fitting for high-dimensional problems.

They propose two algorithms, each consisting of three steps and combining least-squares fitting with hard thresholding. Thresholding supplies a direct selection mechanism by retaining or removing fitted components according to a cutoff. Together, these operations provide a simple route from fitting a large model to selecting its relevant variables. The authors emphasize that the procedures are understandable and can be implemented efficiently.

The methods also have theoretical appeal for consistent model selection. Simulations and data analyses compare them with penalization-based approaches and illustrate their potential. The contribution is a pair of straightforward high-dimensional regression procedures supported by theory and numerical evidence, with the empirical findings presented as promising rather than as a universal superiority claim.
summary.tldr: Two simple algorithms combine generalized least squares with hard thresholding for high-dimensional regression and model selection.

title: No penalty no tears: Least squares in high-dimensional linear models

abstract: In this work, we take a representation learning perspective on hierarchical reinforcement learning, where the problem of learning lower layers in a hierarchy is transformed into the problem of learning trajectory-level generative models. We show that we can learn continuous latent representations of trajectories, which are effective in solving temporally extended and multi-stage problems. Our proposed model, SeCTAR, draws inspiration from variational autoencoders, and learns latent representations of trajectories. A key component of this method is to learn both a latent-conditioned policy and a latent-conditioned model which are consistent with each other. Given the same latent, the policy generates a trajectory which should match the trajectory predicted by the model. This model provides a built-in prediction mechanism, by predicting the outcome of closed loop policy behavior. We propose a novel algorithm for performing hierarchical RL with this model, combining model-based planning in the learned latent space with an unsupervised exploration objective. We show that our model is effective at reasoning over long horizons with sparse rewards for several simulated tasks, outperforming standard reinforcement learning methods and prior methods for hierarchical reasoning, model-based planning, and exploration. This model provides a built-in prediction mechanism, by predicting the outcome of closed loop policy behavior. We propose a novel algorithm for performing hierarchical RL with this model, combining model-based planning in the learned latent space with an unsupervised exploration objective. We show that our model is effective at reasoning over long horizons with sparse rewards for several simulated tasks, outperforming standard reinforcement learning methods and prior methods for hierarchical reasoning, model-based planning, and exploration.

This paper approaches that need by learning continuous latent representations of whole trajectories. Its model, SeCTAR, draws on variational autoencoders and turns the learning of lower-level behavior into a trajectory-level generative modeling problem.

The central mechanism pairs a latent-conditioned policy with a latent-conditioned predictive model. Given the same latent representation, the policy should produce a trajectory matching the model’s prediction. The authors combine planning in the learned latent space with an unsupervised exploration objective. Across several simulated tasks with sparse rewards, the method supports reasoning over long horizons and outperforms the evaluated standard reinforcement learning and prior hierarchical, planning, and exploration methods. The findings show how jointly learning behavior and its predicted outcome can support temporally extended, multistage decisions.
summary.tldr: SeCTAR learns matching trajectory policies and predictions in a latent space to support hierarchical planning on long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks.

title: Self-Consistent Trajectory Autoencoder: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Trajectory Embeddings

abstract: Given a large matrix $A\in\real^{n\times d}$, we consider the problem of computing a sketch matrix $B\in\real^{\ell\times d}$ which is significantly smaller than but still well approximates $A$. We are interested in minimizing the covariance error $\norm{A^TA-B^TB}_2.$We consider the problems in the streaming model, where the algorithm can only make one pass over the input with limited working space. The popular Frequent Directions algorithm of Liberty (2013) and its variants achieve optimal space-error tradeoff. However, whether the running time can be improved remains an unanswered question.In this paper, we almost settle the time complexity of this problem. In particular, we provide new space-optimal algorithms with faster running times. Moreover, we also show that the running times of our algorithms are near-optimal unless the state-of-the-art running time of matrix multiplication can be improved significantly.

paragraphs: Matrix sketching compresses a large matrix into a much smaller one while preserving information needed for later computation. This paper focuses on covariance error: how closely the sketch reproduces the original matrix’s product with its transpose in the specified orientation. The setting is streaming, allowing only one pass over the input and limited working memory.

Frequent Directions and its variants already achieve an optimal tradeoff between memory use and approximation error. The unresolved issue addressed here is speed. The authors introduce faster algorithms that preserve space optimality, improving running time without giving up the established relationship between storage and covariance accuracy.

They also give a conditional account of how much further runtime improvement is possible. Their algorithms are near-optimal unless the state-of-the-art time for matrix multiplication can be improved significantly. This ties the remaining computational room for progress to a broader matrix-computation problem, rather than claiming an unconditional lower bound that rules out all future improvements.
summary.tldr: Faster streaming matrix sketches retain optimal space-error tradeoffs and have conditionally near-optimal running times.

title: Near Optimal Frequent Directions for Sketching Dense and Sparse Matrices

abstract: In classification with a reject option, the classifier is allowed in uncertain cases to abstain from prediction. The classical cost based model of an optimal classifier with a reject option requires the cost of rejection to be defined explicitly. An alternative bounded-improvement model, avoiding the notion of the reject cost, seeks for a classifier with a guaranteed selective risk and maximal cover. We prove that both models share the same class of optimal strategies, and we provide an explicit relation between the reject cost and the target risk being the parameters of the two models. An optimal rejection strategy for both models is based on thresholding the conditional risk defined by posterior probabilities which are usually unavailable. We propose a discriminative algorithm learning an uncertainty function which preserves ordering of the input space induced by the conditional risk, and hence can be used to construct optimal rejection strategies.

paragraphs: A classifier with a reject option can abstain when a prediction is too uncertain. One standard formulation assigns an explicit cost to rejection. Another seeks to predict on as many inputs as possible while keeping the risk among accepted predictions below a target. The second formulation avoids having to specify a rejection cost.

The paper proves that these two formulations share the same class of optimal strategies. It also gives an explicit relationship between the rejection cost and the target risk. This connects two apparently different ways of choosing when to abstain and shows how their controlling parameters relate.

For both formulations, an optimal rejection rule thresholds the conditional risk, which depends on posterior probabilities that are usually unavailable. The authors propose learning an uncertainty function discriminatively so that it preserves the ordering of inputs induced by that risk. Preserving the ordering makes the function usable for constructing optimal rejection strategies. The key learning target is therefore a risk-consistent ranking of inputs, supporting decisions about which predictions to accept.
summary.tldr: Two optimal abstention formulations are equivalent, motivating an uncertainty function that preserves the ordering of conditional prediction risk.

title: On discriminative learning of prediction uncertainty

abstract: We consider decentralized stochastic optimization with the objective function (e.g. data samples for machine learning tasks) being distributed over n machines that can only communicate to their neighbors on a fixed communication graph. To address the communication bottleneck, the nodes compress (e.g. quantize or sparsify) their model updates. We cover both unbiased and biased compression operators with quality denoted by \delta <= 1 (\delta=1 meaning no compression). We (i) propose a novel gossip-based stochastic gradient descent algorithm, CHOCO-SGD, that converges at rate O(1/(nT) + 1/(T \rho^2 \delta)^2) for strongly convex objectives, where T denotes the number of iterations and \rho the eigengap of the connectivity matrix. We (ii) present a novel gossip algorithm, CHOCO-GOSSIP, for the average consensus problem that converges in time O(1/(\rho^2\delta) \log (1/\epsilon)) for accuracy \epsilon > 0. This is (up to our knowledge) the first gossip algorithm that supports arbitrary compressed messages for \delta > 0 and still exhibits linear convergence. We (iii) show in experiments that both of our algorithms do outperform the respective state-of-the-art baselines and CHOCO-SGD can reduce communication by at least two orders of magnitudes.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization across machines that communicate only with neighbors on a fixed graph. Sending model updates can become a bottleneck, so the machines compress those messages through operations such as quantization or sparsification. The analysis accommodates both biased and unbiased compression, with a quality parameter describing how much information the compression preserves.

The authors introduce CHOCO-SGD for stochastic optimization and CHOCO-GOSSIP for average consensus, where machines work toward agreement on an average. For strongly convex objectives, the CHOCO-SGD convergence rate depends on the number of machines, iteration count, graph connectivity, and compression quality. CHOCO-GOSSIP achieves linear convergence with arbitrary compressed messages when their quality parameter is positive.

These guarantees show how communication structure and compression enter the cost of reaching an accurate result. In experiments, both algorithms outperform their respective state-of-the-art baselines, and CHOCO-SGD reduces communication by at least two orders of magnitude. The paper therefore combines theoretical support for compressed neighbor communication with empirical evidence of substantial communication savings in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: CHOCO-SGD and CHOCO-GOSSIP support compressed neighbor communication with convergence guarantees and substantial experimental communication savings.

title: Decentralized Stochastic Optimization and Gossip Algorithms with Compressed Communication

abstract: In distributional reinforcement learning (RL), the estimated distribution of value functions model both the parametric and intrinsic uncertainties. We propose a novel and efficient exploration method for deep RL that has two components. The first is a decaying schedule to suppress the intrinsic uncertainty. The second is an exploration bonus calculated from the upper quantiles of the learned distribution. In Atari 2600 games, our method achieves 483 % average gain across 49 games in cumulative rewards over QR-DQN. We also compared our algorithm with QR-DQN in a challenging 3D driving simulator (CARLA). Results show that our algorithm achieves nearoptimal safety rewards twice faster than QRDQN.

In Atari 2600 games, our method achieves 483 % average gain across 49 games in cumulative rewards over QR-DQN. We also compared our algorithm with QR-DQN in a challenging 3D driving simulator (CARLA). Results show that our algorithm achieves nearoptimal safety rewards twice faster than QRDQN.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates a distribution of values, giving an agent more information than a single expected value. The paper observes that this distribution reflects both uncertainty about model parameters and uncertainty intrinsic to outcomes. Its exploration method uses that distribution while seeking to suppress the influence of intrinsic uncertainty.

The method combines two components: a decaying schedule for suppressing intrinsic uncertainty and an exploration bonus computed from the upper quantiles of the learned distribution. Upper quantiles describe the high-value part of that distribution. Using them to construct a bonus connects exploration decisions to potentially favorable outcomes represented by the learner.

Across 49 Atari 2600 games, the authors report a 483% average gain in cumulative rewards over QR-DQN. In the CARLA driving simulator, they report reaching near-optimal safety rewards twice as fast as QR-DQN. These findings support the exploration strategy in the evaluated settings, showing that a learned value distribution can guide exploration as well as represent possible returns.
summary.tldr: An exploration bonus based on upper value quantiles, combined with suppression of intrinsic uncertainty, improves reported Atari rewards and CARLA learning speed over QR-DQN.

title: Distributional Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Exploration

abstract: Neural networks are difficult to interpret and debug. We introduce testing techniques for neural networks that can discover errors occurring only for rare inputs. Specifically, we develop coverage-guided fuzzing (CGF) methods for neural networks. In CGF, random mutations of inputs are guided by a coverage metric toward the goal of satisfying user-specified constraints. We describe how approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms can provide this coverage metric for neural networks. We then combine these methods with techniques for property-based testing (PBT). In PBT, one asserts properties that a function should satisfy and the system automatically generates tests exercising those properties. We then apply this system to practical goals including (but not limited to) surfacing broken loss functions in popular GitHub repositories and making performance improvements to TensorFlow. Finally, we release an open source library called TensorFuzz that implements the described techniques.
