paragraphs: TensorFuzz targets neural-network errors that occur only on rare inputs. Such failures can be difficult to discover through ordinary testing, especially when a network's behavior is hard to interpret. The paper adapts coverage-guided fuzzing to guide the search for inputs that satisfy user-specified constraints.

The testing process randomly mutates inputs and uses a coverage metric to direct that exploration. The authors explain how approximate nearest-neighbor algorithms can supply a suitable coverage metric for neural networks. They combine this mechanism with property-based testing, in which users state properties a function should satisfy and the system automatically generates tests that exercise those properties.

The authors apply the system to practical debugging work, including finding broken loss functions in popular GitHub repositories and improving TensorFlow performance. They also release the techniques in an open-source library called TensorFuzz. The contribution makes automated input generation responsive to coverage and explicit properties, giving developers a systematic way to search for unusual failures.
summary.tldr: TensorFuzz combines coverage-guided input mutation with property-based testing to discover rare neural-network errors.

title: TensorFuzz: Debugging Neural Networks with Coverage-Guided Fuzzing

abstract: Many real-world problems require trading off multiple competing objectives. However, these objectives are often in different units and/or scales, which can make it challenging for practitioners to express numerical preferences over objectives in their native units. In this paper we propose a novel algorithm for multi-objective reinforcement learning that enables setting desired preferences for objectives in a scale-invariant way. We propose to learn an action distribution for each objective, and we use supervised learning to fit a parametric policy to a combination of these distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on challenging high-dimensional real and simulated robotics tasks, and show that setting different preferences in our framework allows us to trace out the space of nondominated solutions.

We propose to learn an action distribution for each objective, and we use supervised learning to fit a parametric policy to a combination of these distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on challenging high-dimensional real and simulated robotics tasks, and show that setting different preferences in our framework allows us to trace out the space of nondominated solutions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning problems often involve several competing objectives whose numerical values use different units or scales. This makes preferences difficult to express directly: the numerical size of an objective can interfere with the intended tradeoff. The paper proposes a way to specify preferences that is invariant to these scale differences.

The method learns a separate action distribution for each objective. It then combines those distributions and uses supervised learning to fit a parametric policy to the combination. This moves the combination step into the space of action distributions, providing a common basis for bringing together objectives whose original numerical measurements may be difficult to compare.

The authors demonstrate the approach on high-dimensional robotics tasks in both real and simulated settings. Varying the preferences traces out nondominated solutions: choices where improving one objective cannot be achieved without sacrificing another. The results show how the framework can expose different effective tradeoffs, allowing preference changes to select among policies rather than forcing every objective into one native numerical scale.
summary.tldr: Combining objective-specific action distributions enables scale-invariant preferences and effective tradeoffs in multi-objective reinforcement learning.

title: A distributional view on multi-objective policy optimization

abstract: A common strategy in modern learning systems is to learn a representation that is useful for many tasks, a.k.a. representation learning. We study this strategy in the imitation learning setting for Markov decision processes (MDPs) where multiple experts’ trajectories are available. We formulate representation learning as a bi-level optimization problem where the “outer" optimization tries to learn the joint representation and the “inner" optimization encodes the imitation learning setup and tries to learn task-specific parameters. We instantiate this framework for the imitation learning settings of behavior cloning and observation-alone. Theoretically, we show using our framework that representation learning can provide sample complexity benefits for imitation learning in both settings. We also provide proof-of-concept experiments to verify our theory.

paragraphs: When multiple related tasks are available, a shared representation may help each task learn from fewer examples. This paper studies that possibility for imitation learning in Markov decision processes, using trajectories from multiple experts. The central question is whether learning common features can provide provable benefits when acquiring behavior from demonstrations.

The authors express the problem as a bi-level optimization. The outer level learns the shared representation, while the inner level learns task-specific parameters according to the imitation-learning setup. This separates what should transfer across tasks from what must be learned for a particular task, while linking both through a single optimization framework.

The framework is instantiated for behavior cloning and observation-alone imitation learning. In both settings, the theoretical results show that representation learning can reduce sample complexity, meaning fewer observations can be sufficient for learning under the analyzed framework. Proof-of-concept experiments support the theory, illustrating the potential value of shared representations across the two imitation-learning settings.
summary.tldr: A bi-level framework shows that shared representation learning can reduce sample requirements for behavior cloning and observation-alone imitation learning.

title: Provable Representation Learning for Imitation Learning via Bi-level Optimization

abstract: Machine learning and deep learning in particular has been recently used to successfully address many tasks in the domain of code such as finding and fixing bugs, code completion, decompilation, type inference and many others. However, the issue of adversarial robustness of models for code has gone largely unnoticed. In this work, we explore this issue by: (i) instantiating adversarial attacks for code (a domain with discrete and highly structured inputs), (ii) showing that, similar to other domains, neural models for code are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, and (iii) combining existing and novel techniques to improve robustness while preserving high accuracy.
originalAbstract: Machine learning and deep learning in particular has been recently used to successfully address many tasks in the domain of code such as finding and fixing bugs, code completion, decompilation, type inference and many others. paragraphs: Machine learning models increasingly handle programming tasks such as bug detection, code completion, and type inference. This paper investigates whether those models remain reliable when their inputs are deliberately manipulated to cause mistakes. Its central concern is adversarial robustness in a domain where inputs are discrete and governed by substantial structure.

The researchers develop adversarial attacks specifically for code and use them to demonstrate vulnerabilities in neural models. Moving this question into programming requires accounting for the nature of code inputs, rather than assuming that attacks designed for other domains directly apply. The work establishes that successful performance on code tasks can coexist with susceptibility to adversarial attacks.

The paper also combines existing techniques with new ones to improve robustness while maintaining high accuracy. Its contribution therefore covers both exposing weaknesses and addressing them. The stated result is improved resistance to attacks alongside strong task performance, making robustness an additional consideration when assessing the capabilities of models that operate on code.
summary.tldr: The paper demonstrates adversarial vulnerabilities in neural models for code and combines techniques to improve robustness while preserving high accuracy.

title: Adversarial Robustness for Code

abstract: We compare the model-free reinforcement learning with the model-based approaches through the lens of the expressive power of neural networks for policies, Q-functions, and dynamics. We show, theoretically and empirically, that even for one-dimensional continuous state space, there are many MDPs whose optimal Q-functions and policies are much more complex than the dynamics. For these MDPs, model-based planning is a favorable algorithm, because the resulting policies can approximate the optimal policy significantly better than a neural network parameterization can, and model-free or model-based policy optimization rely on policy parameterization. Motivated by the theory, we apply a simple multi-step model-based bootstrapping planner (BOOTS) to bootstrap a weak Q-function into a stronger policy. Empirical results show that applying BOOTS on top of model-based or model-free policy optimization algorithms at the test time improves the performance on benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: The paper compares reinforcement-learning approaches by asking how difficult it is for neural networks to represent dynamics, action values, and policies. It shows theoretically and empirically that many decision processes have optimal policies and Q-functions much more complex than their dynamics. This can happen even with a one-dimensional continuous state space.

For these processes, planning with a model is favorable because the resulting policy can approximate the optimum substantially better than a neural-network policy parameterization. The distinction also applies within model-based learning: policy optimization still depends on how the policy is represented, even when a dynamics model is available.

Motivated by this analysis, the authors introduce BOOTS, a simple multi-step model-based bootstrapping planner that turns a weak Q-function into a stronger policy. Applying it at test time improves benchmark performance on top of both model-based and model-free policy optimization algorithms. The results support planning as a way to overcome representational difficulty in the studied settings, rather than establishing that every environment favors model-based methods.
summary.tldr: Simple dynamics can yield complex optimal policies, motivating a test-time planner that improves policies built from weaker Q-functions.

title: On the Expressivity of Neural Networks for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper we introduce a new approach to topic modelling that scales to large datasets by using a compact representation of the data and by leveraging the GPU architecture. In this approach, topics are learned directly from the co-occurrence data of the corpus. In particular, we introduce a novel mixture model which we term the Full Dependence Mixture (FDM) model. FDMs model second moment under general generative assumptions on the data. While there is previous work on topic modeling using second moments, we develop a direct stochastic optimization procedure for fitting an FDM with a single Kullback Leibler objective. Moment methods in general have the benefit that an iteration no longer needs to scale with the size of the corpus. Our approach allows us to leverage standard optimizers and GPUs for the problem of topic modeling. In particular, we evaluate the approach on two large datasets, NeurIPS papers and a Twitter corpus, with a large number of topics, and show that the approach performs comparably or better than the standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: Topic modeling large text collections can be expensive when repeated optimization work depends on the size of the whole corpus. This paper learns topics directly from word co-occurrence data, using a compact representation that supports GPU computation. The approach aims to make large-scale topic discovery more computationally manageable.

The authors introduce the Full Dependence Mixture model, which represents second-moment information under general generative assumptions. Although earlier topic-modeling methods also used second moments, this paper provides a direct stochastic optimization procedure with a single Kullback–Leibler objective. That formulation allows the model to be fitted using standard optimizers and GPUs.

The key scaling benefit is that an optimization iteration no longer needs to grow with corpus size. The authors evaluate the method with many topics on two large collections, NeurIPS papers and Twitter text, and report performance comparable to or better than standard benchmarks. The contribution combines a compact statistical representation with a fitting procedure designed to make effective use of common optimization tools and hardware.
summary.tldr: Full Dependence Mixtures learn topics from compact co-occurrence statistics using GPU-friendly stochastic optimization, with competitive results on two large corpora.

title: Topic Modeling via Full Dependence Mixtures

abstract: We propose an approach to learning with graph-structured data in the problem domain of graph classification. In particular, we present a novel type of readout operation to aggregate node features into a graph-level representation. To this end, we leverage persistent homology computed via a real-valued, learnable, filter function. We establish the theoretical foundation for differentiating through the persistent homology computation. Empirically, we show that this type of readout operation compares favorably to previous techniques, especially when the graph connectivity structure is informative for the learning problem.

We establish the theoretical foundation for differentiating through the persistent homology computation. Empirically, we show that this type of readout operation compares favorably to previous techniques, especially when the graph connectivity structure is informative for the learning problem.

paragraphs: Graph classification requires turning information about individual nodes into a representation of the whole graph. This paper introduces a new readout operation for that step. Its design uses persistent homology, bringing information about graph structure into the aggregation of node features rather than treating the readout solely as a combination of feature values.

The persistent homology computation is controlled by a learnable function that assigns real-valued filter values. Learning this function allows the structural summary to adapt to the classification problem. The authors establish a theoretical foundation for differentiating through the persistent homology computation, making this component available to gradient-based learning.

Empirically, the resulting readout compares favorably with earlier techniques, particularly when graph connectivity is informative for classification. This qualification explains where its structural emphasis is especially useful: the arrangement of connections must help distinguish the graphs. The contribution links a topological description of structure to a trainable graph-level representation, with both differentiation theory and classification experiments supporting the approach.
summary.tldr: A differentiable persistent-homology readout learns graph-level representations that perform favorably, especially when connectivity helps determine graph classes.

title: Graph Filtration Learning

abstract: Learning from unordered sets is a fundamental learning setup, recently attracting increasing attention. Research in this area has focused on the case where elements of the set are represented by feature vectors, and far less emphasis has been given to the common case where set elements themselves adhere to their own symmetries. That case is relevant to numerous applications, from deblurring image bursts to multi-view 3D shape recognition and reconstruction. In this paper, we present a principled approach to learning sets of general symmetric elements. We first characterize the space of linear layers that are equivariant both to element reordering and to the inherent symmetries of elements, like translation in the case of images. We further show that networks that are composed of these layers, called Deep Sets for Symmetric Elements layers (DSS), are universal approximators of both invariant and equivariant functions. DSS layers are also straightforward to implement. Finally, we show that they improve over existing set-learning architectures in a series of experiments with images, graphs, and point-clouds.

paragraphs: Learning from an unordered set requires a model to handle changes in element order appropriately. This paper considers an additional structure: the elements themselves may have symmetries, such as translations of images. Applications mentioned include image-burst deblurring and multi-view recognition and reconstruction of three-dimensional shapes.

The authors characterize linear layers that are equivariant to both reordering the set and applying the elements’ inherent symmetries. Equivariance means the output changes in a corresponding way when the input is transformed. These layers, called Deep Sets for Symmetric Elements or DSS layers, give a principled way to encode both kinds of structure within one architecture.

The paper proves that networks built from DSS layers are universal approximators of invariant and equivariant functions. It also describes the layers as straightforward to implement and reports improvements over existing set-learning architectures on images, graphs, and point clouds. The contribution combines an expressiveness result with an architectural design that accounts for structure inside each set element.
summary.tldr: DSS layers account for both set reordering and element symmetries, with universal approximation results and reported empirical improvements.

title: On Learning Sets of Symmetric Elements

abstract: We introduce the lookahead-bounded Q-learning (LBQL) algorithm, a new, provably convergent variant of Q-learning that seeks to improve the performance of standard Q-learning in stochastic environments through the use of “lookahead” upper and lower bounds. To do this, LBQL employs previously collected experience and each iteration’s state-action values as dual feasible penalties to construct a sequence of sampled information relaxation problems. The solutions to these problems provide estimated upper and lower bounds on the optimal value, which we track via stochastic approximation. These quantities are then used to constrain the iterates to stay within the bounds at every iteration. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems show that LBQL exhibits faster convergence and more robustness to hyperparameters when compared to standard Q-learning and several related techniques. Our approach is particularly appealing in problems that require expensive simulations or real-world interactions.

paragraphs: Lookahead-bounded Q-learning aims to improve standard Q-learning in stochastic environments by keeping its value estimates within estimated upper and lower bounds. The method uses lookahead calculations to supply these bounds, giving each learning iteration additional information about the optimal value. It is presented as a provably convergent variant of Q-learning.

To construct the bounds, the algorithm combines previously collected experience with the current state-action values. Those values serve as dual feasible penalties in sampled information relaxation problems. Solving these problems supplies upper and lower value estimates, which are tracked using stochastic approximation. The resulting bounds then constrain the Q-learning iterates at every iteration.

On benchmark problems, numerical experiments show faster convergence and greater robustness to hyperparameter choices than standard Q-learning and several related methods. Reusing experience to guide the updates makes the approach particularly appealing where fresh simulations or real-world interactions are expensive. The reported contribution joins a convergence result with an empirical improvement in how efficiently and reliably value estimates develop.
summary.tldr: Lookahead-bounded Q-learning constrains value updates using estimated bounds, with proven convergence and improved convergence speed in benchmark experiments.

title: Lookahead-Bounded Q-learning

abstract: User interests are usually dynamic in the real world, which poses both theoretical and practical challenges for learning accurate preferences from rich behavior data. Among existing user behavior modeling solutions, attention networks are widely adopted for its effectiveness and relative simplicity. Despite being extensively studied, existing attentions still suffer from two limitations: i) conventional attentions mainly take into account the spatial correlation between user behaviors, regardless the distance between those behaviors in the continuous time space; and ii) these attentions mostly provide a dense and undistinguished distribution over all past behaviors then attentively encode them into the output latent representations. This is however not suitable in practical scenarios where a user’s future actions are relevant to a small subset of her/his historical behaviors. In this paper, we propose a novel attention network, named \textit{self-modulating attention}, that models the complex and non-linearly evolving dynamic user preferences. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on top-N sequential recommendation tasks, and the results on three large-scale real-world datasets show that our model can achieve state-of-the-art performance.

This is however not suitable in practical scenarios where a user’s future actions are relevant to a small subset of her/his historical behaviors. In this paper, we propose a novel attention network, named \textit{self-modulating attention}, that models the complex and non-linearly evolving dynamic user preferences. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on top-N sequential recommendation tasks, and the results on three large-scale real-world datasets show that our model can achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Sequential recommendation uses a person's behavior history to anticipate future choices, but interests change over time. The paper identifies two shortcomings of existing attention mechanisms: they can overlook continuous time gaps between behaviors, and they often distribute attention broadly over the history. This is problematic when only a small part of that history is relevant to the next action.

The authors propose self-modulating attention to model preferences that evolve in complex, nonlinear ways. The approach brings temporal dynamics into the attention-based representation of behavior. Its motivation is that relevance depends on more than relationships among past actions: when those actions occurred and which ones matter to the current prediction also deserve attention.

Evaluation focuses on top-N sequential recommendation, where the model produces a ranked selection of candidate items. Results on three large real-world datasets show that the method can achieve state-of-the-art performance. The findings support the usefulness of modeling changing preferences within attention, with the performance claim grounded in the recommendation datasets studied.
summary.tldr: Self-modulating attention models evolving user preferences and achieves strong results on sequential recommendation datasets.

title: Learning Self-Modulating Attention in Continuous Time Space with Applications to Sequential Recommendation

abstract: Instrumental variable methods provide a powerful approach to estimating causal effects in the presence of unobserved confounding. But a key challenge when applying them is the reliance on untestable "exclusion" assumptions that rule out any relationship between the instrument variable and the response that is not mediated by the treatment. In this paper, we show how to perform consistent IV estimation despite violations of the exclusion assumption. In particular, we show that when one has multiple candidate instruments, only a majority of these candidates—or, more generally, the modal candidate-response relationship—needs to be valid to estimate the causal effect. Our approach uses an estimate of the modal prediction from an ensemble of instrumental variable estimators. The technique is simple to apply and is "black-box" in the sense that it may be used with any instrumental variable estimator as long as the treatment effect is identified for each valid instrument independently. As such, it is compatible with recent machine-learning based estimators that allow for the estimation of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) on complex, high dimensional data. Experimentally, we achieve accurate estimates of conditional average treatment effects using an ensemble of deep network-based estimators, including on a challenging simulated Mendelian Randomization problem.

Their use typically relies on an exclusion assumption: an instrument affects the response only through the treatment. This paper develops consistent estimation when some candidate instruments violate that assumption, provided there is suitable agreement among the valid candidates.

A majority of candidates being valid is sufficient; more generally, the modal candidate-response relationship must be valid. The method estimates the modal prediction from an ensemble of instrumental-variable estimators. It is compatible with different underlying estimators, provided each valid instrument independently identifies the treatment effect. These conditions are essential to the stated guarantee.

The ensemble approach can also use machine-learning estimators for conditional average treatment effects on complex, high-dimensional data. Experiments with deep-network estimators produce accurate estimates, including in a challenging simulated Mendelian randomization problem. The contribution makes it possible to use a collection containing invalid instruments under the stated validity structure, while retaining flexibility in how each individual causal estimate is produced.
summary.tldr: An ensemble’s modal prediction supports consistent causal estimation with some invalid instruments when the valid instruments satisfy the stated identification and agreement conditions.

title: Valid Causal Inference with (Some) Invalid Instruments

abstract: We formally study how contrastive learning learns the feature representations for neural networks by investigating its feature learning process. We consider the case where our data are comprised of two types of features: the sparse features which we want to learn from, and the dense features we want to get rid of. Theoretically, we prove that contrastive learning using ReLU networks provably learns the desired features if proper augmentations are adopted. We present an underlying principle called feature decoupling to explain the effects of augmentations, where we theoretically characterize how augmentations can reduce the correlations of dense features between positive samples while keeping the correlations of sparse features intact, thereby forcing the neural networks to learn from the self-supervision of sparse features. Empirically, we verified that the feature decoupling principle matches the underlying mechanism of contrastive learning in practice.

This paper studies a setting where data contain desired sparse features and unwanted dense features. The theoretical question is whether training can select the useful sparse structure while discarding the dense structure.

For ReLU networks, the authors prove that contrastive learning learns the desired features when appropriate augmentations are used. They explain this through feature decoupling: augmentations can weaken correlations in dense features between positive samples while preserving correlations in sparse features. The shared sparse structure then supplies the self-supervised signal that directs learning.

Empirical investigations find that this feature-decoupling principle matches the mechanism observed in practice. The result gives augmentations a specific explanatory role in determining what the representation retains. Its theoretical guarantee depends on the studied feature setting and suitable augmentations, while the experiments support the relevance of that explanation to practical contrastive learning.
summary.tldr: Under the studied sparse-and-dense feature setting, suitable augmentations make contrastive ReLU networks learn desired features through feature decoupling.

title: Toward Understanding the Feature Learning Process of Self-supervised Contrastive Learning

abstract: Inverse kinematic (IK) methods recover the parameters of the joints, given the desired position of selected elements in the kinematic chain. While the problem is well-defined and low-dimensional, it has to be solved rapidly, accounting for multiple possible solutions. In this work, we propose a neural IK method that employs the hierarchical structure of the problem to sequentially sample valid joint angles conditioned on the desired position and on the preceding joints along the chain. In our solution, a hypernetwork $f$ recovers the parameters of multiple primary networks {$g_1,g_2,…,g_N$, where $N$ is the number of joints}, such that each $g_i$ outputs a distribution of possible joint angles, and is conditioned on the sampled values obtained from the previous primary networks $g_j, j<i$. The hypernetwork can be trained on readily available pairs of matching joint angles and positions, without observing multiple solutions. At test time, a high-variance joint distribution is presented, by sampling sequentially from the primary networks. We demonstrate the advantage of the proposed method both in comparison to other IK methods for isolated instances of IK and with regard to following the path of the end effector in Cartesian space.

paragraphs: Inverse kinematics finds joint parameters that place selected parts of a joint chain at desired positions. Several joint configurations can satisfy the same positional target, so a useful method must account for multiple solutions while responding quickly. This paper builds a neural method around the hierarchical structure of the chain.

A hypernetwork produces the parameters of a separate primary network for each joint. Each primary network outputs a distribution over possible joint angles, conditioned on the desired position and the angles already sampled for earlier joints. Sequential sampling therefore represents dependencies along the chain rather than choosing each joint angle independently.

The hypernetwork can be trained using available matching pairs of joint angles and positions without observing multiple solutions for each target. At test time, sequential sampling yields a joint distribution with high variance, supporting a range of configurations. The authors demonstrate advantages over other inverse-kinematics methods both for individual target instances and for following an end-effector path in Cartesian space. These evaluations address isolated solutions as well as movement along a desired path.
summary.tldr: A hypernetwork learns sequential joint-angle distributions to generate multiple inverse-kinematics solutions from ordinary angle-position training pairs.

title: Neural Inverse Kinematic

abstract: We justify the fast equilibrium conjecture on stochastic gradient descent from (Li et al. 2020) under the assumptions that critical points are non-degenerate and the stochastic noise is a standard Gaussian. In this case, we prove an SGD with constant effective learning rate consists of three stages: descent, diffusion and tunneling, and explicitly identify temporary equilibrium states in the normalized parameter space that can be observed within practical training time. This interprets the gap between the mixing time in the fast equilibrium conjecture and the previously known upper bound. While our assumptions do not represent typical implementations of SGD of neural networks in practice, this is the first description of the three-stage mechanism in any case. The main finding in this mechanism is that a temporary equilibrium of local nature is quickly achieved after polynomial time (in term of the reciprocal of the intrinsic learning rate) and then stabilizes within observable time scales; and that the temporary equilibrium is in general different from the global Gibbs equilibrium, which will only appear after an exponentially long period beyond typical training limits. Our experiments support that this mechanism may extend to the general case.

paragraphs: This paper explains how stochastic gradient descent can appear to settle quickly even when reaching its ultimate equilibrium would take far longer. Under non-degenerate critical points and standard Gaussian stochastic noise, the authors prove a three-stage evolution for SGD with a constant effective learning rate: descent, diffusion, and tunneling.

The analysis identifies temporary equilibrium states in normalized parameter space that can arise within practical training time. A local temporary equilibrium is reached after time polynomial in the reciprocal of the intrinsic learning rate and then remains stable over observable timescales. In general, this state differs from the global Gibbs equilibrium, which emerges only after an exponentially long period beyond typical training limits.

The distinction helps reconcile fast observed stabilization with earlier, much longer mixing-time bounds. The authors explicitly note that their assumptions do not describe typical neural-network SGD implementations. Their experiments support the possibility that the mechanism extends more broadly, but do not establish that extension as a theorem. The contribution is a proved account of the three stages in a specific setting and a concrete explanation of temporary equilibrium.
summary.tldr: Under specific assumptions, SGD quickly reaches a temporary local equilibrium long before its global equilibrium becomes observable.

title: Three-stage Evolution and Fast Equilibrium for SGD with Non-degerate Critical Points

abstract: We study adversarial attacks on linear stochastic bandits: by manipulating the rewards, an adversary aims to control the behaviour of the bandit algorithm. Perhaps surprisingly, we first show that some attack goals can never be achieved. This is in a sharp contrast to context-free stochastic bandits, and is intrinsically due to the correlation among arms in linear stochastic bandits. Motivated by this finding, this paper studies the attackability of a $k$-armed linear bandit environment. We first provide a complete necessity and sufficiency characterization of attackability based on the geometry of the arms’ context vectors. We then propose a two-stage attack method against LinUCB and Robust Phase Elimination. The method first asserts whether the given environment is attackable; and if yes, it poisons the rewards to force the algorithm to pull a target arm linear times using only a sublinear cost. Numerical experiments further validate the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of the proposed attack method.

paragraphs: An adversary can try to manipulate a bandit learner by altering the rewards it observes. This paper shows that, in linear stochastic bandits, some attack goals are impossible. The correlations among arms constrain what reward manipulation can accomplish, creating a different situation from context-free stochastic bandits.

The authors give a necessary-and-sufficient characterization of attackability based on the geometry of the arms' context vectors. This makes attackability a property that can be assessed from the environment's structure. They then propose a two-stage method against LinUCB and Robust Phase Elimination: first determine whether the environment is attackable, and then carry out reward poisoning when that condition holds.

In attackable environments, the method forces selection of a target arm a number of times growing linearly with the interaction horizon, while its attack cost grows sublinearly. Numerical experiments support the method's effectiveness and cost efficiency. The central result combines a boundary on adversarial power with an attack construction inside that boundary; it does not claim that every target can be forced in every linear-bandit environment.
summary.tldr: Arm geometry determines when linear bandits are attackable, and a conditional attack can force frequent target-arm selections at sublinear cost.

title: When Are Linear Stochastic Bandits Attackable?

abstract: The speed of gradient descent for convex Lipschitz functions is highly dependent on the choice of learning rate. Setting the learning rate to achieve the optimal convergence rate requires knowing the distance D from the initial point to the solution set. In this work, we describe a single-loop method, with no back-tracking or line searches, which does not require knowledge of D yet asymptotically achieves the optimal rate of convergence for the complexity class of convex Lipschitz functions. Our approach is the first parameter-free method for this class without additional multiplicative log factors in the convergence rate. We present extensive experiments for SGD and Adam variants of our method, where the method automatically matches hand-tuned learning rates across more than a dozen diverse machine learning problems, including large-scale vision and language problems. Our method is practical, efficient and requires no additional function value or gradient evaluations each step. An implementation is provided in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Gradient descent can be highly sensitive to its learning rate. For convex Lipschitz functions, choosing a rate with optimal convergence requires information about the distance from the starting point to the solution set. This paper introduces D-Adaptation to achieve the desired asymptotic rate without knowing that distance in advance.

The method uses a single optimization loop without backtracking or line searches. Its theoretical result reaches the optimal convergence rate for this function class without the extra multiplicative logarithmic factors present in earlier parameter-free methods. It also requires no additional function-value or gradient evaluations at each step, making the adaptation computationally practical.

The authors test SGD and Adam variants on more than a dozen machine learning problems, including large-scale vision and language tasks. In these experiments, the method automatically matches hand-tuned learning rates. The theory and experiments establish different parts of the case: the convergence guarantee concerns convex Lipschitz optimization, while the broader machine learning evaluations demonstrate the practical behavior of the proposed variants.
summary.tldr: D-Adaptation removes learning-rate tuning while achieving an optimal asymptotic convex convergence rate and matching hand-tuned rates in reported experiments.

title: Learning-Rate-Free Learning by D-Adaptation

abstract: Selecting hyperparameters in deep learning greatly impacts its effectiveness but requires manual effort and expertise. Recent works show that Bayesian model selection with Laplace approximations can allow to optimize such hyperparameters just like standard neural network parameters using gradients and on the training data. However, estimating a single hyperparameter gradient requires a pass through the entire dataset, limiting the scalability of such algorithms. In this work, we overcome this issue by introducing lower bounds to the linearized Laplace approximation of the marginal likelihood. In contrast to previous estimators, these bounds are amenable to stochastic-gradient-based optimization and allow to trade off estimation accuracy against computational complexity. We derive them using the function-space form of the linearized Laplace, which can be estimated using the neural tangent kernel. Experimentally, we show that the estimators can significantly accelerate gradient-based hyperparameter optimization.
authors: Tycho F. A. Van Der Ouderaa

paragraphs: Hyperparameters strongly influence neural network performance, but selecting them often requires manual effort. Bayesian model selection with a Laplace approximation provides a way to optimize them using gradients on training data. The scalability problem addressed here is that previous estimators require a full dataset pass for each hyperparameter gradient.

The authors introduce lower bounds on the linearized Laplace approximation to marginal likelihood. These bounds support stochastic gradient optimization, providing a way to estimate useful updates without the same full-data requirement. Their derivation uses a function-space formulation that can be estimated through the neural tangent kernel.

The resulting estimators allow a tradeoff between estimation accuracy and computational cost. This matters because the objective being optimized is already an approximation, and the method explicitly exposes another computational choice within its estimation. Experiments show that the proposed estimators can substantially accelerate gradient-based hyperparameter optimization. The contribution is therefore a more scalable way to use Bayesian selection objectives, supported by empirical speed improvements rather than a claim that every hyperparameter search becomes faster.
summary.tldr: Neural tangent kernel-based bounds enable stochastic hyperparameter optimization and can substantially reduce its computational cost.

title: Stochastic Marginal Likelihood Gradients using Neural Tangent Kernels

abstract: Weighting methods in causal inference have been widely used to achieve a desirable level of covariate balancing. However, the existing weighting methods have desirable theoretical properties only when a certain model, either the propensity score or outcome regression model, is correctly specified. In addition, the corresponding estimators do not behave well for finite samples due to large variance even when the model is correctly specified. In this paper, we consider to use the integral probability metric (IPM), which is a metric between two probability measures, for covariate balancing. Optimal weights are determined so that weighted empirical distributions for the treated and control groups have the smallest IPM value for a given set of discriminators. We prove that the corresponding estimator can be consistent without correctly specifying any model (neither the propensity score nor the outcome regression model). In addition, we empirically show that our proposed method outperforms existing weighting methods with large margins for finite samples.

paragraphs: Weighting methods for causal inference try to make treated and control groups more comparable in their observed characteristics. The paper highlights two difficulties with existing methods: their theoretical guarantees depend on correctly specifying a treatment-assignment or outcome model, and their estimates can have high variance even when that specification is correct.

The proposed approach chooses weights by directly comparing the groups’ weighted empirical distributions. It uses an integral probability metric, or IPM, which measures distributional differences through a selected collection of discriminator functions. The optimization finds weights that make the two groups as similar as possible according to that collection. This places distributional balance at the center of weight selection.

The authors prove that the resulting estimator can be consistent without correctly specifying either a propensity-score model or an outcome-regression model. Consistency concerns approaching the target as the amount of data grows. They also report substantial improvements over existing weighting methods in finite-sample experiments. Together, these findings address both large-sample justification and the practical difficulty of unstable estimates with limited data.
summary.tldr: Choosing causal-inference weights through a distributional distance can yield consistent estimation without correctly specified propensity or outcome models.

title: Covariate balancing using the integral probability metric for causal inference

abstract: We present a dynamic model in which the weights are conditioned on an input sample x and are learned to match those that would be obtained by finetuning a base model on x and its label y. This mapping between an input sample and network weights is approximated by a denoising diffusion model. The diffusion model we employ focuses on modifying a single layer of the base model and is conditioned on the input, activations, and output of this layer. Since the diffusion model is stochastic in nature, multiple initializations generate different networks, forming an ensemble, which leads to further improvements. Our experiments demonstrate the wide applicability of the method for image classification, 3D reconstruction, tabular data, speech separation, and natural language processing.

This mapping between an input sample and network weights is approximated by a denoising diffusion model. The diffusion model we employ focuses on modifying a single layer of the base model and is conditioned on the input, activations, and output of this layer. Since the diffusion model is stochastic in nature, multiple initializations generate different networks, forming an ensemble, which leads to further improvements. Our experiments demonstrate the wide applicability of the method for image classification, 3D reconstruction, tabular data, speech separation, and natural language processing.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model whose weights change according to the input sample. The target behavior comes from fine-tuning a base model on an individual input and its label. Instead of treating one fixed set of weights as suitable for every sample, the method learns to approximate the sample-specific weights produced by that fine-tuning process.

A conditional denoising diffusion model learns the mapping from an input to network weights. It focuses on modifying a single layer, using that layer's input, activations, and output as conditioning information. The construction concentrates the adaptation in a particular part of the base model while learning how its parameters should vary with the sample.

Because diffusion sampling is stochastic, different initializations produce different networks for the same conditioning process. Combining those networks forms an ensemble, which the authors report yields further improvements. Experiments demonstrate applicability across image classification, 3D reconstruction, tabular data, speech separation, and natural language processing. The contribution is a learned route to input-dependent adaptation, with stochastic weight generation also providing a source of ensemble variation.
summary.tldr: OCD uses conditional diffusion to generate input-specific layer weights that imitate per-sample fine-tuning and support ensembling.

title: OCD: Learning to Overfit with Conditional Diffusion Models

abstract: The study of Neural Tangent Kernels (NTKs) has provided much needed insight into convergence and generalization properties of neural networks in the over-parametrized (wide) limit by approximating the network using a first-order Taylor expansion with respect to its weights in the neighborhood of their initialization values. This allows neural network training to be analyzed from the perspective of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), which is informative in the over-parametrized regime, but a poor approximation for narrower networks as the weights change more during training. Our goal is to extend beyond the limits of NTK toward a more general theory. We construct an exact power-series representation of the neural network in a finite neighborhood of the initial weights as an inner product of two feature maps, respectively from data and weight-step space, to feature space, allowing neural network training to be analyzed from the perspective of reproducing kernel Banach space (RKBS). We prove that, regardless of width, the training sequence produced by gradient descent can be exactly replicated by regularized sequential learning in RKBS. Using this, we present novel bound on uniform convergence where the iterations count and learning rate play a central role, giving new theoretical insight into neural network training.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernel theory studies neural networks through a first-order approximation around their initial weights. This helps explain very wide networks, but the approximation becomes less suitable for narrower networks whose weights move more during training. This paper seeks a mathematical description that extends beyond that linear approximation.

The authors construct an exact power-series representation within a finite neighborhood of the initial weights. It expresses the network using two feature maps, one for data and one for weight changes, and connects training to a reproducing kernel Banach space. This provides a different functional framework from the Hilbert-space treatment associated with neural tangent kernels.

They prove that gradient descent's training sequence can be reproduced exactly by regularized sequential learning in this framework, regardless of network width. The finite-neighborhood setting remains part of the construction. They then derive a uniform convergence bound in which the learning rate and number of iterations play central roles, connecting training choices to a theoretical account of generalization.
summary.tldr: An exact local power-series representation connects neural-network gradient descent at any width to sequential learning in a Banach space.

title: Gradient Descent in Neural Networks as Sequential Learning in Reproducing Kernel Banach Space

abstract: Devoted to interpreting the explicit behaviors of machine learning models, explanation methods can identify implicit characteristics of models to improve trustworthiness. However, explanation methods are shown as vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, implying security concerns in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we investigate when robust explanations are necessary and what they cost. We prove that the robustness of explanations is determined by the robustness of the model to be explained. Therefore, we can have robust explanations for free for a robust model. To have robust explanations for a non-robust model, composing the original model with a kernel is proved as an effective way that returns strictly more robust explanations. Nevertheless, we argue that this also incurs a robustness-faithfulness trade-off , i.e., contrary to common expectations, an explanation method may also become less faithful when it becomes more robust. This argument holds for any model. We are the first to introduce this trade-off and theoretically prove its existence for SmoothGrad. Theoretical findings are verified by empirical evidence on six state-of-the-art explanation methods and four backbones.

Therefore, we can have robust explanations for free for a robust model. To have robust explanations for a non-robust model, composing the original model with a kernel is proved as an effective way that returns strictly more robust explanations. Nevertheless, we argue that this also incurs a robustness-faithfulness trade-off , i.e., contrary to common expectations, an explanation method may also become less faithful when it becomes more robust. This argument holds for any model. We are the first to introduce this trade-off and theoretically prove its existence for SmoothGrad. Theoretical findings are verified by empirical evidence on six state-of-the-art explanation methods and four backbones.

paragraphs: An explanation can be unstable under adversarial perturbations, raising questions about how reliably it describes a model. This paper asks when explanation robustness requires additional intervention and what that intervention costs. It proves that explanation robustness is determined by the robustness of the model being explained, making robust explanations available for a robust model.

For a non-robust model, the authors prove that composing it with a kernel produces strictly more robust explanations. However, this improvement can introduce a trade-off with faithfulness: an explanation may become more stable while describing the original model less accurately. Robustness and faithfulness therefore need to be assessed as separate properties.

The authors argue that this trade-off can apply to any model and theoretically establish its existence for SmoothGrad. Experiments involving six explanation methods and four backbones support the theoretical findings. The result does not say that every robustness improvement necessarily reduces faithfulness; it establishes that greater robustness can carry that cost, challenging the expectation that stabilizing explanations is automatically beneficial.
summary.tldr: Explanation robustness depends on model robustness, and making explanations more robust can reduce their faithfulness to the model.

title: Robust Explanation for Free or At the Cost of Faithfulness

abstract: In Reinforcement Learning (RL), Laplacian Representation (LapRep) is a task-agnostic state representation that encodes the geometry of the environment. A desirable property of LapRep stated in prior works is that the Euclidean distance in the LapRep space roughly reflects the reachability between states, which motivates the usage of this distance for reward shaping. However, we find that LapRep does not necessarily have this property in general: two states having a small distance under LapRep can actually be far away in the environment. Such a mismatch would impede the learning process in reward shaping. To fix this issue, we introduce a Reachability-Aware Laplacian Representation (RA-LapRep), by properly scaling each dimension of LapRep. Despite the simplicity, we demonstrate that RA-LapRep can better capture the inter-state reachability as compared to LapRep, through both theoretical explanations and experimental results. Additionally, we show that this improvement yields a significant boost in reward shaping performance and benefits bottleneck state discovery.

Distances between represented states are often used for reward shaping because they are expected to reflect reachability. The paper shows that this expectation need not hold: nearby points in the representation can correspond to states that are far apart in the environment.

The proposed Reachability-Aware Laplacian Representation rescales each dimension of the original representation. This directly changes how distances are computed without abandoning the Laplacian representation itself. The aim is to make closeness in the learned space better reflect how reachable one state is from another.

The authors provide theoretical explanations and experimental evidence that the rescaled representation captures reachability better. They also report a substantial improvement in reward shaping and benefits for discovering bottleneck states. The contribution links a specific geometric mismatch to downstream learning behavior and shows that correcting the relative scales of representation dimensions can improve the usefulness of distance-based guidance.
summary.tldr: Rescaling Laplacian representation dimensions better aligns distances with state reachability, improving reward shaping and bottleneck discovery in the reported results.

title: Reachability-Aware Laplacian Representation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many recent machine learning tasks focus to develop models that can generalize to unseen distributions. Domain generalization (DG) has become one of the key topics in various fields. Several literatures show that DG can be arbitrarily hard without exploiting target domain information. To address this issue, test-time adaptive (TTA) methods are proposed. Existing TTA methods require offline target data or extra sophisticated optimization procedures during the inference stage. In this work, we adopt N on- P arametric C lassifier to perform the test-time Ada ptation ( AdaNPC ). In particular, we construct a memory that contains the feature and label pairs from training domains. During inference, given a test instance, AdaNPC first recalls $k$ closed samples from the memory to vote for the prediction, and then the test feature and predicted label are added to the memory. In this way, the sample distribution in the memory can be gradually changed from the training distribution towards the test distribution with very little extra computation cost. We theoretically justify the rationality behind the proposed method. Besides, we test our model on extensive numerical experiments. AdaNPC significantly outperforms competitive baselines on various DG benchmarks. In particular, when the adaptation target is a series of domains, the adaptation accuracy of AdaNPC is $50$% higher than advanced TTA methods.

It then stores the new example’s features together with that predicted label. Repeating this process gradually shifts the memory toward the test distribution, with little additional computation.

For adaptation across a sequence of domains, it reports accuracy 50% higher than advanced test-time adaptation methods. This is a reported comparison in that setting, not a percentage-point claim. The central result is that updating a memory can provide effective adaptation without a complicated inference-time optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: AdaNPC adapts to incoming data by predicting from nearby stored examples and adding its predictions to memory.

title: AdaNPC: Exploring Non-Parametric Classifier for Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Efficiently generating statistically independent samples from an unnormalized probability distribution, such as equilibrium samples of many-body systems, is a foundational problem in science. In this paper, we propose Iterated Denoising Energy Matching (iDEM), an iterative algorithm that uses a novel stochastic score matching objective leveraging solely the energy function and its gradient—and no data samples—to train a diffusion-based sampler. Specifically, iDEM alternates between (I) sampling regions of high model density from a diffusion-based sampler and (II) using these samples in our stochastic matching objective to further improve the sampler. iDEM is scalable to high dimensions as the inner matching objective, is simulation-free, and requires no MCMC samples. Moreover, by leveraging the fast mode mixing behavior of diffusion, iDEM smooths out the energy landscape enabling efficient exploration and learning of an amortized sampler. We evaluate iDEM on a suite of tasks ranging from standard synthetic energy functions to invariant $n$-body particle systems. We show that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on all metrics and trains $2-5\times$ faster, which allows it to be the first method to train using energy on the challenging $55$-particle Lennard-Jones system.

These findings demonstrate the approach’s practical reach on the tested sampling problems.
summary.tldr: iDEM trains diffusion samplers directly from energy functions and gradients, reporting faster training and strong results on demanding particle systems.

title: Iterated Denoising Energy Matching for Sampling from Boltzmann Densities

abstract: Combining discrete and continuous data is an important capability for generative models. We present Discrete Flow Models (DFMs), a new flow-based model of discrete data that provides the missing link in enabling flow-based generative models to be applied to multimodal continuous and discrete data problems. Our key insight is that the discrete equivalent of continuous space flow matching can be realized using Continuous Time Markov Chains. DFMs benefit from a simple derivation that includes discrete diffusion models as a specific instance while allowing improved performance over existing diffusion-based approaches. We utilize our DFMs method to build a multimodal flow-based modeling framework. We apply this capability to the task of protein co-design, wherein we learn a model for jointly generating protein structure and sequence. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art co-design performance while allowing the same multimodal model to be used for flexible generation of the sequence or structure.

They report state-of-the-art performance for joint sequence and structure generation. The same multimodal model also supports flexible generation of either sequence or structure. The contribution therefore includes both a discrete generative formulation and a demonstration that it can connect different data types within one model, rather than requiring a separate modeling framework for each.
summary.tldr: Discrete Flow Models use continuous-time Markov chains to enable joint discrete and continuous generation, demonstrated in protein co-design.

title: Generative Flows on Discrete State-Spaces: Enabling Multimodal Flows with Applications to Protein Co-Design

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) methods often struggle in highly statistically heterogeneous settings. Indeed, non-IID data distributions cause client drift and biased local solutions, particularly pronounced in the final classification layer, negatively impacting convergence speed and accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce Federated Recursive Ridge Regression (Fed3R). Our method fits a Ridge Regression classifier computed in closed form leveraging pre-trained features. Fed3R is immune to statistical heterogeneity and is invariant to the sampling order of the clients. Therefore, it proves particularly effective in cross-device scenarios. Furthermore, it is fast and efficient in terms of communication and computation costs, requiring up to two orders of magnitude fewer resources than the competitors. Finally, we propose to leverage the Fed3R parameters as an initialization for a softmax classifier and subsequently fine-tune the model using any FL algorithm (Fed3R with Fine-Tuning, Fed3R+FT). Our findings also indicate that maintaining a fixed classifier aids in stabilizing the training and learning more discriminative features in cross-device settings. Official website: https://fed-3r.github.io/.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes difficult when participating devices hold very different data. Local training can pull models toward solutions that suit individual clients, slowing convergence and reducing accuracy. The paper identifies the final classification layer as a particularly important source of this problem and proposes Federated Recursive Ridge Regression, or Fed3R, to address it.

Fed3R uses features from a pretrained model and computes a ridge regression classifier in closed form. For this classifier construction, the method is immune to statistical heterogeneity and does not depend on the order in which clients are sampled. Those properties make it especially relevant when learning across devices whose participation and data differ.

The authors report communication and computation requirements up to two orders of magnitude below competing approaches. They also introduce Fed3R+FT, which uses the resulting parameters to initialize a softmax classifier before federated fine-tuning. Their findings further indicate that keeping the classifier fixed can stabilize cross-device training and help the model learn features that distinguish classes more clearly.
summary.tldr: Fed3R computes a classifier from pretrained features in closed form, reducing federated training costs while avoiding sensitivity to client data heterogeneity and sampling order.

title: Accelerating Heterogeneous Federated Learning with Closed-form Classifiers

abstract: The partial monitoring (PM) framework provides a theoretical formulation of sequential learning problems with incomplete feedback. At each round, a learning agent plays an action while the environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The agent then observes a feedback signal that is only partially informative about the (unobserved) outcome. The agent leverages the received feedback signals to select actions that minimize the (unobserved) cumulative loss. In contextual PM, the outcomes depend on some side information that is observable by the agent before selecting the action. In this paper, we consider the contextual and non-contextual PM settings with stochastic outcomes. We introduce a new class of PM strategies based on the randomization of deterministic confidence bounds. We also extend regret guarantees to settings where existing stochastic strategies are not applicable. Our experiments show that the proposed RandCBP and RandCBPside* strategies have competitive performance against state-of-the-art baselines in multiple PM games. To illustrate how the PM framework can benefit real world applications, we design a use case on the real-world problem of monitoring the error rate of any deployed classification system.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring describes sequential decisions where an agent sees only an incomplete signal about what happened. The agent must use those signals to reduce cumulative loss even though the outcomes and losses themselves are unobserved. In the contextual version, additional information is available before acting and helps determine the distribution of outcomes.

The paper studies both contextual and non-contextual settings with stochastic outcomes. It introduces strategies that randomize otherwise deterministic confidence bounds, producing the RandCBP and RandCBPside* methods. It also extends regret guarantees to settings where existing stochastic strategies do not apply. These guarantees address learning performance despite the restricted feedback available to the agent.

Experiments across several partial-monitoring games show performance competitive with state-of-the-art baselines. The authors also design a use case for monitoring the error rate of a deployed classifier. That example illustrates how the framework can describe a practical monitoring problem in which the information needed to evaluate a system is only partially available.
summary.tldr: Randomized confidence bounds yield competitive partial-monitoring strategies and extend regret guarantees to additional stochastic settings.

title: Randomized Confidence Bounds for Stochastic Partial Monitoring

abstract: Stochastic gradients have been widely integrated into Langevin-based methods to improve their scalability and efficiency in solving large-scale sampling problems. However, the proximal sampler, which exhibits much faster convergence than Langevin-based algorithms in the deterministic setting (Lee et al., 2021), has yet to be explored in its stochastic variants. In this paper, we study the Stochastic Proximal Samplers (SPS) for sampling from non-log-concave distributions. We first establish a general framework for implementing stochastic proximal samplers and establish the convergence theory accordingly. We show that the convergence to the target distribution can be guaranteed as long as the second moment of the algorithm trajectory is bounded and restricted Gaussian oracles can be well approximated. We then provide two implementable variants based on Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) and Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA), giving rise to SPS-SGLD and SPS-MALA. We further show that SPS-SGLD and SPS-MALA can achieve $\epsilon$-sampling error in total variation (TV) distance within $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\epsilon^{-2})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{1/2}\epsilon^{-2})$ gradient complexities, which outperform the best-known result by at least an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{1/3})$ factor. This enhancement in performance is corroborated by our empirical studies on synthetic data with various dimensions, demonstrating the efficiency of our proposed algorithm.

summary.tldr: Stochastic proximal samplers offer improved gradient-complexity bounds under stated moment and oracle-approximation conditions.

title: Faster Sampling via Stochastic Gradient Proximal Sampler

abstract: In this paper, we present DetKDS, the first framework that searches for optimal detection distillation policies. Manual design of detection distillers becomes challenging and time-consuming due to significant disparities in distillation behaviors between detectors with different backbones, paradigms, and label assignments. To tackle these challenges, we leverage search algorithms to discover optimal distillers for homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Firstly, our search space encompasses global features, foreground-background features, instance features, logits response, and localization response as inputs. Then, we construct omni-directional cascaded transformations and obtain the distiller by selecting the advanced distance function and common weight value options. Finally, we present a divide-and-conquer evolutionary algorithm to handle the explosion of the search space. In this strategy, we first evolve the best distiller formulations of individual knowledge inputs and then optimize the combined weights of these multiple distillation losses. DetKDS automates the distillation process without requiring expert design or additional tuning, effectively reducing the teacher-student gap in various scenarios. Based on the analysis of our search results, we provide valuable guidance that contributes to detection distillation designs. Comprehensive experiments on different detectors demonstrate that DetKDS outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detection and instance segmentation tasks. For instance, DetKDS achieves significant gains than baseline detectors: $+3.7$, $+4.1$, $+4.0$, $+3.7$, and $+3.5$ AP on RetinaNet, Faster-RCNN, FCOS, RepPoints, and GFL, respectively. Code at: https://github.com/lliai/DetKDS.

These choices vary across detector architectures, detection paradigms, and label assignments, making manual design difficult. DetKDS automates the search for distillation policies for both similar and structurally different teacher-student pairs.

Its search space includes global image features, foreground and background features, instance features, classification responses, and localization responses. It also searches transformations, distance functions, and loss weights. To manage this large space, a divide-and-conquer evolutionary procedure first develops distillers for individual information sources, then optimizes how their losses are weighted together.

Experiments across several detectors show improvements over leading distillation methods in detection and instance segmentation. Reported gains over baseline detectors range from 3.5 to 4.1 AP across five named architectures. The search results also yield guidance for designing detection distillers. The broader contribution is a systematic way to adapt knowledge transfer to the particular teacher and student without requiring expert-designed policies or additional tuning.
summary.tldr: DetKDS searches automatically for detector-specific knowledge distillation policies and reports gains in object detection and instance segmentation.

title: DetKDS: Knowledge Distillation Search for Object Detectors

abstract: Neural operators (NOs) have emerged as effective tools for modeling complex physical systems in scientific machine learning. In NOs, a central characteristic is to learn the governing physical laws directly from data. In contrast to other machine learning applications, partial knowledge is often known a priori about the physical system at hand whereby quantities such as mass, energy and momentum are exactly conserved. Currently, NOs have to learn these conservation laws from data and can only approximately satisfy them due to finite training data and random noise. In this work, we introduce conservation law-encoded neural operators (clawNOs), a suite of NOs that endow inference with automatic satisfaction of such conservation laws. ClawNOs are built with a divergence-free prediction of the solution field, with which the continuity equation is automatically guaranteed. As a consequence, clawNOs are compliant with the most fundamental and ubiquitous conservation laws essential for correct physical consistency. As demonstrations, we consider a wide variety of scientific applications ranging from constitutive modeling of material deformation, incompressible fluid dynamics, to atmospheric simulation. ClawNOs significantly outperform the state-of-the-art NOs in learning efficacy, especially in small-data regimes.

If a model must discover these laws solely from finite, noisy observations, its predictions may satisfy them only approximately, even when the underlying physical system obeys them exactly.

The paper introduces conservation law-encoded neural operators, or clawNOs, that automatically satisfy the encoded conservation laws during inference. Their construction uses a divergence-free prediction of the solution field, which guarantees the continuity equation. They report substantial improvements in learning efficacy over state-of-the-art neural operators, especially with small datasets. The findings indicate that incorporating known physical structure can make data-driven learning more effective, while ensuring consistency with the conservation relationships represented by the construction.
summary.tldr: ClawNOs build conservation constraints into neural-operator predictions and report improved learning, particularly when training data are limited.

title: Harnessing the Power of Neural Operators with Automatically Encoded Conservation Laws

abstract: It is vital to learn effective policies that can be transferred to different domains with dynamics discrepancies in reinforcement learning (RL). In this paper, we consider dynamics adaptation settings where there exists dynamics mismatch between the source domain and the target domain, and one can get access to sufficient source domain data, while can only have limited interactions with the target domain. Existing methods address this problem by learning domain classifiers, performing data filtering from a value discrepancy perspective, etc. Instead, we tackle this challenge from a decoupled representation learning perspective. We perform representation learning only in the target domain and measure the representation deviations on the transitions from the source domain, which we show can be a signal of dynamics mismatch. We also show that representation deviation upper bounds performance difference of a given policy in the source domain and target domain, which motivates us to adopt representation deviation as a reward penalty. The produced representations are not involved in either policy or value function, but only serve as a reward penalizer. We conduct extensive experiments on environments with kinematic and morphology mismatch, and the results show that our method exhibits strong performance on many tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dmksjfl/PAR.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy may need to transfer between environments whose dynamics differ. This paper considers abundant source-domain data but only limited interaction with the target domain. The challenge is to use the available source experience while accounting for behaviors that do not carry over reliably.

This separation makes the adaptation signal an explicit correction to how source experience is valued. Experiments involving kinematic and morphology differences show strong performance on many tasks. The results support representation deviation as a useful transfer signal when target interaction is limited.
summary.tldr: Target-domain representation deviations provide a reward penalty that helps policies adapt from abundant source data to different target dynamics.

title: Cross-Domain Policy Adaptation by Capturing Representation Mismatch

abstract: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) have shown promise in learning continuous dynamics. However, their slow training and inference speed hinder wider applications. In this paper, we propose to optimize Neural ODEs from a spatial and temporal perspective, drawing inspiration from control theory. We aim to find a reasonable depth of the network, accelerating both training and inference while maintaining network performance. Two approaches are proposed. One reformulates training as a minimum-time optimal control problem directly in a single stage to search for the terminal time and network weights. The second approach uses pre-training coupled with a Lyapunov method in an initial stage, and then at a secondary stage introduces a safe terminal time updating mechanism in the forward direction. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of speeding up Neural ODEs.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations learn continuous dynamics, but their training and inference can be slow. This paper approaches that cost through control theory, asking how much depth the model needs to maintain its performance. It treats the terminal time of the dynamics as something to optimize alongside the network, connecting the duration of computation with the learning problem.

The second approach separates the process into stages. It begins with pretraining and a Lyapunov method, then applies a safe mechanism for updating terminal time in the forward direction. Their shared contribution is to make depth selection an explicit part of training, with the aim of improving both training and inference speed while maintaining network performance.
summary.tldr: Two control-theoretic approaches optimize neural ODE terminal time to accelerate training and inference while aiming to maintain performance.

title: How Deep Do We Need: Accelerating Training and Inference of Neural ODEs via Control Perspective

abstract: Pufferfish privacy is a flexible generalization of differential privacy that allows to model arbitrary secrets and adversary’s prior knowledge about the data. Unfortunately, designing general and tractable Pufferfish mechanisms that do not compromise utility is challenging. Furthermore, this framework does not provide the composition guarantees needed for a direct use in iterative machine learning algorithms. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a Rényi divergence-based variant of Pufferfish and show that it allows us to extend the applicability of the Pufferfish framework. We first generalize the Wasserstein mechanism to cover a wide range of noise distributions and introduce several ways to improve its utility. Finally, as an alternative to composition, we prove privacy amplification results for contractive noisy iterations and showcase the first use of Pufferfish in private convex optimization. A common ingredient underlying our results is the use and extension of shift reduction lemmas.
