paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions while retaining independence from a particular discretization. Standard deterministic versions produce one prediction, leaving uncertainty unmodeled. Diffusion last layer, or DLL, adds a modular probabilistic output head so an operator backbone can represent a distribution of possible target fields.

DLL expresses each target field through a compact, input-dependent expansion inspired by the Karhunen–Loève expansion. A conditional diffusion model learns the distribution of the expansion’s coefficients. Modeling uncertainty in this smaller coefficient space makes distributional prediction efficient while preserving the structural advantages of the underlying operator.

On stochastic partial differential equation benchmarks with random forcing, DLL captures output distributions well and competes with pixel-space and conventional latent diffusion approaches. In deterministic tasks involving long autoregressive rollouts, it improves stability over the backbone and provides useful uncertainty estimates as prediction errors accumulate. These results suggest that a learned coefficient space can serve as a practical interface between operator learning and probabilistic diffusion modeling.
summary.tldr: DLL adds diffusion over compact field coefficients to neural operators, enabling uncertainty estimates and improving reported rollout stability.

title: Generative Neural Operators through Diffusion Last Layer

abstract: With the rise of reasoning language models and test-time scaling methods as a paradigm for improving model performance, substantial computation is often required to generate multiple candidate sequences from the same prompt. This enables exploration of different reasoning paths toward the correct solution, however, allocates the same compute budget for each prompt. Grounded on the assumption that different prompts carry different degrees of complexity, and thus different computation needs, we propose EAGer, a training-free generation method that leverages model uncertainty through token-wise entropy distribution to reduce redundant computation and concurrently improve overall performance. EAGer allows branching to multiple reasoning paths only in the presence of high-entropy tokens, and reallocates the saved compute budget to instances where exploration of alternative paths is most needed. We validate EAGer across multiple open-source models on complex reasoning benchmarks, with gains specifically demonstrated on AIME 2025. When target labels are accessible – as in RLVR training pipelines – EAGer achieves up to +37% in Pass@k and 59% fewer tokens; in test-time settings it still yields +12% in Pass@k and 64% fewer tokens compared to Full Parallel Sampling.

EAGer starts from the assumption that prompts differ in complexity and therefore in how much exploration they need. It adjusts generation without additional model training.

The method uses token-level entropy as a signal of model uncertainty. It branches into multiple reasoning paths only when uncertainty is high, rather than repeatedly generating whole sequences independently. Computation saved on less uncertain portions can then be allocated to instances where alternative paths are more useful. This connects the amount of exploration to uncertainty during generation.

These distinct settings show how label access affects the reported gains from adaptive exploration.

title: EAGer: Entropy-Aware GEneRation for Adaptive Inference-Time Scaling

abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning have largely been driven by foundation models (FMs) trained on large, diverse datasets, enabling them to generalize effectively to new, related tasks. However, extending this paradigm to reinforcement learning (RL), where an agent interacts with an environment to select actions, remains a significant challenge. Most existing approaches train FMs directly on sets of control tasks, but developing diverse RL environments and scaling training across them can be costly and complex. In this study, we explore a simpler alternative approach based on a classical reduction from RL to regression. We demonstrate that a foundation model pre-trained for regression tasks, when used as an in-context regression (ICR) model, can be directly applied to RL problems. Building on this insight, we introduce a gradient-free method, ICR-RL, that requires no additional training and leverages an ICR foundation model to tackle RL tasks. We evaluate our approach by applying the ICR model with the recently proposed TabPFN, which is trained on a wide range of regression tasks. Experiments conducted on the Gymnasium classic-control benchmark indicate that ICR-RL matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including DQN and PPO. These results show that ICR foundation models can effectively solve RL tasks without fine-tuning, demonstrating their potential as a foundation for RL-oriented models

paragraphs: Building foundation models directly from many reinforcement-learning tasks can require expensive environment development and training. This paper explores another route: using a foundation model already trained for regression. Its starting point is the classical connection that allows reinforcement-learning problems to be approached through regression subproblems.

The proposed method, ICR-RL, uses in-context regression to apply that connection without further training or fine-tuning the foundation model. It is gradient-free and draws on the model's existing ability to solve regression tasks from supplied context. The authors instantiate the approach with TabPFN, which was pretrained on a broad range of regression problems.

On the Gymnasium classic-control benchmark, ICR-RL matches or outperforms evaluated state-of-the-art methods, including DQN and PPO. These experiments show that a model pretrained outside the control-task setting can serve as a useful component for reinforcement learning. The result supports regression pretraining as a possible foundation for RL-oriented systems, with the demonstrated performance grounded in the classic-control tasks evaluated in the paper.
summary.tldr: ICR-RL applies a pretrained regression foundation model to reinforcement learning without additional training, with strong classic-control results.

title: ICR-RL: Deep Reinforcement Learning via In-Context-Regression

abstract: Attention is the critical component of a transformer. Yet the quadratic computational complexity of vanilla full attention in the input size and the inability of its linear attention variant to focus have been challenges for computer vision tasks. We provide a mathematical definition of generalized attention and formulate both vanilla softmax attention and linear attention within the general framework. We prove that generalized attention disperses, that is, as the number of keys tends to infinity, the query assigns equal weights to all keys. Motivated by the dispersion property and recent development of Mamba form of attention, we design Scalable and Efficient Mamba like Attention (SEMA) which utilizes token localization to avoid dispersion and maintain focusing, complemented by theoretically consistent arithmetic averaging to capture global aspect of attention. We support our approach on Imagenet-1k where classification results show that SEMA is a scalable and effective alternative beyond linear attention, outperforming recent vision Mamba models on increasingly larger scales of images at similar model parameter sizes. Source code can be found at: https://github.com/nhatthanhtran/SEMA.

paragraphs: Full attention becomes expensive as an image’s token count grows, while linear attention can struggle to concentrate on relevant information. This paper studies both within a mathematical framework called generalized attention. Within that framework, the authors prove a dispersion result: as the number of keys tends to infinity, a query’s weights become equal across keys.

SEMA responds by combining token localization with arithmetic averaging. Localization is designed to preserve focus and avoid dispersion, while averaging captures the global aspect of attention in a theoretically consistent way. The architecture draws inspiration from Mamba-style attention and assigns complementary roles to localized processing and global information aggregation.

ImageNet-1k classification experiments support the resulting design as a scalable alternative beyond linear attention. At similar parameter counts, SEMA outperforms recent vision Mamba models as image scales increase. The reported findings connect the theoretical concern about attention losing focus to a practical architectural response, with evidence that combining local concentration and global averaging can improve classification at larger image scales.
summary.tldr: SEMA combines localized tokens and global averaging to preserve attention focus and improve image classification at increasing scales.

title: SEMA: a Scalable and Efficient Mamba like Attention via Token Localization and Averaging

abstract: Loss spikes remain a persistent obstacle in large-scale language model pretraining. While previous research has attempted to identify the root cause of loss spikes by investigating individual factors, we observe that, in practice, such spikes are typically triggered by the confluence of heterogeneous factors. Empirically, loss spikes may arise from a combination of data outliers, hardware or transient computational faults, numerical precision issues, and hyperparameter settings. Regardless of the underlying cause, these spikes manifest as unstable optimizer updates, as abnormal gradients contaminate both first- and second-moment states. In this paper, we propose a principled gradient-centric remedy: AdaGC, an adaptive per-tensor gradient clipping scheme that mitigates such contamination by bounding gradient norms relative to a tensor-wise exponential moving average of their historical clipped values. AdaGC is optimizer-agnostic, introduces negligible memory overhead, and reduces communication costs compared to GlobalGC, particularly in hybrid-parallel distributed training. Experiments on Llama-2 7B, Mixtral 8$\times$1B, and ERNIE 10B-A1.4B demonstrate that AdaGC robustly eliminates training instabilities, consistently reducing spike scores to zero for all models and improving downstream accuracy over GlobalGC by 1.32%, 1.27%, and 2.48%, respectively. Furthermore, AdaGC seamlessly integrates with optimizers such as Muon and Lion, consistently yielding higher average accuracy and zero spike scores. The code is available at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleFleet (see Research/AdaGC).

Their approach targets a shared consequence: abnormal gradients can corrupt the optimizer’s running estimates of both gradients and their squared magnitudes, making subsequent updates unstable.

These findings support addressing instability through adaptive gradient control across the evaluated training configurations.
summary.tldr: AdaGC adapts gradient clipping separately for each tensor, eliminating measured loss spikes and improving downstream accuracy in the reported pretraining experiments.

title: AdaGC: Enhancing LLM Pretraining Stability via Adaptive Gradient Clipping

abstract: Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) adapts Vision-Language Models to privacy-sensitive medical imaging, typically via a textual tuning paradigm that assumes the frozen visual encoder provides a discriminative feature geometry. We argue this assumption breaks down in medical settings, leading to two geometric pathologies: (1) Intra-client: Medical Manifold Collapse, where high morphological similarity reduces the effective rank of visual features; and (2) Inter-client: Medical Topological Misalignment, where heterogeneous acquisition protocols induce inconsistent geometry across clients. To address these, we propose FedMAP, which shifts the paradigm to Visual Manifold Anchoring. FedMAP utilizes an LLM-derived codebook as a client-invariant synchronization signal to restructure the visual space, via Manifold Semantic Anchoring (MSA) and Topology Structural Alignment (TSA) to enforce consistent inter-class relations. Experiments on FedISIC, FedCamelyon17, and a private ultrasound dataset show that FedMAP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially in high-noise regimes where manifold collapse is most severe.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts vision-language models across medical-data clients, commonly by tuning text while freezing the visual encoder. This relies on visual features already separating relevant categories. The authors argue that medical images can violate this assumption because similar morphology compresses feature diversity and differing acquisition protocols create inconsistent feature geometry across clients.

FedMAP addresses these issues by restructuring the visual representation through Visual Manifold Anchoring. An LLM-derived codebook provides a shared synchronization signal that is invariant across clients. Manifold Semantic Anchoring and Topology Structural Alignment use this signal to organize the visual space and enforce consistent relationships between classes.

The authors evaluate FedMAP on FedISIC, FedCamelyon17, and a private ultrasound dataset. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, particularly under high noise, where the identified feature collapse is most severe. The findings support addressing the visual geometry itself when adapting these models to medical imaging, with a shared semantic reference helping coordinate clients whose image-acquisition conditions differ.
summary.tldr: FedMAP uses a shared LLM-derived codebook to restructure medical-image features and align class relationships across federated clients.

title: Rethinking Federated Prompt Learning for Medical Images: From Textual Tuning to Visual Manifold Anchoring

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) increasingly relies on hierarchical indexing, yet existing frameworks are bottlenecked by the high cost and information loss of recursive, LLM-based summarization. We propose SeRAG, a novel token-free hierarchical indexing framework that replaces textual summaries with an information-theoretic knowledge taxonomy. SeRAG first transforms a corpus into a multi-perspective graph capturing semantic, logical, and sequential dependencies, then minimizes structural entropy to induce a topologically-faithful encoding tree. To bridge the gap between abstract themes and granular facts, we introduce localized structural weight-based vector aggregation for token-free community consolidation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeRAG significantly reduces indexing overhead while outperforming state-of-the-art methods in complex multi-hop reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Hierarchical retrieval indexes help connect broad themes with detailed evidence, but building them through repeated language-model summaries can be costly and lose information. SeRAG replaces those textual summaries with a graph-derived knowledge taxonomy. Its token-free indexing approach organizes the corpus through relationships among its contents rather than generating new summary text at successive levels.

The framework first constructs a graph capturing semantic, logical, and sequential dependencies. It then minimizes structural entropy to produce an encoding tree that preserves the graph’s topology. To connect abstract communities with granular facts, it aggregates vectors using localized structural weights. This consolidates community representations without requiring generated textual descriptions of those communities.

Experiments report substantially reduced indexing overhead and stronger performance than state-of-the-art methods on complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. The result matters because the index must support both efficient organization and retrieval across connected pieces of evidence. SeRAG ties those functions to the corpus’s relational structure, with the reported gains suggesting that hierarchical retrieval need not depend on recursive language-model summarization.
summary.tldr: SeRAG builds hierarchical retrieval indexes from graph structure and vector aggregation, reducing indexing overhead while improving reported multi-hop reasoning performance.

title: Token-Free Hierarchical Indexing for RAG beyond LLM-based Summarization

abstract: Driven by the pressing demand for graph anomaly detection (GAD) in high-stakes domains, the generalist GAD paradigm, which trains a single detector transferable across new graphs, has recently gained growing attention. However, existing methods often rely on scarce and costly annotations for training and sometimes even require few-shot support at inference, which limits their robustness to diverse and unseen anomaly patterns. To address this limitation, we introduce ProMoS, the first unsupervised generalist GAD framework, which detects anomalies by modeling the abundant normality in unlabeled data. ProMoS adopts a knowledge-distillation paradigm to distill normality priors from a frozen self-supervised graph neural network (GNN) teacher to a mixture-of-students model with shared global and lightweight personalized branches, enabling efficient and expressive normality modeling without learning from scratch. We further propose prototype-guided soft-label distillation to align teacher and student in a shared prototype space, enhancing cross-graph generalizability. During inference, ProMoS performs zero-shot anomaly detection on unseen graphs via distillation bias and prototype geometric deviation. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness and efficiency of ProMoS, charting a practical path toward label-free, zero-shot generalist GAD.

paragraphs: A generalist graph anomaly detector should transfer to unfamiliar graphs without requiring new labeled examples. Existing approaches often depend on costly anomaly annotations or a few support examples at inference. ProMoS instead learns from the abundance of normal patterns in unlabeled data, pursuing unsupervised training and zero-shot detection.

Its teacher is a frozen, self-supervised graph neural network. A mixture of student models learns normality priors from that teacher, using a shared global branch alongside lightweight personalized branches. Prototype-guided soft labels place teacher and student outputs in a common prototype space, helping align their representations in a form intended to transfer across graphs.

At inference, ProMoS detects anomalies on unseen graphs using distillation bias and geometric deviation from prototypes. This connects its anomaly signals to how well an input agrees with the learned model of normality. Experiments report effectiveness and efficiency, supporting a practical approach to transferable graph anomaly detection without anomaly labels or inference-time support examples.
summary.tldr: ProMoS distills normal graph patterns into prototype-aligned students for label-free anomaly detection on unseen graphs.

title: Generalist Graph Anomaly Detection via Prototype-Based Distillation

abstract: Modern neural networks derive much of their effectiveness from rich connectivity patterns. Yet, existing architectures often fix the topology at either the sparse or dense extremes, thereby limiting structural flexibility and analysis. We propose Kronecker Generative Networks (KGNs), an algebraic framework that constructs neural network topologies via recursive generation rules, treating topology as a first-class design object. KGNs generate families of directed acyclic graphs with controllable connectivity complexity, enabling systematic interpolation between sparse and dense aggregation regimes. Under this formulation, architectures such as FractalNet and DenseNet arise as specific instantiations corresponding to different generation rules. We provide theoretical analysis of acyclicity, connectivity scaling, and expressiveness, and demonstrate experimentally that KGN instantiations achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple domains.

KGNs generate families of directed acyclic graphs with controllable connectivity complexity, enabling systematic interpolation between sparse and dense aggregation regimes. Under this formulation, architectures such as FractalNet and DenseNet arise as specific instantiations corresponding to different generation rules. We provide theoretical analysis of acyclicity, connectivity scaling, and expressiveness, and demonstrate experimentally that KGN instantiations achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple domains.

paragraphs: A neural network’s connections determine how information can move and combine across its layers. Many architectures commit to relatively sparse or dense connectivity, making the structure itself less flexible to study. Kronecker Generative Networks place connectivity at the center of architectural design by generating network graphs through recursive rules.

The framework constructs families of directed acyclic graphs with controllable connection complexity. Changing the generation rules allows systematic movement between sparse and dense aggregation patterns. FractalNet and DenseNet appear as particular instances of this broader construction, linking established architectures through a common way of describing how their connections are produced.

The authors analyze whether the generated graphs remain acyclic, how connectivity scales, and what the resulting networks can express. Experiments across multiple domains report favorable trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a design framework and an analytical one: it makes connection patterns adjustable through explicit rules and provides tools for understanding their consequences, with empirical results supporting useful parameter-efficient instantiations.
summary.tldr: Kronecker Generative Networks use recursive rules to build controllable connectivity patterns, yielding favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across classification domains.

title: Kronecker Generative Networks: A General Neural Architecture for Parameter-Efficient Learning Across Classification Tasks

abstract: Incremental object detection (IOD) aims to extend detectors to new categories while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Existing methods often adopt a class incremental learning perspective, separating feature spaces to sharpen decision boundaries. However, this separation-oriented paradigm may overlook object symbiosis in detection, where co-occurrence and occlusion introduce spatial and semantic dependencies that benefit from shared representations. Ignoring these dependencies distorts the shared representations, exacerbates confusion between old and new classes, and accelerates catastrophic forgetting. To address this, we propose Symbiosis-Inspired Knowledge Distillation (SIKD), which explicitly leverages object symbiosis at two complementary levels. Spatial Symbiosis Distillation (SpSD) focuses on symbiotic regions where the old model responds with high overlap to objects in the new task. It preserves generalizable old class cues, suppresses class-specific bias and redundancy, and distills the refined evidence to the new model at matched spatial locations with slot-aligned supervision. Semantic Symbiosis Distillation (SeSD) maintains class level structure by forming confidence weighted prototypes for old classes and aligning their inter class soft ranks over the old class logits, which stabilizes the semantic topology during adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Incremental object detection adds new categories while trying to preserve recognition of old ones. The paper argues that separating class representations can overlook useful dependencies created by objects appearing together or occluding one another. SIKD transfers knowledge in ways that preserve these shared spatial and semantic relationships during adaptation.

Its spatial component identifies regions where the old detector's responses overlap strongly with objects in the new task. It preserves transferable old-class cues while suppressing class-specific bias and redundancy, then teaches the new model using matched spatial locations and aligned slots. This targets shared evidence that remains useful as categories change.

The semantic component builds confidence-weighted prototypes for old classes and aligns their relative soft rankings over old-class outputs. This helps stabilize relationships among previously learned categories. Together, the two components address preservation at both image-region and class-structure levels. Experiments report the method's effectiveness and superiority over compared approaches. The findings support using object dependencies as a resource for retaining knowledge when a detector learns additional categories.
summary.tldr: SIKD preserves spatial cues and semantic class relationships to reduce forgetting as object detectors learn new categories.

title: Symbiosis-Inspired Knowledge Distillation for Incremental Object Detection

abstract: Discrete biological sequence optimization often requires goal-directed, parser-valid edits to an existing protein or molecule. Diffusion models support iterative refinement but do not expose a controllable discrete-edit interface, while autoregressive LLMs can be myopic when planning constrained edits over multiple steps. We introduce STRIDE (Sequence Trajectory Refinement via Iterative Discrete Editing), a post-training framework that trains an LLM to emit executable INSERT/DELETE/REPLACE trajectories for variable-length refinement. STRIDE first learns Levenshtein-aligned shortest-edit demonstrations, then uses supervised fine-tuning and group-based policy optimization to align trajectories with task rewards while preserving coherent editing. On an oracle-based full-action protein stress test, STRIDE raises success over Vanilla SFT from 42% to 89% and novelty among unique improvements from 47% to 97%. On instruction-conditioned molecular editing, the GSPO-aligned variant improves strict success, controllability, and SMILES validity over the SFT-only STRIDE model (code: https://github.com/daiheng-zhang/STRIDE).

On instruction-conditioned molecular editing, the GSPO-aligned variant improves strict success, controllability, and SMILES validity over the SFT-only STRIDE model (code: https://github.com/daiheng-zhang/STRIDE).

paragraphs: Refining an existing protein or molecular representation requires edits that pursue a goal while remaining executable and syntactically valid. STRIDE trains a language model to produce sequences of INSERT, DELETE, and REPLACE operations. This provides an explicit interface for multistep changes, including changes in sequence length, while addressing difficulties in planning constrained edits.

Training starts with shortest-edit demonstrations aligned using Levenshtein edits. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model coherent editing trajectories, and group-based policy optimization then aligns those trajectories with task rewards. The approach combines learning how to carry out edits with learning which sequences of edits better satisfy the task.

On an oracle-based protein stress test covering the full action set, STRIDE increases success from 42% for Vanilla SFT to 89%, and novelty among unique improvements from 47% to 97%. For instruction-conditioned molecular editing, the GSPO-aligned version improves strict success, controllability, and SMILES validity over STRIDE trained only with supervised fine-tuning. These results support explicit edit trajectories and reward alignment in the evaluated sequence-refinement tasks.
summary.tldr: STRIDE trains language models to refine biological sequences through executable edit trajectories aligned with task rewards.

title: STRIDE: Post-Training LLMs to Reason and Refine Bio-Sequences via Edit Trajectories

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) guides large language models (LLMs) to generate recommendations aligned with user historical behavior distributions by minimizing preference alignment loss. However, our systematic empirical research and theoretical analysis reveal that DPO tends to amplify spurious correlations caused by environmental confounders during the alignment process, significantly undermining the generalization capability of LLM-based generative recommendation methods in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. To mitigate this issue, we propose CausalDPO, an extension of DPO that incorporates a causal invariance learning mechanism. This method introduces a backdoor adjustment strategy during the preference alignment phase to eliminate interference from environmental confounders, explicitly models the latent environmental distribution using a soft clustering approach, and enhances robust consistency across diverse environments through invariance constraints. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that CausalDPO can effectively capture users’ stable preference structures across multiple environments, thereby improving the OOD generalization performance of LLM-based recommendation models. We conduct extensive experiments under four representative distribution shift settings to validate the effectiveness of CausalDPO, achieving an average performance improvement of 24.10% across four evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization can train a language model to recommend items in ways that match historical user behavior. The paper finds that this alignment can also strengthen misleading associations created by the environment in which the behavior was recorded. When that environment changes, recommendations based on those associations can generalize poorly.

CausalDPO extends preference optimization with mechanisms intended to recover more stable preferences. It uses backdoor adjustment during alignment to address environmental confounding, soft clustering to represent an unobserved distribution of environments, and invariance constraints to encourage consistency across them. Together, these components seek to separate enduring preference structure from environment-dependent patterns.

The theoretical analysis supports CausalDPO's ability to capture stable preferences across multiple environments. Experiments cover four representative distribution-shift settings and report an average performance improvement of 24.10% across four evaluation metrics. The findings suggest that matching historical preferences becomes more robust when the training objective also accounts for how the environment shaped the observed behavior, rather than treating every observed association as equally dependable.
summary.tldr: CausalDPO adds environmental adjustment and invariance constraints to preference optimization to improve recommendation robustness under distribution shifts.

title: Causal Direct Preference Optimization for Distributionally Robust Generative Recommendation

abstract: AI-generated image detectors achieve high accuracy on in-distribution data but often fail on unseen generators. A key obstacle to understanding this failure is the black-box nature of current detectors: they do not reveal which evidence drives their decisions. We propose ForensicConcept, a framework that extracts explicit forensic concepts from detectors and enables their transfer across backbones. Our method localizes decision-critical patches via Transformer attribution, clusters them into a compact concept codebook, and uses a concept-aligned projection to produce auditable evidence readouts. Motivated by prior studies showing that DINO representations can guide diffusion generation and exhibit concept-level correspondence with diffusion features, we introduce a generation-trace reference based on CleanDIFT diffusion features and quantify backbone-trace alignment via neighborhood-structure consistency (CKNNA). We further propose concept codebook injection to transfer diffusion-derived concepts into target backbones. Experiments on GenImage, GAN-family, and Chameleon benchmarks show consistent improvements over prior methods. We also find that CKNNA alignment predicts transfer effectiveness, providing a principled explanation for why some backbones yield more transferable forensic evidence than others.

paragraphs: Detectors of AI-generated images can perform well on familiar generators yet struggle with unseen ones. Understanding that failure is harder when a detector does not reveal its evidence. ForensicConcept addresses both interpretability and transfer by extracting explicit forensic concepts and moving those concepts between different model backbones.

The framework first uses Transformer attribution to locate image patches important to a detector’s decision. It clusters those patches into a compact concept codebook and projects representations into concept-aligned evidence readouts. It also builds a generation-trace reference from CleanDIFT diffusion features. A neighborhood-consistency measure, CKNNA, evaluates how closely a backbone’s representation structure aligns with that reference.

Concept codebook injection then transfers diffusion-derived concepts into target backbones. Experiments on GenImage, GAN-family, and Chameleon benchmarks report consistent improvements over prior methods. The authors also find that CKNNA alignment predicts transfer effectiveness. Together, these results connect interpretable evidence with transfer behavior: the organization of a backbone’s features helps explain which forensic concepts can carry over effectively.
summary.tldr: ForensicConcept extracts auditable image-forensics concepts and transfers them between backbones, with representation alignment predicting transfer effectiveness.

abstract: Learning sparse Markov networks based on the maximum margin principle remains an open problem in structured prediction. In this paper, we proposed the Laplace max-margin Markov network (LapM 3 N), and a general class of Bayesian M 3 N (BM 3 N) of which the LapM 3 N is a special case and enjoys a sparse representation. The BM 3 N is built on a novel Structured Maximum Entropy Discrimination (SMED) formalism, which offers a general framework for combining Bayesian learning and max-margin learning of log-linear models for structured prediction, and it subsumes the unsparsified M 3 N as a special case. We present an efficient iterative learning algorithm based on variational approximation and existing convex optimization methods employed in M 3 N. We show that our method outperforms competing ones on both synthetic and real OCR data.

The BM 3 N is built on a novel Structured Maximum Entropy Discrimination (SMED) formalism, which offers a general framework for combining Bayesian learning and max-margin learning of log-linear models for structured prediction, and it subsumes the unsparsified M 3 N as a special case. paragraphs: This paper addresses sparse learning for maximum margin Markov networks in structured prediction. The goal is to combine the maximum margin principle with a representation that uses parameters sparsely. The authors introduce the Laplace maximum margin Markov network, or LapM3N, as a model that provides this sparse representation.

LapM3N belongs to a broader family of Bayesian maximum margin Markov networks developed in the paper. That family rests on Structured Maximum Entropy Discrimination, a framework combining Bayesian learning and maximum margin learning for structured log-linear models. It also includes the existing unsparsified maximum margin Markov network as a special case, connecting the new formulation to an established approach.

For learning, the authors present an efficient iterative algorithm combining variational approximation with convex optimization methods already used for maximum margin Markov networks. Their method outperforms competing approaches on synthetic and real optical character recognition data. The contribution thus spans both modeling and computation: it supplies a framework for Bayesian margin-based learning, a sparse instance, and a practical training procedure.
summary.tldr: Laplace maximum margin Markov networks combine Bayesian and margin-based structured learning with sparse representations.

title: Laplace maximum margin Markov networks
